The preference spoken of here is a preference over the people of that age, the Children of Israel and their neighbours, and not over every man of every age.

Beyond that, the ranking of the messengers is set out in a way that keeps the matter in its place. Muhammad ﷺ stands at the head of all the children of Adam, those who came before him and those who came after. That is why Allah chose him to be the last of the prophets and messengers, carrying a law that remains in force until the last hour begins. With him came a following larger than the following of every prophet and messenger before him put together. After him, the next in rank of honour and virtue is Ibrahim, and after Ibrahim comes Musa son of Imran, the one who spoke with the Most Beneficent directly. So the man who spoke with his Lord is honoured above the rest of creation and still stands below the chief of the children of Adam in rank.

### The two speeches and what is left unsaid

The first time Allah spoke with Musa was when he was given prophethood, at the fire by the side of the Mount. The second time was here, at the occasion of the giving of the Torah. The wording of this verse indicates that the later speech had some additional characteristics over the first one, since the message and the speech are both named together in the statement of preference.

What the nature of that speech was, and how the hearing of it took place, cannot be settled by anyone but Allah. The explanations that the learned have given are suppositions of the mind, and only those of them can be entertained that do not go against any rule of the sacred law. None of them can be taken as certain unless it is carried by a valid argument. The safest practice in a matter like this is the one followed by the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, by their students, and by the elders who came after them. They left such questions to Allah, and they did not set out ungrounded suppositions in order to settle them.

### What the honoured position carries

The inner reading of the answer is put as a word spoken to Musa in his own situation. It is said to him that he had been held back from one thing, which is the sight. But he had been marked out for many virtues. He had been chosen for the carrying of the message, and honoured with standing and nearness. He was told to give thanks for all of it and to recognise the gifts as gifts, and he was told not to open the door of complaint about what had been withheld. What was sung of this meaning is that the ones who turn away are the ones who came in tenderness. They were loyal, so he should be patient with them if they should break away.

There is a lesson in the whole exchange for the one who is asked to believe in the unseen. The gift given to Musa was the speech and not the sight, and the sight belongs to the life to come. So the servant is asked to hold to what he has been given in this world, and to thank his Lord for it. He is to wait for the reward of looking until the place where looking is possible.

### In short

- Allah told Musa that He had preferred him over the people of his time by two things. They are the messages sent down to him and the speech given to him directly.
- The word for the messages is read in the plural as bi-risālātī or in the singular as bi-risālatī.
- The commands that follow are to hold firmly to what he was given and to be grateful. The thanks includes not asking for what is beyond his capacity to bear.
- The preference was over the people of his own age. Musa stands in rank after Muhammad ﷺ and Ibrahim among the children of Adam, honoured as the one who spoke with his Lord.
- The first speech came when he was given prophethood and the second when the Torah was given. The nature of that speech is left to Allah, following the practice of the companions and the elders. They left such questions alone.

145.text:
The writing of the law is placed in his hands, and with it the instruction to hold on and the promise of what would be shown. "We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything; commandments and explanations of all things. ˹We commanded,˺ “Hold to this firmly and ask your people to take the best of it. I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious""

### Phrase by phrase

**"We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything"** records the giving of the law in written form. What was written on the Tablets was instruction for all things and an explanation of all things. That is the lessons to be drawn, and the detailing of what was commanded and what was forbidden. One explanation says the Tablets carried advice for the people and the details of the rulings for the lawful and the unlawful. Another says that what was on them was the Torah itself. The Book describes that book elsewhere, as the Scripture given to Musa once the generations of old had been destroyed, a light for mankind (28:43). And a further view holds that the Tablets were given to him before the Torah came down and were not a part of it.

Of the Tablets themselves the reports say that the wood of them is given as the Lote-tree of Paradise, and the stone of them as chrysolite or emerald. The number of them is put at either seven or ten.

**"commandments and explanations of all things"** is the description of the content. It was a laying out of what was required and a spelling out of what it all meant. The people would have both the rule and the reason for it, the command and the guidance that goes with the command.

**"Hold to this firmly"** is the instruction to Musa himself. The sense is that he was to take hold of it seriously, earnestly and diligently, and to be firm in the obedience it laid down.

**"and ask your people to take the best of it"** hands the same thing on to the community. The command was that he should enjoin his people to take the better of what was in it, and to hold to the fairest of its precepts. One reading of that instruction is that they were to act upon what was clear and unambiguous. What was ambiguous they were to believe in without forcing a meaning upon it. Ibn 'Abbas, in a report carried from 'Ikrimah, said that Musa was commanded to hold to the toughest of what had been laid on his people. In that way the effort of the following would be real. And it was promised that the greatest reward would be for those who carried out what they were instructed in the most complete way. The carrying out was to be done with patience and with a forgiving spirit.

**"I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious"** is the promise that follows the command. What would be shown is the recompense of those who set aside the command of Allah and turn away from obedience to Him. The words name the destruction and the loss and the ruin they would meet. One reading takes the abode of the transgressors to be Hell itself. Another takes it as the abode of the wicked among the people of Pharaoh together with their followers, which is Egypt. The purpose of showing it would be that the Israelites take their example from it.

### The two views about that home

The sentence is a promise, and it says that the Israelites would soon take over the land of the sinners. What land is meant has been taken in two ways, and the disagreement rests on a question of history. Had the Israelites gone back to Egypt after the destruction of the king and his people, or had they not?

If they did go back at that time and rule the land, then this promise refers to Syria. Verse 137 indicates as much when it speaks of Allah making them inherit the land. The land of Egypt had already passed into their hands before the light appeared on the mount. If they did not go back to Egypt after the king was destroyed, then the reference may be to Egypt and to Syria together. And one report names Iraq, just as others name Egypt.

### What was written among the admonitions

Among the traditions about the Tablets, some carry the admonitions written for Musa as words of counsel. One of them says that if he wanted to be respected at the threshold of his Lord's exaltation and to be marked out for nearness to Him, then he should act beautifully toward orphans. He was not to abase the poor. It says that the Lord is the caresser and the well-wisher of orphans, and the kindly bestower of bounty on the poor. So the command was to caress those whom He caresses and not to drive away those whom He calls.

On the poor, Al-Mustafa, the chosen Prophet ﷺ, said that the poor who hold out in patience are the ones who will sit in the company of God on the Day of Resurrection. On the orphan he said that the Throne of the All-Merciful is set trembling by the crying of an orphan. God then says that whoever brings the orphan to contentment will himself be brought to contentment. Another of the admonitions says that if Musa wanted his Lord to speak of him with pride among the angels, then he should be without harm. He should keep stones and thorns away from the road of those who submit. Of that same meaning the Prophet ﷺ said that faith has more than seventy branches. The greatest of them is the declaration that there is no god but God, and the smallest of them is the taking of a harmful thing off the road. And another says that if he wanted his supplications to be answered, then he should deal with people beautifully, learn knowledge, and teach knowledge to others. The knowers have been honoured by being given knowledge, and there is more in store for them. Their dust is made sweet, their graves are lit and made wide, and on the day of rising they will be gathered among the companies of the prophets.

What the Prophet ﷺ said on this last point came with a report from Gabriel. Gabriel said to him that he should not count as lowly a servant whom God has given knowledge, since God did not count him as lowly when He gave it to him. The word from God on that day will be that He had placed His knowledge with the knowers only for a good that He desired for them. He forgives them for what has come out of them.

### Why the examples are shown to a people on the way

The promise that they would be shown the home of the rebellious was to be fulfilled during the journey itself. They would pass through the ruins of communities that had been destroyed before them. Those communities had been given guidance and had turned aside from it. They could not stay firm in the belief they had been given, and they could not withstand the pressure of the circumstances around them. They gave way to their own desires and ambitions, and so they earned the displeasure of God and were destroyed. The children of Israel were told to look at what was left of them and to take the lesson. The same end waited for them if they went the same way. God is not partial to any community in the balance of His justice, and there is no difference between one people and another.

There is a further point in how the guidance was given to Musa at all. A prophet is a man like other men. He is not a creature of another kind, and his only special quality is that he is able to keep intact the nature he was born with. Because of that he is chosen to carry the message of God and may be trusted to represent Him among the people. In that sense Musa was the best person of his community, and that is why he was chosen and given the message.

The messages themselves come down in the form of words. In this world of trial there is always the possibility that a person will put a wrong construction on the words, bending them to suit his own desires. But one who is serious and sincere in the matter of guidance, and who stands in awe of the censure of his Lord, will be able to draw from the words the same meaning that God intended by them. It is only the one who is genuinely looking for the true path who receives true guidance from the words of God.

### The honour and the warning together

The two verses before this one had placed Musa above the people of his time. This verse puts the law in his hands, and warns the same people about the home of the rebellious in the same breath. The honour was not a shield. Musa was the most honoured among the children of Adam after Muhammad ﷺ and Ibrahim, and his people were still told that they would be shown where the disobedient ended. No rank and no book in the hand exempts a community from the rule that God deals justly with all of them.

### In short

- The law was written for Musa on the Tablets, carrying instruction for all things and an explanation of all things. The Tablets are described in the reports as made of the wood of Paradise, or of chrysolite, or of emerald, and as seven or ten in number.
- One view holds that what was on the Tablets was the Torah itself, and another that they were given before the Torah. The Book describes the Scripture given to Musa after the earlier generations had been destroyed as an enlightenment for mankind.
- Musa was told to hold to it firmly and to enjoin his people to take the best of it. That best is read as acting on what is clear and believing in what is ambiguous, and the reward is promised for carrying it out in the best way.
- The home of the rebellious is read as Hell, or as the land of the people of Pharaoh, which is Egypt. The two views about whether the promise refers to Egypt or Syria, or both, rest on whether the Israelites returned to Egypt after the king was destroyed.
- The traditions of the Tablets carry admonitions about orphans and the poor and the removal of harm from the road. They join the knowledge of God to the kind treatment of people. The promise to show the ruined homes of the destroyed communities warns that no honour exempts a people from the justice of God.

146.text:
The law has been written on the Tablets, and the warning that goes with it is set out in full. "I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land." The next sentences explain the state such people are left in. "And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them." Then the two paths are put side by side. "If they see the Right Path, they will not take it. But if they see a crooked path, they will follow it." The reason is given at the end. "This is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them"

### Phrase by phrase

**"I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land."** is a statement of what is done to the proud, not only of what they do. The words say that the hearts of those who are too proud to obey Allah, and who behave as tyrants over people with no right on their side, will be kept from the understanding of the signs and the proofs that stand as witness to His might and His law and His commands. Because they lifted themselves up with no justification, they were brought low with ignorance. The Book says in another place that the hearts and the eyes of such people are turned away from guidance, as they refused to believe in it the first time (6:110). And it says that when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away from the right path (61:5). The turning away of the servant is answered with a turning away from his Lord, and the two things are of the same kind.

What the signs of Allah are has been taken in a wide sense. They may be the revealed verses of the Torah, of the Gospel and of the Qur'an, and they may also be the signs placed in the heavens and the earth and in the human being himself. Whichever sense is taken, the proud person is turned away from them all.

**"without any right"** is a phrase worth stopping over. It names the fault that turns a strong feeling into a sin, and it leaves open the case where the feeling is deserved. Arrogance in the face of the arrogant is a justified act, since what appears as arrogance there is not arrogance in reality but a putting of things in their place. The dictum is carried in one of the treatises of the path, Masail as-Suluk, that showing arrogance to the arrogant is itself an act of humbleness.

**"And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them."** describes a condition that has already gone past the reach of evidence. The Book says of such people in another place that those against whom the word of the Lord has been justified will not believe, even if every sign were to come to them, until they see the painful punishment (10:96-97). So the refusal to believe is not a shortage of proof. It is the settled state of the heart that the proof cannot move.

**"If they see the Right Path, they will not take it. But if they see a crooked path, they will follow it."** is where that state becomes visible in action. The right path is the way of guidance and of safety, and if it is laid out plainly in front of them they will not take it as their way. The crooked path is the way that ends in destruction and in misguidance, and they take it at once. One explanation names the right path as the way of Islam and of goodness, and the crooked path as the way of disbelief and of the worship of idols.

**"This is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them."** gives the reason plainly. They rejected the Book and the Messenger, and they were heedless of the signs, so the signs gave them no lesson. Denial in the heart and heedlessness in the conduct between them explain the whole picture that the verse has drawn.

### What one of the early teachers said

Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah read the opening of verse 146 in a way that shows what this turning away comes to. He said that the sense of it is that the understanding of the Book is snatched away from such people, and that they are turned from the signs. Ibn Jarir drew a conclusion from that statement, holding that this part of the verse is addressed to the community of the Prophet ﷺ. The conclusion does not have to be pressed that far, since what was meant is that the pattern runs in every ummah, and that no ummah is treated differently from another in this matter. And Allah knows best.

### What arrogance does to a person

There are two ways of living in this world, and the verse divides them.

The first way is to keep one's eyes and ears open. A person who lives that way sees things as they really are, and when the truth comes into view he takes it, since the signs of God lie open in every part of the universe and the lesson is there for whoever will read it. The second way is to live with a sense of being above others. Such a person lives as though the world belonged to him. He cares for nothing except his own interests, and he takes the good things that come to him as the fruit of his own ability and his own effort, so the needs of other people carry no weight with him. That attitude stands between him and the truth. The first man is open to what is around him, and because his mind is open he understands what the signs of God point to and sets himself straight without delay. The second man is closed, because pride and self-righteousness have shut him in. The truth stands right in front of him and he pays it no attention, since it has no importance in his own scale. The world of the Hereafter is not for the people of that second kind. As they ignored the message of God in the world of trial, so will they be left out in the world that never ends, while the first kind are given richly by God.

What lies at the root of it is desire. Treading the path of misguidance is the work of a man who follows the wishes of his own self. The path of guidance opens when a person rises above the pull of the self and the pull of his surroundings, and takes a road for the sake of God alone. The self-centred man who values nothing but the fulfilling of his own wants rushes along the road of transgression. Right guidance looks strange to his temperament, and so he cannot follow it. One who feels himself superior finds it easy to accept any proposal that leaves his superiority intact, and where he sees that he will not be given his due importance he turns away with no interest in the matter.

The explanation known as Ruh al-Bayan puts the same point in another figure. Arrogance is a habit so destructive that it raises a wall between a person and the knowledge that comes from Allah. Knowledge of divine things is given only out of the mercy of Allah, and the mercy of Allah visits the humble. Jalal al-Din Rumi put the same law into a saying, that water flows down towards the slope and the remedy appears where the difficulty is.

### Where the warning is placed

One reading takes the words "if they see" as pointing at the people of Pharaoh, and another takes them as pointing at Abu Jahl and his companions. On that second reading the promise that the abode of the evil-doers would be shown was fulfilled at Badr, and there is also a report that names Makkah as the abode meant. Read either way, the verse is telling the community of the Prophet ﷺ that the pattern it describes is not the property of any one nation.

### The two kinds of pride

Pride has been divided into two sorts, and the division settles what the verse is blaming.

The first is pride with the Real. It is the pride of the poor man toward the rich, of the one who is high in his aspiration and rich in his heart through his Lord. Such a person has turned his aspiration away from the throne and from everything beneath it, cut his heart off from creatures, and given himself to the love of his Lord. His aspiration is greater than this world and better than the world to come, and his longing is for the sight of his Patron. Al-Wasiti put it that when the pride is the pride that belongs with the Real, it is the poor man's bearing toward the wealthy and the sinful, and toward the unbelievers and the people of new-fangled ways. He recalled that the reports carry the instruction to meet the ungodly with a dark face.

The second is pride without the Real. It is the pride of the wealthy and of the rulers of the world toward the poor, and it is this second sort that the words name when they speak of those who lift themselves in the land with no right from Him.

Ibn Ata'i said of the verse that their hearts and their secret cores and their spirits would be held back from roaming in the dominion of holiness. Their own being would become the veil over them. They would be turned away from the road of their Lord, so that their secret cores could not travel in the world of holiness and the dominion. They would be kept from seeing the wonders of that dominion, and left to find their company in their own souls and in the creatures of this world. They would not taste the flavour of finding, and would stay unaware of the gifts given to the people who are chosen. No day of good fortune would come to them, and the rose of union would not open for them. And the poor wretch who has never caught the scent of these words at all, how could he have anything of the ocean when he has no stream running into him?

### In short

- The proud are turned away from the signs of Allah, and the turning of their hearts is the answer to their own turning away, as the Book says in the sixth surah and the sixty-first.
- The phrase "without any right" leaves room for the case where standing up to the arrogant is itself humbleness, as the treatise Masail as-Suluk records.
- The verse describes a state that has gone past proof, and it names its cause, that they denied the signs and were heedless of them.
- Two ways of living are set against each other, the open way that reads the signs and the closed way that lives on its own sense of superiority, and the root of the second is the following of the self.
- Pride is of two kinds, the pride of the poor man toward the rich which is pride with his Lord, and the pride of the wealthy and the rulers toward the poor, which is the pride the verse condemns.

147.text:
The warning closes on the fruit of denial. "The deeds of those who deny Our signs and the meeting ˹with Allah˺ in the Hereafter will be in vain." Then the question is put. "Will they be rewarded except for what they have done?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The deeds of those who deny Our signs and the meeting ˹with Allah˺ in the Hereafter will be in vain."** states what comes of work done without faith. Those who reject the signs that prove the truth of the messengers, and who deny that they will meet Allah on the Day of Judgement, find that their good deeds come to nothing. The reason is that those deeds were never built on faith, and so there is no foundation under them to hold them up. What is recorded against them instead is their denial of Allah and their joining of partners with Him, and the repayment for that is a life that goes on in the fire.

The words say more than that good deeds are lost. One explanation holds that the works in question are the acts a person would count as his best, the keeping of the ties of kinship and the giving of voluntary alms, and that all of it fails and brings no reward, since such acts are not binding in this case. The reward of a deed follows the faith of the one who does it, and when the faith is gone the deed has nothing to stand on.

**"Will they be rewarded except for what they have done?”"** is put as a question, and the answer is folded into it. The recompense of a people is drawn from the deeds they have sent ahead, good repaid with good and evil repaid with evil. It is said of this that a person reaps only the harvest of what he has brought forth, so that the question leaves no room for complaint on the day when the account is settled.

### Where these words are placed

The verses around this one are speaking of the people of the calf, and the sentence is set here to name the end of what they did. The Israelites had been left with Harun while Musa was away at the meeting with his Lord, and the sin that came out of that interval was the worship of the calf. The verse tells them that the deed done in those days was not a small lapse that would be forgotten. Deeds that are done while denying the signs and the meeting with Allah do not survive, and the people who did them would be repaid for exactly what they had done.

There is a lesson in the arrangement of the passage for every community that comes after. The warning about the proud in the verse before this one, and the account of the calf that follows, are placed side by side with a statement that no community carries a privilege that exempts it from this rule. What a people sends ahead is what a people meets.

### In short

- The deeds of those who deny the signs and the meeting with Allah in the Hereafter come to nothing, since they were never built on faith.
- One explanation names the deeds as the acts a person takes most pride in, the ties of kinship and the voluntary alms, and says that none of it brings reward in that case.
- The closing question establishes that the recompense of a people is drawn from what they have done, with no injustice in it.
- The words are placed among the verses of the calf, so that the sin of that interval is answered by the statement that such deeds do not survive.

148.text:
The story turns back to the people left behind on the plain. "In the absence of Moses, his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound." Two questions follow it. "Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path?" And then the verdict. "Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers"

### Phrase by phrase

**"In the absence of Moses, his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound."** brings in the man behind it. Among the Israelites there was a person named As-Samiri, a man of standing among them, and one who held to superstitions. He told the people that the jewels and the ornaments of the Egyptians which they had with them were not lawful for them, and the plunder taken from an enemy after a defeat was not lawful for the Israelites either. So they gathered all their jewellery and handed it over to him. He melted the ornaments down and forged from them the shape of a calf.

What he did next is reported in more than one way. He had collected some dust from under the hooves of the horse of the angel Gabriel, and Allah had placed in that dust the effect of life. He threw it into the molten metal as the calf was made, and the figure gave out a sound like the lowing of a cow. The ornaments themselves had been borrowed from the people of Pharaoh on the pretext of a wedding celebration, and it was from those borrowed things that the calf was made.

The reports differ on what the calf actually was. One view holds that it became a living body of flesh and blood, which is how it lowed. What the Book says of the same days in another place is that Allah told Musa that his people had been put to trial after he left them, and that As-Samiri had led them astray (20:85). Verse 148 gives a short account of that event, while the fuller account is carried elsewhere. Another holds that it stayed a figure of gold, and that the air entering it as it passed through made the sound that seemed to come from its mouth. Knowledge of the exact matter rests with Allah.

**"Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path?"** is the question put to the makers of it. The calf could not answer them with a single word. It could not return a reply to anyone who spoke to it, and it had no power to bring them harm or to bring them benefit. It could not lead them to any good way, whether in the affairs of this world or in the affairs of the spirit. The Book says of the same calf in another place that it could not give them back a word in reply, and that no power lay in its hands either for their hurt or for their benefit (20:89).

**"Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers"** is what happened after all of that. They took it for worship, and by that act they wronged themselves. Their own sense of reason was blinded by ignorance and misguidance, and they turned to a statue in the shape of a calf while leaving the Creator of the heavens and the earth out of the account.

### How the people were drawn in

What brought the whole people in was not argument but spectacle, and the account explains the way it worked.

When the statue lowed, the people began to dance around it, and they fell into misguidance because they had come to adore it. They said that this was their god and the god of Musa, and that Musa had forgotten. As-Samiri had been a man of respect among them before that day, and the strange thing he had made raised their trust in him still higher, so they began to gather around him. He told them that Musa had gone up the mountain to speak with God, and that God had now come to them in the shape of the calf itself. He invited them to worship it, and they took it as their god.

By that time, the account says, the people were gathered around him in great numbers, and only Harun and a few of his companions were standing apart. Nobody dared to raise an objection openly. In the face of that mass following, even the protests of Harun were not strong enough to turn them, and no other person in the community had the courage to speak up. This has been the way of crowds from ancient times to the present day. A clever man, by the sheer flow of his words, can draw a great crowd after him even on a matter that carries no weight at all. The public, drawn to the small and the striking and the things that have nothing to do with the facts, has not the ability to think the matter through and separate what is true from what is not. And if anyone does stand up to show the truth, he is simply passed by, in the way that Harun was passed by.

There was also the art of it. The sculpting of the ancient Egyptians was of the kind that allows air to pass through a figure and come out as sound, and it was by that means that the sound came out of the calf's mouth. A people can be brought to worship a thing because a noise comes out of it, and the verse asks them afterwards whether that thing could speak to them or guide them anywhere.

### The calf in every age

The story was read by the people of the path for the meaning it carries into every life. Sahl ibn 'Abdullah said of it that whatever in this world turns a servant from the Real, and keeps him from obedience to Him, is his calf, and he is the one who worships it. The idol changes shape with the age, and the worship stays where it was.

The account adds where deliverance is found. The worshippers of the calf among the Children of Israel were freed when they were commanded to kill themselves, and the Book records that command in the words "So kill your own souls!" (2:54). In the same way, the servant finds deliverance on the road of truth when he is made clean of his own portions and of the secondary causes, or rather when he disowns everything other than his Lord.

The verse also carries a contrast in it. The calf could not speak, and this is set against the One whose description is that of a speaker who addresses the creatures. The kings of the earth count it beneath them to address their servants with their own tongue, because of their high rank, and their way of dealing with the lowly is to keep silent. The Lord of the worlds acted in the opposite way with His faithful servants. To the enemies in the fire He will say, "Slink into it, and do not talk to Me" (23:108). To the faithful the Prophet ﷺ gave the glad news that there is not one of them who will not be spoken to by his Lord with no interpreter between them.

### In short

- As-Samiri gathered the jewellery of the people, which he had told them was not lawful for them, and forged from it the shape of a calf that gave out a lowing sound.
- The dust from under the hooves of the horse of the angel Gabriel was placed in the metal, and the reports differ on whether the calf became a living body or stayed gold with air passing through it.
- The people were drawn in by spectacle and by the standing of the man, and only Harun and a few companions stood apart, with nobody daring to object openly.
- The verse asks whether the calf could speak to them or guide them to the right path, and records that they took it as a god and wronged themselves.
- Sahl ibn 'Abdullah said that whatever turns a servant away from his Lord and holds him back from obedience is his calf, and he is its worshipper.

149.text:
The story closes on what the people did once the truth came home to them. "Later, when they were filled with remorse and realized they had gone astray, they cried," The plea that follows is all they had left. "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Later, when they were filled with remorse and realized they had gone astray, they cried,"** records a change of state. They regretted what they had done. In the words of verse 149 they came to know for certain that they had wandered from the truth and from guidance by taking the calf as a god besides Allah. Their regret came when they saw the consequences of the deed and understood that they did not know how to make up for the wrong they had done.

**"If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers.”"** is the plea itself, and it carries an admission. They ask for mercy, which would enable them to do what they were instructed to do, and they ask forgiveness for having worshipped the calf. Then they name the outcome of being left without either. If mercy and forgiveness are not given, they are of the losers both in this life and in the world to come.

It is worth noting what the sentence is not. It is not a bargain, and it is not an argument. The people who had just made a god out of their own ornaments have nothing to offer and nothing to plead. All they can do is put the whole matter into the hands of their Lord and name their own condition truthfully. Repentance in the Book at this point is made of exactly these two parts, the recognition of the sin and the seeking of salvation from Allah.

**Where the words sit in the story.** The remorse came after Musa returned from the meeting with his Lord, since the account of the calf belongs to the time of his absence. So the people who had been left with a prophet among them to guide them came back to their senses and, finding nothing in their hands, turned to the door they should have used from the beginning.

### In short

- The people came to regret the worship of the calf and knew that they had gone astray from the truth and the guidance.
- Their plea asked for mercy that would let them do what they had been commanded and for forgiveness for the worship of the calf.
- They named the outcome of being left without mercy, that they would be of the losers in this life and in the world to come.
- The words carry the two parts of repentance, the admission of the sin and the asking of salvation from Allah, and they came after Musa had returned from the meeting with his Lord.

150.text:
Musa comes down from the mountain and finds his people around the calf. "Upon Moses’ return to his people, ˹totally˺ furious and sorrowful, he said," and the first words are for the people. "What an evil thing you committed in my absence! Did you want to hasten your Lord’s torment?”" Then he turns. "Then he threw down the Tablets and grabbed his brother by the hair, dragging him closer." The answer of Harun follows. "Aaron pleaded, “O son of my mother! The people overpowered me and were about to kill me." And he asks for two things. "So do not ˹humiliate me and˺ make my enemies rejoice, nor count me among the wrongdoing people.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Upon Moses’ return to his people, ˹totally˺ furious and sorrowful, he said,"** describes the state he came back in. Verse 150 opens with what happened once the meeting on the mount was over. He was angry, and he was filled with regret. One of the companions, Abu Ad-Darda, said of this that the grief which comes with anger is the severest kind of anger there is.

**"What an evil thing you committed in my absence!"** is said to the people first. What they had done after he went up the mount was to worship the calf, and the words name it as an evil thing in the plainest terms. He told them that the condition they had fallen into led only to ruin and misery.

**"Did you want to hasten your Lord’s torment?”"** is the second part of the question. One sense of it is that they wanted him to come back to them sooner than the appointment Allah had set, and another is that they were in a hurry for the judgement of their Lord and brought it on themselves by worshipping the calf. Some of those who explained the Book said the words mean that they had quickly decided that Musa was dead, and that the decision was made before the book of Allah had come to them.

**"Then he threw down the Tablets and grabbed his brother by the hair, dragging him closer."** is what he did next. He had left Harun among them as his deputy, and seeing the people as they were, he turned on his brother. In the report of the words it is said that he took hold of him by the head, seizing the hair itself with his right hand, and taking the beard with his left, and then drew him toward himself in his anger.

### The Tablets and the question of respect

What Musa did with the Tablets has been taken up carefully. The word used in the verse is one that carries the sense of putting a thing down or letting it fall, and it has raised the question whether a prophet showed disrespect to the book of the Torah by his action. The answer given is that every prophet is free of sin, so the act must be understood in its setting. He was putting the Tablets aside quickly in order to free his hands to take hold of his brother, and the effect of haste made it look as though they had been thrown down. The Book uses that word as a gesture of warning, and not as a record of disrespect. In one report it is added that two of the Tablets were broken in the process.

### Why Harun was taken to task

Musa took hold of his brother because he feared that Harun had not tried hard enough to forbid the people from the evil they had fallen into. That fear was answered in the words that came back to him.

**"Aaron pleaded, “O son of my mother!"** is where Harun begins. He called on the mother rather than on the father, although the two of them were full brothers, so that mercy and gentleness would come into the heart of Musa. The form of address was chosen for its effect on his brother's feelings, and it did its work.

**"The people overpowered me and were about to kill me."** is his account of what he had been through. He had stood against them and had forbidden the calf, and the people had counted him weak and had not respected him. They were so set on what they were doing that they came close to killing him. In another place in the Book the fuller exchange is recorded, where Musa asked him what had kept him from following after the people when he saw them going astray, and Harun answered that he should not take him by his beard or by his head, since he had feared that Musa would say that he had caused a division among the Children of Israel and had not respected his word (20:92-94).

**"So do not ˹humiliate me and˺ make my enemies rejoice, nor count me among the wrongdoing people.”"** is the plea he ends with. He asked his brother not to punish him in a way that the enemy, that is the people of the calf, would gloat over. He asked not to be placed on the same level as the wrongdoers, which would be a reproach laid on him by his brother. What he had said to the people beforehand was already on record, that they were being tried in this matter and that their Lord was the Most Gracious, so they should follow him and obey his order (20:90). When Musa had been satisfied that his brother was innocent, he turned to his Lord.

### Information is not the same as observation

The passage carries a lesson about the difference between hearing of a thing and seeing it. Allah had told Musa on the mountain that his people had been put to trial after he left them, and As-Samiri had led them astray. The news of it did not move him to throw the Tablets. It was when he came down and saw the calf and the people around it with his own eyes that he threw them down. So the verse demonstrates the meaning of a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, that information is not the same as observation.

Ibn 'Abbas reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of this, asking that Allah grant His mercy to Musa, and noting that one who observes a thing is nothing like one who is told about it. His Lord had told him that his people had been tried after him, and he did not throw the Tablets, and when he saw it with his eyes he threw them.

### The two brothers and the way of the believer

What happened between the two of them is also read as a lesson for every community. Musa held Harun responsible for what had happened, under the impression that his brother had failed in the duty of a reformer. He took hold of him in anger, and Harun answered by setting out the facts of the matter, saying that he had done everything in his power to show the people the right path. Then Musa checked himself and began to pray for his brother. Misunderstandings arise between believers, and once the matter is clarified they return to where they were, as though nothing had come between them.

There is an allusion in the passage that was drawn out by the people of the path. In this verse the servant of God is shown asking forgiveness in every state, and it is worth noticing that the Children of Israel were the ones who sinned, while Musa and his brother were the ones who asked forgiveness. From this it is taken that all of creation belongs to its Lord, and that the owner's disposal runs through everything that He owns. This is the path of the chevaliers and the road of those who travel the inner way, that they lay the sin upon themselves and ask pardon for wrongs they did not commit.

### In short

- Musa came back to his people angry and grieved, and Abu Ad-Darda said that the grief which comes with anger is the most severe form of anger.
- He charged the people with the evil they had done in his absence and asked whether they had wanted to hurry the judgement of their Lord, and one explanation is that they had quickly decided he was dead.
- He put the Tablets aside in haste to free his hands, and the word used in verse 150 is read as a gesture of warning rather than as disrespect, with two of the Tablets broken in the report.
- He seized Harun because he feared his brother had not forbidden the evil, and Harun answered that the people had counted him weak and had come close to killing him, and asked not to be humiliated in front of the enemy.
- The scene is read as proof that information is not the same as observation, and as a lesson in the way believers clear a misunderstanding and return to where they were.

151.text:
The anger is put down and the two brothers ask together. "Moses prayed," and the supplication is short and complete. "My Lord! Forgive me and my brother! And admit us into Your mercy. You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses prayed,"** marks the turn. He had held his brother responsible, heard the account of what Harun had been through, and then turned from the dispute to his Lord. What the words say is that the one who had been sent to lead the people put the matter back into the hands that it belonged to.

**"My Lord! Forgive me and my brother!"** brings the two of them into one request. He asks forgiveness for his brother for whatever shortcoming there may have been in the duties laid on him. Harun had been left among the people to keep them on the way of the Torah while his brother was away, and it was against that charge that Musa measured him. Then he asks forgiveness for himself. The reasons given for his own part differ and they sit together. One is that he put the Tablets aside in haste, which the Book described in the way it did in order to give a warning. Another is that the request was meant to teach people to include themselves whenever they ask forgiveness for someone else, so that they do not fall into a sense of being above the fault.

The mention of the brother inside the same supplication carries a purpose of its own. By bringing Harun into his prayer in that public setting, he reconciled his brother to himself and shut the door on any gloating over what Harun had suffered. The two of them had been through an argument in front of the people, and the prayer ended it in the sight of everyone.

**"And admit us into Your mercy."** asks for more than forgiveness. In one reading it is a request to be brought into the Garden of their Lord, and it takes in the two of them together as the forgiveness did. The mercy here is wide enough to cover the man who had been carried away by anger and the man who had been carried away by nothing at all and had still been blamed for it.

**"You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”"** is the close of the supplication, and it names the ground on which the request is made. It is the attribute of Allah that the two of them are relying on, and the words leave the outcome entirely with Him.

### What the supplication teaches

The state of the two brothers at this point is worth noticing. One of them had come down the mountain to find the people in the middle of a great sin, and the other had stood in front of those people and had nearly been killed for it. Neither of them had done the evil, and both of them asked for pardon. The lesson drawn from that is that a person should ask forgiveness in every condition he may be in, and not only when he is aware of a fault. It is the way of those who take the inner road, that they put the fault upon themselves and ask pardon for things they did not commit, and the account of this verse is given as the pattern for it.

The supplication also shows how a disagreement between two believers closes. It closes with the two of them standing in the same request, asking for the same mercy, and naming the same Lord over them both.

### In short

- Musa turned from the dispute with his brother to his Lord, and asked forgiveness for himself and for Harun together.
- The forgiveness he sought for himself is read either as covering the hasty setting down of the Tablets or as a lesson teaching people to include themselves when they ask pardon for others.
- Bringing his brother into the supplication reconciled the two of them in front of the people and ended any gloating over what Harun had been through.
- The request for mercy asks to be admitted into it together, and the close names the attribute of Allah on which the whole prayer rests.
- The prayer marks the way believers leave a misunderstanding behind, and the way a servant asks forgiveness in every state he is in.

152.text:
The sentence on the calf and its makers comes down hard. "Those who worshipped the calf will certainly be afflicted with Allah’s wrath as well as disgrace in the life of this world." Then the wider rule is stated. "This is how We reward those who invent falsehood"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who worshipped the calf will certainly be afflicted with Allah’s wrath"** names the punishment that followed the sin. The wrath that came on the Children of Israel for the worship of the calf was not lifted at once. It stayed until some of them put others of them to death, and the ones who did the killing were those who had kept away from the calf. That story is told in full in Al-Baqarah. They were told to turn in repentance to the One who had made them. They were told also to put the guilty among them to death, since that would be better for them with their Maker. Their turning was accepted after that (2:54).

**"as well as disgrace in the life of this world"** adds to the wrath something that was carried in this world. The words speak of the humiliation and the shame that fell on the people in their own lifetime. One reading takes it as the abasement that was stamped upon them until the Day of Resurrection. Another names the capitation tax by which the humiliation was imposed on them.

**"This is how We reward those who invent falsehood"** turns the matter from one nation to a rule. The sentence is taken to cover everyone who invents a new thing in the religion. A person who does that has added to the law of Allah what Allah did not send. The disgrace that follows such an invention is described as being placed in the heart of the man first, and from the heart it moves to his shoulders. Al-Hasan Al-Basri said of this that the shame of an invented practice sits on a man's shoulders. It stays there whether he rides out on a mule or gallops along on a horse kept for work.

Ayyub As-Sakhtiyani carried from Abu Qilabah Al-Jarmi the statement that, by Allah, this verse covers every person who invents a lie. It will go on doing so until the Day of Resurrection. Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah said that every person who invents an innovation in the religion will taste disgrace.

### Where the punishment was seen in this life

A part of the punishment of certain sins is given in this very life, and the case of As-Samiri is given as the example of it. Musa commanded him to live apart from the people, so that he would not touch anyone and no one would touch him. For the rest of his life he lived a deserted life, walking about among the animals, and no human being came near him. Al-Qurtubi carried from the companion Qatadah a report about the punishment of the man. If he touched anyone, or anyone touched him, fever came on both of them. The author of Ruh al-Bayan observed that the marks of that illness are still found in his descendants.

The rule drawn from the verse was applied by the scholars in the widest way. Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah said that those who invent new things in the shariah have committed the sin of fabrication and deserve that punishment. Imam Malik took from this verse that whoever invents new practices in the shariah deserves the wrath of Allah in the world to come and disgrace in this one.

### Why the act is called a fabrication

The act of the calf is named as a fabrication because of the way it was done, and not only because of what it was. The people had done a wrongful thing in the name of the truth. Their case was not a plain rejection of the truth, but the use of the truth in order to gain benefit. They used to justify such acts in religious language. Like the idol worshippers they said that God had taken form in the idol they had made with their own hands. On their own account, worshipping it was the same as worshipping God.

There is more of the same in the account of As-Samiri. He made up a dream, saying that he had seen the angel Gabriel in it. In the dream he had taken up a handful of earth from the footprint of the horse and placed it in the statue, and that, he said, was what caused the sound to come out of its mouth. So the maker and the people with him invented falsehoods and attributed them to God, and that is what fabricating against God means.

### The shame that is at the heart of repentance

How the punishment fell on the people themselves is also recorded. Musa told the leaders of each tribe to search out the ones who had been responsible for the act. The guilty were found and put to death by their own tribesmen. Only those who were greatly ashamed of what they had done, admitted their guilt and repented sincerely were not punished. So the Israelites were punished for their wrongdoing by their own people. Punishment of that kind is sometimes given through other people or other communities, above all where the shame of it can be made plain to them.

Being truly ashamed of sin is the essence of repentance, and that shame is what makes the verse stand. The strong feeling of shame is the guarantee that the one who repents resolves in the deepest part of his heart never to go back to the act. When a person who has sinned shows that shame and proves his determination not to repeat the sin, it is as if he has taken up the faith afresh. After a time of slipping back, he returns into the fold of the religion of God, and the door stays open while the shame is real.

### In short

- The worshippers of the calf were struck with the wrath of Allah and with disgrace. Their repentance was not accepted until some of their own people put the guilty to death, as the account in Al-Baqarah records.
- The wrath is followed by humiliation in this life, and the words are read as the abasement carried by the people, or as the capitation tax imposed on them.
- The rule at the end covers everyone who invents a lie about the religion. Al-Hasan Al-Basri said the shame of it would weigh on the shoulders of such a person however he travelled.
- Ayyub As-Sakhtiyani carried from Abu Qilabah Al-Jarmi that the verse holds for every inventor of a lie until the Day of Resurrection. Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah said every inventor of an innovation will taste disgrace.
- As-Samiri was punished in this life by separation from people and by fever on contact. Al-Qurtubi reported it from Qatadah, while the author of Ruh al-Bayan said the marks of the illness remained in his line.
- The calf is called a fabrication because the people dressed their act in the name of the truth, and the shame which they felt afterwards is the essence of their repentance.

153.text:
The door is held open in the same breath. "But those who commit evil, then repent and become ˹true˺ believers, your Lord will certainly be All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful"

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those who commit evil, then repent and become ˹true˺ believers"** describes the change the verse is speaking of, and verse 153 names it in two parts. The first part is tawbah, the turning back. The second is the entry into belief. The people meant are the ones who turned back from their sin after their prophet had warned them. They met the hard condition that had been laid on them for forgiveness. It is also taken to cover everyone who does wrong. One reading names the wrong as the joining of partners with Allah, and the repentance as the turning away from that to the oneness of Allah and the belief in Him alone. Repentance in that reading carries a second turn with it, away from disobedience and towards good deeds, with the giving up of sin and the seeking of forgiveness from the Lord.

The words say that turning back is enough, whatever the sin has been. Allah tells His servants that He accepts the repentance of the one who turns to Him. That holds for any sin at all, whether it is shirk or kufr or hypocrisy or plain disobedience. That includes the worship of the calf, which the verse before this one had punished, and it includes the sins that come after it.

**"your Lord will certainly be All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful"** is the promise that closes the verse. The two names are placed after the description of the sin on purpose. So no one reads the promise as though the sin were small, and no one reads the sin as though the door were shut. The Prophet ﷺ is called in this connection the Messenger of Repentance and the Prophet of Mercy, since that invitation stands at the front of his message.

### What the two verses do together

The two verses put a punishment and a promise side by side, and the pairing is what the passage is teaching. The first says that the people who made a god out of their ornaments were struck with wrath and with shame. Their repentance passed through a hard command before it was accepted. The second says that those who sin and afterwards turn back and believe find their Lord forgiving and merciful. The seriousness of the deed is not softened, and the mercy that follows a real turning is not withdrawn.

**What the words say** about the order of the two things is worth keeping in view. The turning comes before the promise, and the belief comes with the turning. Nothing in the sentence lets a man hold on to the sin and take the mercy as a cover for it. What is named is the one who did the evil and then left it, and the Book measures the sincerity of that leaving by the shame and the resolve it produces.

### The report of Ibn Mas'ud

Abdullah bin Mas'ud was asked about a man who commits fornication with a woman and afterwards marries her. He recited this verse in answer, and he recited it ten times, neither permitting the marriage in that case nor forbidding it. The report shows how the companions handled a question when they did not wish to give a ruling on it. It also shows the place this verse held in their minds as the answer to the question of a sin followed by a change of life.

### After the killing, a people forgiven

What happened among the Israelites after the command is given in the account of the verse that comes before this one. The people met the condition that had been laid on them, and Musa called them together and told them that Allah had accepted their repentance. Those of them who were killed in the affair were given the rank of martyrs, and those who survived were forgiven. The matter ends there, and it teaches what the Book says plainly in this verse. A person who becomes caught up in a sinful act and then turns to Allah and puts his belief right is forgiven by the mercy of his Lord. The weight of the deed does not shut the door on him. It is therefore wise to turn to Allah at once after every sinful act, and not to let the delay build a wall where the verse has left a door.

### In short

- The verse promises forgiveness and mercy to those who committed evil, then repented and believed, and it follows the punishment of the calf in the verse before it.
- Repentance here is read as turning from joining partners with Allah to His oneness, and from disobedience to good deeds, with the sin given up and forgiveness sought.
- The two names of forgiveness and mercy are placed after the description of the sin, so that neither the sin is treated as small nor the door as shut.
- Abdullah bin Mas'ud recited this verse ten times when asked about a man who fornicated with a woman and then married her, neither permitting nor forbidding the marriage.
- The Israelites who met the hard condition had their repentance accepted. Those killed were counted as martyrs, and those who lived were forgiven. The verse holds out the same door for every sin afterwards.

154.text:
The anger passes and the Tablets are taken up again. "When Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the Tablets whose text contained guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When Moses’ anger subsided"** marks the end of the state he had come down the mountain in. He had thrown the Tablets down out of zeal for Allah and out of anger for His sake, and the cause of it was the worship of the calf by his people. Verse 154 opens with the anger going quiet, and one reading has the calm coming over him with his people.

**"he took up the Tablets"** is what he did once he was himself again. What he had cast down he now lifted up. Some of those who explained the Book said that when the Tablets were thrown on the ground they were shattered, and that Musa gathered up the pieces afterwards. The reports add that two of them had broken, and one account says that Allah then gave him the Torah written on other material. The word rendered here as the text of them carries the sense of a copy, that is a writing taken from a book or from other writings.

**"whose text contained guidance and mercy"** describes what was in them. Guidance from error and mercy that holds back torment are the two things named. Musa found in what was written there a guide for the people and a mercy laid over them, and the loss of the physical Tablets did not take either of those things away. One view holds that what remained after the breaking was enough, and another that the guidance and the mercy were in what was given back to him.

**"for those who stand in awe of their Lord"** names the people the Book works for. What is written there is guidance and mercy, and it reaches the one who holds his Lord in awe and stands in fear of Him. The Book of God is the best guide in this life and a certain cause of grace in the life to come, but it benefits only the person who fears God and keeps before his mind the account he will one day give. Such people are the real seekers after the truth, and when the truth is set in front of them they take it, without the twistings that come of wanting a different answer.

### What the two sentences say about the reader

There is a description of the man who is changed by the Book in the verse, and it is worth drawing out. His fear of God does not sit still in him. It wakes up his awareness, it clears the barriers from his eyes, and it keeps him ready to recognise the signs of God whenever they appear before him. God becomes the centre of his hopes and his fears together, and his life and his possessions are given over to his Lord. He does not settle into ease and think himself safe with what he holds. He lives in fear, and not in comfort with himself.

### Where the passage has come from

The book in his hands is the same one that had been laid down in anger a few verses earlier, and that is the point of the sentence being placed here. The law of the people is in the hands of a messenger who has just been angry, and the verses before this one have recorded the sin of the people, the taking of the brother to task, and the supplication of the two of them for forgiveness. After all of that, the Tablets are taken up again, and what is in them is described as guidance and mercy for the people who fear their Lord. The warning and the mercy stand in the same writing, and the passage closes its account of the calf with both.

### In short

- When the anger of Musa went quiet he took up the Tablets he had thrown down in zeal for Allah and in anger for His sake over the worship of the calf.
- The reports say the Tablets were shattered when they were thrown, that he gathered up the pieces afterwards, and that the Torah was then given to him written on other material, with knowledge of the details resting with Allah.
- What their text carried was guidance from error and mercy that holds back torment, and one reading places both in what was given back to him.
- The guidance and the mercy reach those who stand in awe of their Lord, and the verse describes how such a person is woken by his fear of God rather than settled into ease.

155.text:
Seventy men are chosen, and the earth shakes under them. "Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment and, when they were seized by an earthquake, he cried," Then the plea begins. "My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well." The argument of the plea follows. "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?" Then the confession of the whole matter. "This is only a test from You—by which You allow whoever you will to stray and guide whoever You will." And it closes with the asking. "You are our Guardian. So forgive us and have mercy on us. You are the best forgiver"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment"** records the choosing and the reason for it. Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said that Allah commanded Musa to choose seventy men. He chose them and went on with them so that they would supplicate to their Lord. The supplication they made asked Allah to give them what He had never given to anyone before them or after them. Allah disliked that supplication, and the violent earthquake came on them. As-Suddi said that the command given to Musa was to bring thirty men out of the Children of Israel with him, to offer apology for the worship of the calf. A time and a place were appointed for them, while the verse itself speaks of seventy.

Muhammad bin Ishaq gave the account in more detail. Musa chose seventy of the best of the Children of Israel and said to them that they should go to the meeting with Allah, repent for what they had done. They were also to beg forgiveness for their people whom they had left behind. He told them to fast, to purify themselves and to clean their clothes. Then he went with them to Mount Tur in Sinai, to the place and the time that had been appointed by his Lord. He went only with the leave and the knowledge of Allah. According to what was told to him, when the seventy had done what he ordered, they said that they wished to hear the words of their Lord themselves. He told them that he would ask for it.

What happened at the mountain is given in that account. When Musa came near the mountain it was covered over completely with columns of cloud, and he went in among them, and he said to the people to come forward. When Allah spoke to Musa, a brilliant light came round his cloak which no human being could bear to look at, so a barrier was placed below him, and the people came forward. They entered the cloud and fell down prostrate, and the words of their Lord reached them as He spoke with Musa. He laid commands and prohibitions on him and set out what was to be done and what was to be left. When He had finished the command and the cloud was lifted from Musa, he turned to face the people. They said to him that they would not believe in him unless they saw Allah directly.

**"and, when they were seized by an earthquake, he cried,"** is what came of that demand. The Book records the demand itself in the words that they would never believe in him, O Musa, until they saw Allah plainly, and they asked that He be shown to them (2:55). In the other place it is recorded that a bolt of lightning struck them (4:153) and they died. One account of the events says that the demand came out of ignorance and obstinacy. They were caught by the earthquake from beneath and by the thunderclap from above, and they fell to the ground at once as senseless as the dead. Whether they looked like dead men or were in fact dead is left in the reports, and what is certain is that they were taken away in front of Musa.

**"My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well."** is the first sentence of the plea, and it carries an argument in it. One reading of the words is that if He had willed He could have destroyed them before this day, and Musa with them. One report explains the sense as being that they could have been drowned with Pharaoh, or killed at the time of the calf, and that none of that happened. One detail in the explanation is that Musa counted himself with them in the words, remembering the day he killed the Egyptian.

The grief that drove the plea is described. Musa was deeply grieved by what had happened. The men who had died were the leading figures of the Children of Israel, and on top of that he did not know how he would face his people when he came back without them. They would lay the death of all those men at his door, and there was a real danger that they would turn on him.

**"Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?"** is the request that the punishment should not fall on all for the act of some. The question is not put as a demand, and it carries its own submission inside it. What it asks for is compassion, and what it refuses to accept is that the many should be wiped out for the deed of the few.

**"This is only a test from You—by which You allow whoever you will to stray and guide whoever You will."** names the whole event as a trial. The word used in the verse is fitnah, and it carries the sense of an affliction and a testing. That reading is given by Ibn 'Abbas, and by Sa'id bin Jubayr, by Abu Al-'Aliyah, by Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, and by a number of the early generations. What Musa was saying is that the decision belongs to Allah and the judgement belongs to Him, and that whatever He wills comes to pass. He leads astray whom He wills and He guides whom He wills, and no one can guide the one He has led astray, or lead astray the one He has guided. No one can give what He withholds or hold back what He gives, and the sovereignty and the judgement and the creation are all His.

**"You are our Guardian. So forgive us and have mercy on us. You are the best forgiver"** closes the supplication. Forgiveness here is the covering of the mistake and the not punishing for the sin. Where mercy is named along with forgiveness, as it is in this supplication of Musa, it carries a further hope, that the one forgiven will not be allowed to fall into the same act again. The last words state the ground of the request, that there is none besides Him who can forgive the sin.

### Why the seventy were taken

Why the punishment fell on that particular group has been answered in more than one way, and the answers are not far apart.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and Ibn Jarir At-Tabari said that they were seized by the tremor, or by the lightning. Their fault was that they had neither shunned the worship of the calf nor forbidden their people from it. Ibn 'Abbas added that the earthquake came on them because they did not break away from their people on the day the people took to the worship of the calf. He added a further detail, that these were not the same men who had asked to see God and were struck by the thunderbolt. So two events are being kept apart in his report, the demand of the seventy at this meeting, and the demand of another group among the Children of Israel at another time.

The wider lesson stands out of both. The making of the calf had shown that the people did not have in their hearts the conviction they should have had about God. The answer to that weakness was to call them to the mount, where thunder and lightning and the shaking of the earth brought them back with everything they had. They cried out and wailed before God, and they repented as one body, and they made a solemn undertaking to carry out the commandments of the Torah.

### The two accounts of what struck them

The two places in the Book use two different words for what came on the men. The word in this verse points to the earthquake, and the word in Al-Baqarah points to the thunderbolt. The two accounts have been reconciled by taking it that both punishments came on them, the shaking from below and the crash from above.

In one telling of the events, the demand that was made at the mountain was not the first step. Musa had brought the Torah to his people and had told them to follow it. They answered as a crooked and pretentious people, saying that they were not sure it was the word of Allah, and that Musa might have written it himself. He prayed to Allah to make them certain. Allah told him to choose seventy men of his people and to bring them to Sinai, where He would let them hear His word, and that was done as promised. It was after hearing the voice that they said they would not be certain the voice was from God, and that they would believe only when they saw Allah vividly. So the demand came after the hearing, and the punishment followed the demand.

### What the choosing of the two communities shows

The difference between the community of Musa and the community of Muhammad has been drawn from this verse. Musa chose his own people, as the words say. Of those whom Musa chose it is recorded that they said, show us God openly, and the thunderbolt took them for their wrongdoing (4:153). The community of Muhammad was chosen by God and not by any man, and the Book says of them that they were chosen with knowledge above the worlds (44:32). Here He says of the men whom Musa chose that the earthquake took them. Of the ummah whom God chose for Himself the Book says that their faces on that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord (75:22-23).

The point of the comparison is that the want is the want of the Real and the choosing is the choosing of the Real. The Book states it in the words that your Lord creates what He wills and chooses, and they have no choice (28:68).

### What the supplication shows of the one praying

The state Musa was in when he made this supplication has been described in some detail. He was bold on the carpet of nearness, standing in the station of whispered prayer, and he spoke out of the realisation that had come to him in his brokenness and his need. Then he saw himself as he was, and came back to his own incapacity and need, entering by the door of awe and reverence. So he threw the decree back entirely to his Lord, saying that He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. He was not content to leave it there, so he set his tongue to praise. He joined the praise to his asking and his weeping, saying that his Lord is his Guardian and that He should forgive and have mercy. He laid his need and his lowliness before Him, and asked, and ended on the note that the best of all who forgive is the One he was addressing.

It is also reported that Musa came to the edge of Mount Sinai on the day of the whispered prayer. At each step along that road he praised God, called upon Him and showed his need. And of the same meaning the Pir of the Tariqah said that the one in need is never turned away. Behind the door of need there is no deceit, and no road brings a man nearer to the Friend than his own need.

### In short

- Musa chose seventy of the best of the Children of Israel for the appointed meeting, on the command of Allah, so that they should apologise for the calf and ask forgiveness for their people.
- The demands of verse 155 follow the hearing of the divine speech. The words of the people at that point were that they would not believe unless they saw Allah plainly, as Al-Baqarah and the fourth surah record.
- The two accounts of what struck them use the word for the earthquake and the word for the thunderbolt, and the two are reconciled by taking it that both came on them at once.
- They were seized because they had neither shunned the calf nor forbidden their people from worshipping it. One report from Ibn 'Abbas keeps the men of this meeting apart from those who were struck by the thunderbolt on another day.
- Musa pleaded that the many should not be destroyed for the deed of the few. He named the whole event as a trial from his Lord, and asked for forgiveness and mercy, since there is no forgiver besides Him.
- The difference between the community of Musa and the community of Muhammad is drawn from the choosing. Musa chose his people, while God chose the followers of the last Prophet ﷺ. The decree and the choice belong to Allah, as the Book says in the forty-fourth surah and the twenty-eighth.

156.text:
The plea widens out from forgiveness to the whole of life, and the answer comes back naming the limits of mercy. "Ordain for us what is good in this life and the next." The ground of the asking is stated next. "Indeed, we have turned to You ˹in repentance˺.”" Then the answer of the Lord. "Allah replied, “I will inflict My torment on whoever I will. But My mercy encompasses everything." And the condition is given. "I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ordain for us what is good in this life and the next."** is the second half of the supplication, and it asks for something rather than turning something away. The first part of the plea had been aimed at holding off what should be avoided, and this part seeks what is wanted. In one reading the good asked for in this world is knowledge, worship, and protection from sin, and the good asked for in the life to come is Paradise and its bliss. The meaning of the sentence is that Allah should grant them everything good in both of the lives, and what that good is had already been set out in the explanation of Al-Baqarah.

**"Indeed, we have turned to You ˹in repentance˺.”"** is the ground on which the request is made. The word used here in the Book carries the sense of turning back and returning. That is the meaning given by Ibn 'Abbas, and by Sa'id bin Jubayr, and by Mujahid, and by Abu Al-'Aliyah, and by Ad-Dahhak, and by Ibrahim At-Taymi, and by As-Suddi, and by Qatadah. Several others besides them said the same.

The inner reading of it is put in a way that fills out the sense. The words mean that they have turned towards the religion of their Lord and come home to Him entirely, leaving nothing over for themselves. It is the speech of one who has come back to his Lord with nothing of his own. He is quit of his own power and his own strength, and content with whatever has been decreed for him. The prayer of Al-Mustafa in the same spirit was that he should not be left to himself for the blink of an eye, or for less than that. He also asked to be shielded as a son is shielded.

The same meaning was given to David in revelation, in the words that his friends have nothing to do with the sorrow of this world. The sorrow of this world, it says, takes the sweetness of whispered prayer out of their hearts. What the Lord loves in His friends is that they should be spiritual. They should not grieve over anything. They should detach their hearts from this world, throw all their work and business upon Him, and approve of what He decrees. The Messenger of God said on this last point that the approval of the decree is the greatest gate that leads to God.

A worshipper among the Children of Israel once spent long days in worship, and it was shown to him in a dream that his close friend in Paradise would be a certain man he knew. He set off to find him, to see what worship the man had. He found that the man kept no night prayer and no fasting beyond the obligatory acts. He asked him to tell him what he did, and the man said that he had never done much beyond what had been seen. He had one trait.
