When he was in a trial or an illness he did not wish to be well, and when he was standing in the sun he did not wish to be in the shade. Whatever God decreed, he approved of it, and he did not add his own want to the want of God. The worshipper said to him that this was what had carried him to that station.

He, God, says in verse 156 that He will strike with His torment whoever He wills, and the answer holds the door of punishment open while it narrows it. The sense is that though all the disobedient deserve the punishment of Allah, out of His mercy, which takes in everything, He strikes with His punishment only whom He wills. So the men who had been taken were not punished because a whole people had sinned. The Lord punishes whom He wills for their transgression, and no one can overturn His decision.

**"But My mercy encompasses everything."** states the breadth of the mercy. The angels who carry the Throne and those around it supplicate with the words that their Lord comprehends all things in mercy and knowledge (40:7). The mercy spoken of here reaches every created thing in this world. It is also remembered that even those who are punished are not cut off from mercy altogether, since the punishment they receive could have been harder than it was. In a similar place the Book says that your Lord has written mercy upon Himself (6:54).

The word of the Prophet ﷺ on this came with two reports. Ahmad recorded from Jundub bin 'Abdullah Al-Bajali that a bedouin came, made his camel kneel, tied it, and prayed behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the prayer was finished the man untied the camel and mounted it. Then he called out aloud in prayer that Allah should grant His mercy to him and to Muhammad, and give no share of it to anyone else. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked his companions whether they thought that man or his camel was the more misguided, and whether they had heard what he said. Then he told them that the man had put a limit on a mercy that has no limit. God's Messenger said that Allah had made the mercies a hundred in number, and that one of them was sent down. By that one the created beings show kindness among themselves, men and jinn and animals alike, while the ninety-nine that remain stay with Him. Ahmad and Abu Dawud collected that hadith. Ahmad also recorded from Salman that the Prophet ﷺ said that the mercies of Allah come to a hundred. One of them is at work among the creatures, so that even a beast is gentle with its young. The other ninety-nine are held back with Him for the Day of Resurrection. Muslim recorded that report.

**"I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations."** sets out where the mercy is placed. The first condition is that a person keep clear of shirk and of the major sins, which is what the fear of Allah means here in practice. The second is the giving of the alms-tax, which has been read either as the purifying of the self or as the alms-tax on wealth. It is possible that both senses are meant, since this passage was revealed in Makkah before the fixed shares of the alms-tax had been ordained. The third is belief in the signs of Allah, that is in His Book, in His Messenger and in the verses themselves.

What the answer amounts to is that the mercy is ordained for the ummah of the Prophet ﷺ, since those who carry the three qualities are the people of that faith. Moses had asked for the good of his own community. The answer given to him names the people who will receive it, and it does not make the matter depend on belonging to any one group. Salvation and success are decided for each person on the basis of his own deeds, and the mercy of God does not carry anyone past the demand for righteous action.

### The claim that the mercy covered everyone

A dispute arose over the reach of the sentence, and it is worth stating plainly.

The Satan claimed a share in the mercy on the basis of these words, arguing that he too is one of the things that everything covers. The answer given to him is that the verse does not say that His mercy shall take in everything. It says that it has taken in everything, and the condition that follows closes the door on his claim. In another place the Book says it in clearer words, that the Lord has an all-encompassing mercy, and that His punishment cannot be turned away from the people of evil (6:147). So the breadth of the mercy does not save the sinner from being punished.

The people of the Book made a claim of the same shape. They said that they believed in Allah and gave the alms-tax, and that the perfect mercy would therefore be written for them. The verse that follows this one names belief in the last Prophet and in the verses of the Book among the conditions, and by that the claim is shut out.

### Whether the supplication was granted

A question was raised about the answer that Musa received, and the answer to it turns on what exactly he had asked. There is no clear statement in this place that his prayer was accepted, unlike other places where the acceptance is stated. On one occasion he was told that he had been given what he asked for (20:36), and on another that the prayer of Musa and Harun had been accepted (10:89). Here no such word is given. On that basis some suggested that this particular prayer of Musa was not accepted on behalf of the Children of Israel, and that it was accepted instead on behalf of the Muslim community. Ruh al-Ma'ani said that this is a remote possibility.

The better reading is that the supplication had two requests in it. The first was for mercy and forgiveness for those who had been punished. The second was for the good of this world and the next to be written for him and for his people. The first request was granted at once, and the answer to the second is given in the verse that follows this one. As for the first, the answer was that Allah does not punish everyone who acts sinfully. He punishes whom He wills, and these people accordingly were shown mercy. His mercy is wide enough to cover the whole of creation. Even those who are punished are not shut out of the mercy of Allah entirely, since a harder punishment than theirs was possible and was not given. He has power over all things and does whatever He wills.

The two conditions belong to the two lives separately. In this world the mercy of Allah reaches every creature without regard to belief or disbelief. The world to come is a different place. There the mercy is written for those who carry the fear of Allah. They fulfil their obligations and keep away from what is forbidden. They give the alms-tax regularly out of what they earn, and they believe firmly in the verses of their Lord without turning them aside by false readings. For the people who carry those qualities the perfect favour is written in both worlds.

### In short

- The second half of the supplication asks for what is good in this world and the next. The good is read as knowledge and worship and protection from sin, and then Paradise and its bliss.
- The turning back to Allah named in the verse means coming to Him entirely with nothing of one's own left over. The reports from the companions and the early generations give it the sense of repentance and return.
- The answer keeps the punishment of Allah within His will and describes His mercy as having taken in everything. The angels around the Throne supplicate with the words that their Lord comprehends all things in mercy and knowledge.
- The report of the bedouin who asked for mercy for himself and the Prophet ﷺ alone, collected by Ahmad and Abu Dawud, shows how vast the mercy is. The report of Salman in Muslim says that a hundred mercies were created and one of them was sent down.
- The mercy is written for those who keep clear of shirk and major sins, give the alms-tax, and believe in the signs of their Lord. The passage was revealed in Makkah before the fixed shares of the alms-tax were ordained.
- The Satan and the people of the Book both claimed a share in the mercy on the strength of its breadth. Both claims are answered by the conditions attached to it and by the verse that follows.

157.text:
The people who receive the mercy are named, and the man they follow is described. "˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet," The next words send them back to their own books. "whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel." Then his work among them is set out. "He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil, permits for them what is lawful and forbids to them what is impure," and then comes the lifting of the load. "and relieves them from their burdens and the shackles that bound them." The verse closes on the four things that make a man successful. "˹Only˺ those who believe in him, honour and support him, and follow the light sent down to him will be successful.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet"** describes the people who deserve the perfect mercy. That mercy, and the complete favour of it, is what Musa had asked for on behalf of his own nation. The people who fulfil the conditions set out in the verse before this one are, in truth, those who follow the Messenger of Allah. The verse names him with the word that means a man who does not know the art of reading and writing.

The Book refers to the Arabs as the unlettered ones, because the Arabs in general had very little to do with reading and writing. Being unable to read and write is, in itself, plainly not a quality. It is an indication of a shortcoming. What makes the word remarkable here is that the same lack, which is a defect in others, has become for this Prophet a sign of the highest perfection.

A demonstration of wisdom and sound practice coming from a man of letters is taken as the fruit of his education. The same things, and many more of the same order, stand as a proof as clear as daylight. They come from a man who did not know how to read and write. It is more striking still that he lived in Makkah el-Mukarramah for forty years without ever having an occasion to learn. Then, at the age of forty, he began to speak in words of such wisdom and such a style. No one in the world could produce a match for the smallest part of them. That is a witness standing on its own, that he was truly the Messenger of Allah and that the Book he brought is truly the word of Allah. In another place the Book puts the challenge to the whole world to produce a surah to match it (2:23). The inability of the Arabs to answer it, in a nation as boastful of its speech as they were, is proof of the miraculous character of the Book.

The quality of being unlettered, then, may be a defect for other men, and for this Prophet it is a praiseworthy attribute. In the same way, the words of the verse calling him a messenger and a prophet are witness enough that his being unlettered was itself a sign. Not a weakness in the claim made for him.

### The description in the earlier books

**"whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel."** is the verse's claim about the earlier Books. The Gospel here is the book revealed to Jesus, and the Torah is the book revealed to Musa. What is found in them is not merely a set of attributes or a set of indications. The words say that they find him in their books, and that carries an implicit meaning of its own. The qualities named in the Torah and the Gospel are described in such detail that seeing them written there is like seeing the Prophet himself.

The mention of the Torah and the Gospel, without a reference to the Zabur, the Book revealed to Dawud, is because the Jews and the Christians believed in those two books. The Zabur also carried the description of the Prophet, as the reports that follow make clear.

The present copies of the Torah and the Gospel have passed through great changes and distortions, and have lost the quality of being original and trustworthy. Even so, they still carry expressions that point to him. Beyond that, the Book stated in definite terms that those two books contained his description. The Jews and the Christians of his own time would have used the claim against him if it could have been shown to be false. and neither group ever tried to refute it. That silence is itself a witness that the Torah and the Gospel of that period carried clear references to him.

Some of the attributes named in those books have been reported in the Book itself. Others have come down in the hadith through men who read them in those books before they entered Islam.

Ibn Jarir recorded that Al-Muthanna said that 'Ata' bin Yasar met 'Abdullah bin 'Amr and asked him about the description of the Messenger of Allah in the Torah. He answered, by Allah, that he is described in the Torah just as he is described in the Book. He is a witness to them, one who brings good news and one who gives warning (33:45). He is a safe refuge for the unlettered ones. The description continued in his words. He is My servant and My Messenger, he is called Al-Mutawakkil, the one who trusts in Allah, he is neither hard nor harsh, and he does not utter foul speech in the markets. Nor does he return an evil deed with one of the same kind. Rather, he forgives and he forgoes. Allah will not end his life until He has straightened through him the crooked religion, so that they proclaim that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. Through him He will open sealed hearts, and deaf ears, and blind eyes.

'Ata' then said that Ka'b was asked the same question by him, and his answer did not differ from the answer of 'Abdullah by a single letter. Al-Bukhari recorded it from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr. He mentioned that our Salaf were in the habit of calling the Books of the People of the Two Scriptures the Tawrah, as some hadith support.

The People of the Book had been told of the coming of the last prophet by their own prophets. The report of it was left in their books so that, when he appeared, they would recognise him readily and gather to his cause. It was also foretold that he would be unlettered, so that no one could raise a doubt about his credibility. A man with schooling would have been suspected of inventing what he brought and attributing it to God. To the knowledge of the Israelites, whichever prophets had come had all, without exception, been raised from their own community. By the plan of God the last prophet was to be raised from the children of Isma'il. This had already been conveyed to them through their prophets. Many of the predictions on the subject are still to be found in their books.

### The reports of those who read the description

Several reports have come down about people who read the description and tested it against the man himself.

Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Sakhr Al-'Uqayli said that a bedouin told him he had brought a milk-producing camel to Al-Madinah during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah. After he had sold it he said to himself that he would meet the man and hear from him. The man came across him walking between Abu Bakr and 'Umar. He kept behind them until they reached a Jewish man, who sat reading from an open copy of the Tawrah. The man was mourning a son of his who was dying, and the boy was one of the most handsome of children. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked the father whether he did not find the description of him and of his advent in his book. He put the question to him by the One who had sent down the Tawrah. The man nodded his head in the negative. His son said that the truth was otherwise, by the One who sent down the Tawrah. He said that they found his description and his advent in their book. He bore witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. He also bore witness that this man is the Messenger of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ told the companions to take the boy from the Jew, and he took care of the funeral himself and led the prayer over him. That hadith is sound, and it is supported by a similar report in the Sahih narrated from Anas.

Al-Baihaqi reported the same kind of event in his Dalail al-Nubuwwah. The wording there has Anas telling of a Jewish boy who was in the service of the Prophet ﷺ. When the boy fell sick the Prophet ﷺ came to his house, and there he found the father reciting parts of the Torah beside the bed. The Prophet ﷺ asked him, by the pledge of Allah, whether he found in the Torah a description of his coming as a prophet. The father said no, and the son at once said that his father was wrong, and that they found him and his attributes mentioned in the Torah. Then he bore witness that there is no god but Allah and that he is the Messenger of Allah. When the boy died, the Prophet ﷺ told his companions to carry out the funeral rites for him as a Muslim.

Ali reported an affair of a different kind. The Prophet ﷺ owed some money to a Jew. The man asked for it back and told him in a harsh tone that he would not let him go until he was paid. The Prophet ﷺ said that the man had a right over him. He sat down beside him and said that he would not leave until the man let him go willingly. He stayed there a whole day and night, and offered the midday, the afternoon, the sunset and the night prayers, and the dawn prayer of the next day. The companions were greatly annoyed at the behaviour of the Jew, and they began, quietly, to press him to let the Prophet ﷺ go. The Prophet ﷺ, who had some idea of what they were doing, asked them what it was. Their answer was that they could not bear the sight of the Prophet ﷺ standing held by a Jew. He told them that his Lord had forbidden him to do wrong to anyone under a covenant.

Next morning the Jew came to him, deeply impressed by what he had seen. He declared that he bore witness that there is no god but Allah, and that this man is the Messenger of Allah. After that declaration he said that he had detained the Prophet ﷺ for no other purpose than to test the truth of the attributes he had read about him in the Torah. He gave half of his wealth away for the sake of Allah. The description he said he had read was this. The man's name was Muhammad the son of 'Abdullah, his birth would be in Makkah, the place of his migration would be Madinah, and his country would be Syria. He would be neither a man of harsh temperament nor a man of rough speech, and he would make no noise in the markets. It said that he would be far from the acts of immodesty. The report comes through Al-Baihaqi in Dalail al-Nubuwwah.

Al-Baghawi reported from Ka'b Ahbar a description that the Torah carried. Muhammad is the Messenger and the chosen servant of Allah, neither harsh nor disagreeable in speech. He does not cry out in the markets, and he does not return ill for ill. It said also that he forgives or passes over the wrongdoing of others. His birthplace is Makkah, his migration is to Taybah, which is Madinah, and his country is Syria. His people will be a praising people, who praise Allah in comfort and in trouble. They say the takbir when they rise in their travels, and they watch the shadows to work out the times of their prayers. They wear a sheet of cloth round the waist, and they keep their hands and feet clean with the wudu. The man who calls them to prayer will raise his voice in the air. In the field of battle they will stand in lines as close as they stand in prayer. At night their recitation will be heard like the humming of bees.

Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Sa'd cited a full chain of narrators. Sahl, the freedman of Khuthaimah, said that he had read the following description of the Prophet ﷺ in the Injil. He would be neither short nor tall, of a fair colour, with his hair in two locks. He would carry the seal of prophethood on his body between the shoulders. He would not accept alms, he would ride a camel, he would milk the goat with his own hands, and he would wear patched clothes. He would be of the line of Isma'il, and his name would be Ahmad.

Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat, Darimi in his Musnad and Al-Baihaqi in Dalail al-Nubuwwah reported from 'Abdullah bin Salam, who had been a great scholar among the Jews. He reported that the Torah contained this description. O Prophet, We have sent you to bear witness over every nation on the earth, as a bearer of glad tidings to the righteous, as a warner to the wrongdoers. As a protector of the unlettered Arabs. You are My Messenger and My servant. I have named you Al-Mutawakkil, the one who trusts in Allah. You are neither harsh in temperament, nor quarrelsome, nor one who cries out in the markets. You do not return evil in exchange for evil. Rather, you forgive and you pass over the wrongdoing of others. Allah will not let him die until the crooked has been set right and the people have come to believe in Allah alone. That will not come to pass until blind eyes see, deaf ears hear and sealed hearts are opened. A similar description is carried in the Sahih of Al-Bukhari from Amr ibn al-'As.

Al-Baihaqi also reported in his Dalail al-Nubuwwah from Wahb ibn Munabbih, a great scholar and a man learned in the early books. Ruh al-Ma'ani carried that report. The wording is that Allah revealed to Dawud in the Zabur that a prophet would come after him whose name would be Ahmad. Allah would never be displeased with him, he would never disobey his Lord, and his errors and omissions had been forgiven. His people had been given the optional and the obligatory prayers that had been laid on the earlier prophets. On the Day of Judgement they will come before their Lord carrying a light like the light of the early prophets. Dawud was told that Muhammad and his people had been given excellence over the people of the other prophets. They had been favoured further with six concessions that were not given to the peoples before them. They will not be punished for inadvertent omissions. Their unintentional sins will be forgiven if they ask for forgiveness. The money they spend willingly in the way of their Lord will be repaid to them many times over in this world as well. When they are struck by distress and they say that they belong to Allah and that to Him they are returning. Their distress will be turned into a blessing and a mercy and a means of guidance towards Paradise. Their prayers will be answered, at one time by handing them the very thing they asked for and sometimes by storing the prayer to be granted on the Day of Judgement.

The reports of this kind have been gathered by scholars into separate volumes, and what has been cited here is a small part of what they collected. The book Izhar al-Haqq dealt with the subject thoroughly. It gave specific examples of such descriptions still found in the present versions of the Bible, even after all the changes and distortions they have been through.

### He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil

**"He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil,"** names the work he does among the people he is sent to. The word for the good he commands carries the sense of what is known and acknowledged. The word for the evil he forbids carries the sense of what is strange and not recognised.

Among the greatest of these commands is that Allah sent the Messenger ﷺ to order the worship of Him alone. No partner is to be joined to Him, and the worship of anything besides Him is forbidden. That is the message with which every messenger was sent before him. The Book says it in the words that a messenger was raised in every ummah, calling people to worship Allah and to keep away from false deities (16:36).

The way this command is understood has consequences. What was recognised as good by the people of the first century of Islam is what is taken as a good deed. Anything else falls on the side of the rejected. Any act that was not approved by the companions and their students cannot be counted as a good deed, however agreeable or positive it may look to a person. On that basis the authentic hadith called such acts innovated ones.

The attribute of commanding good and forbidding evil was common to all the prophets. The very purpose of their being raised was to guide people to what is good and to keep them from what is evil. So there must be something distinctive in the way it is said of this Prophet. A little reflection on the way he spoke to people according to the state they were in makes the distinction clear. The Arab bedouins, who knew nothing beyond grazing camels and goats, were addressed in such simple and candid terms that they understood matters of a complex and speculative kind without effort. He received delegations from the powers of the age, from Rome and Persia and from the other tribes. They were struck by the directness of his approach and by how easily his point came across. His God-given ability to reach people in his speech was something his enemies themselves acknowledged. The earlier books carried the same thing in the promise that through him blind eyes would see, deaf ears would hear and sealed hearts would open. That verse has been taken as a reference to the way he made matters understood.

### He permits the good things and forbids the impure

**"permits for them what is lawful and forbids to them what is impure,"** describes what he does with the law itself. He makes lawful the good things that the people had been forbidden, and he makes unlawful the things that are foul. One report from Ibn 'Abbas, carried through Ali bin Abi Talhah, says that the good things include the kinds of livestock the people had declared off limits for themselves. The same report says that the impure things include the flesh of the pig and riba. They include foods that they had treated as lawful although Allah had forbidden them.

The first part of it means that many things which were good in themselves had been made unlawful for the Israelites as a punishment. Those same things were made lawful for the people of this Prophet. The fat of a properly slaughtered animal is one of them. It had been forbidden for the Israelites, and it was made lawful for the Muslims. The examples given for the impure things include blood, dead animals, liquor, and the animals that are forbidden. They also include the means of earning that are not permitted, such as gambling, riba, and bribes. Some have added immorality and bad manners to the list, and one of the works on the subject, Al-Siraj Al-Munir, is cited on the point.

### He relieves them of burdens and shackles

**"and relieves them from their burdens and the shackles that bound them."** is the lifting of the load that had been laid on the nations before. The word used for the burden points to a weight heavy enough to stop a man moving. The word used for the shackles is the plural of a word for the iron that binds the hands of a criminal to his neck. Both words point to things that were, in themselves, a punishment and not a religious requirement.

The examples given are of that kind. The Israelites were required to cut away the piece of cloth that had impurity on it, and were not allowed simply to wash it. The spoils taken in a jihad from the enemies of religion were not lawful for them. It is reported that a fire used to come down from heaven and burn them up. They were not allowed to hunt on the Sabbath. A human organ that had been involved in a sin had to be cut off. A murderer had to be killed in retaliation whatever the nature of the killing, whether deliberate or by mistake. There was no concession of paying a ransom in place of the killing. All of that has been taken as the burden and the shackles spoken of in this verse. The Prophet ﷺ came to set such things aside and to replace them with commands that can be carried out without hardship.

The Messenger ﷺ described this side of the law himself. He said that he was leaving among a people a law that is easy and practicable, neither burdensome nor such as would lead them astray. In another report he said plainly that the religion is easy. When he sent Mu'adh and Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari to Yemen as commanders, he told them to bring glad tidings and not drive people away, and to make matters easy and not difficult. He said too that they should agree with one another and not fall into disagreement among themselves.

Abu Barzah Al-Aslami, a companion of the Prophet, said that the Messenger of Allah was with him on a journey and that he saw how light the man's way was. The nations before had things made difficult for them in their laws, and Allah made the law wide and easy for this ummah. Out of that came the word of the Messenger of Allah. Allah has forgiven his ummah for what passes within themselves, as long as they do not speak it or act on it. The word that his ummah has been forgiven for unintentional errors, for forgetfulness, and for what a man is driven to do under duress. This is why Allah has guided this ummah to a supplication that asks the Lord not to punish its people if they forget or fall into error. It asks Him not to lay on them a burden like the burden laid on those before them, and not to place on them a load greater than they can bear. The same supplication asks for pardon, forgiveness and mercy, and it names Him as its Patron and Protector (2:286).

It is recorded in Sahih Muslim that Allah answered every one of those requests with the words that He would accept it. A supplication whose every request is granted is the plainest sign that the load on this people has been made light.

Now the verse says that the Prophet ﷺ came with leniency and with an easy religion. The well-known report carries the words that he was sent with the easy way of the one who turns to his Lord alone.

Abdullah bin Mas'ud gave a rule to the believers on this matter. He said that when a person hears the words, O you who believe, he should give them his full attention. What follows is either a good that he is being commanded to do or an evil that he is being forbidden.

### Those who believe, honour, support and follow the light

**"˹Only˺ those who believe in him, honour and support him. Ollow the light sent down to him will be successful.”"** sets out four conditions. Uccess is tied to all of them.

The first is belief in him. The next is reverence of him. The word used for reverence is derived from a root that carries the sense of stopping a person, out of love and affection, from doing something, and of guarding him. Ibn 'Abbas explained it as reverence, and one of the early authorities on the language said that it denotes the highest degree of reverence there is. The third is help. In the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ the help spoken of was given to him in person. After his departure the same help is given to his message, and the support given to the sacred law stands in the same place. The fourth is the following of the light, which is the Book sent down with him and the revelation that he delivered to mankind. The light has been taken as the Book itself, since it was sent down with Gabriel.

What the light means is worth setting out. Light does not need an outside proof to show that it exists, and the Book is in the same position. It is its own evidence that it is from Allah, since the highest order of wisdom and eloquence is in it, as plain as the light of the sun. It was spoken by a man who could not read or write. In another respect the Book is unlike any other light, since light not only shows itself but makes other things bright. The Book has brought out of darkness a people who had been lost in it.

There is a further point in the way the verse is built. It opens with those who follow the Messenger and it closes with those who follow the light that was sent down with him. The first phrase lays on the people the obedience of the Prophet ﷺ and the second lays on them the obedience of the Book. Eternal success is therefore tied to both of them together, and obedience to the Prophet ﷺ is reached only by following the way of his life, which is the sunnah. Between those two phrases sits the command to honour and to help him. The point of that arrangement is that the obedience owed to the Prophet ﷺ is not the obedience a man gives to a high official out of necessity. It is an obedience that comes out of love and reverence.  A person should carry as much love and reverence for him as will make that obedience the dearest thing to him. The Prophet stands to his people in more than one relation. He is a prophet, a teacher and a commander. He is an object of deep love as well. The fulfilment of the demands of all of those positions falls on the believer.

The companions took this seriously, and the reports show how. In another verse the words come that the people should help him and honour him (48:9). In another, the believers are told not to raise their voices above the voice of the Prophet ﷺ and not to speak to him in a loud voice as they speak to one another. The warning is that their works may come to nothing while they are not aware (49:2). In another, they are told not to go ahead of Allah and His Messenger (49:1). Sahl ibn 'Abdullah took that to mean that a person should not begin to speak before the Prophet of Allah speaks, and should keep silent when he is speaking. In another, they are told not to treat the calling of the Messenger among them as the calling of one of them to another (24:63). The warning attached to it is that a failure of respect towards him can bring a man's good deeds to nothing.

The companions who had his company most of the time kept to that instruction. It is reported that after the revelation of the verse Abu Bakr used to speak to the Messenger of Allah in a low voice. He spoke the way a man does when he is telling a secret. Umar al-Faruq did the same. Amr ibn al-'As said that no one on the face of the earth was dearer to him than the Messenger of Allah. He said at the same time that he could not bring himself to look at him directly. He said that if he were asked to describe him he would find it difficult, since he had never looked at him long enough to give a description. Anas reported that whenever the Prophet ﷺ came into the assembly of the companions they kept their eyes down out of respect. He said that only Abu Bakr and Umar raised their eyes and smiled at him.

The respect of the Muslims for their Prophet was noticed by those who came from outside. Urwah ibn Mas'ud was once sent to Madinah to spy on the Muslims. When he returned to Makkah he reported that he had seen the courts of great kings, of the king of Rome and of Persia. He had met the Negus as well. The reverence he saw in the hearts of the Muslims for their prophet was something he had never seen anywhere in the world. He told his people that they would never succeed against such a people. Mughirah ibn Shu'bah reported the same care in another form. When the companions wanted the Prophet ﷺ and he was inside his house, they would not call out to him from the street. They knocked at his door with their fingernails, so as to make no loud sound. Even after he had left them, the companions avoided raising their voices in his mosque, and they avoided it in the sermons given there as well. When the Prophet ﷺ was mentioned among them, a number of them could not help weeping.

It was that love and that reverence which let the companions take a large share of the perfection of prophethood. It gave them the highest religious standing there is, next to the prophets themselves.

### The spirit of the religion and the shape of it

The verse also speaks to a matter that comes up in every age. The real spirit of the religion is the fear of God and a concern for the Hereafter. In later generations, after a prophet or a reformer has gone, the inner spirit grows less ardent and the greatest weight comes to be placed on the outward form. The Prophet ﷺ brought the pure religion, free of the additions that people had made to it.

When a prophet appears, the greatest virtue for a person lies in believing in him. That faith is not the reciting of a few words as though it were a ritual. It means leaving behind a structure of rituals that has lost its spirit and taking up a living religion that speaks directly to human nature. A man's link with the older structure rests on nothing more than inherited tradition and the customs of his people. When he accepts a new religion, he makes a conscious decision, and he leaves the shell behind for the reality. That looks like a simple matter, and in every age it has proved the hardest step for people to take, since people find it hardest to see past appearances.

There is a further thing in the verse that was noted in the report of 'Abdullah bin Salam. The people of the earlier books had been told of the coming of the last prophet. The purpose was that they should not face a great trial when he came, but should recognise him readily and gather to his cause. Many of the predictions on the matter are still there in their books. The early Muslims who came from those communities read them and recognised him before they entered Islam. The obligation on the one who reads them is the same in every age, that he should take the man when he finds him described.

### In short

- The people who receive the perfect mercy are those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet. He had no schooling, and that lack became by his wisdom and eloquence a sign of the highest perfection rather than a defect.
- The verse claims that his description is found in the Torah and the Gospel, and the claim was never refuted by the Jews and the Christians of his own time. The reports gathered by Al-Baihaqi in Dalail al-Nubuwwah, by Al-Baghawi, by Ibn Sa'd and by Ibn 'Asakir give the descriptions from those books. They name Makkah as his birthplace, Madinah as the place of his migration and Syria as his country.
- He commands the good and forbids the evil, which is the call to the oneness of Allah that every messenger was sent with. He makes lawful the good things that had been forbidden to the Israelites as a punishment, and makes unlawful the impure things, among them riba and the earnings that are not permitted.
- The burdens and the shackles he lifted are the hard requirements laid on the nations before, and he came with a law that the Prophet ﷺ himself described as easy. His ummah was forgiven for what passes within them, for error, and for what a man is driven to do against his will. That is what the supplication of Al-Baqarah asks and what Sahih Muslim records the answer to.
- Success is tied to four things together, belief in him, reverence for him, help given to him and following the light sent down with him. The reverence placed in the middle is what turns obedience into love, as Abu Bakr and Umar and the rest of the companions showed in their conduct towards him.

158.text:
The verse is a command to the Prophet to address the whole of mankind. "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity! I am Allah’s Messenger to you all." The right of the One who sent him follows at once, since He owns all that exists. "To Him ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth." His sole right to worship is stated next. "There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him." His power over life and death comes after that. "He gives life and causes death.”" The verse then names what the hearers owe the Messenger. "So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and his revelations." The last words promise the result of following him. "And follow him, so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say"** is addressed to the Prophet himself. The instruction that follows it, **"O humanity! I am Allah's Messenger to you all,"** is the declaration he was told to make. The word for mankind here is taken to cover people of every colour, and the Arabs and the non-Arabs alike. It leaves out no one.

The verse names the honour and the greatness of the Prophet in that declaration. He is the final prophet, and he was sent to all mankind, and to the jinn as well. The Holy Qur'an says it in other places. One passage has the words that the Book has been revealed to him so that he may warn whoever it reaches (6:19). Another says that the sects which reject it have the Fire as their promised meeting place (11:17). Another has the command to say to those who were given the Scripture, and to the unlettered, whether they submit themselves. The words that follow say that the duty of the Messenger is only to convey the message (3:20). Reports on the subject are more than can be counted, and the universality of his mission is well known in the religion itself.

**"To Him ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He gives life and causes death."** describes the One who sent him. The words point to the Creator, the Lord, the King of all things, in whose hand lies the control of everything, and life, and death, and the decision.

**"So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and his revelations."** is the command that follows the declaration. Belief in Allah is joined here with belief in His Messenger, and the Messenger is named as the one who could neither read nor write. The description adds that he believes in Allah and in His words. This is read to mean that his actions agree with what he says, and that he believes in what he was given from his Lord. The words of Allah that he believes in are the Books revealed to the prophets. They include the Torah, the Gospel revealed to Jesus, and the Book given to him.

**"And follow him, so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided"** names the second demand. Belief in him is asked for first, and the following of him is asked for after it. The order of the two tells a reader that a bare belief, or the saying of the words of belief with the tongue, is not enough by itself for guidance. Putting the shariah into practice is what the verse is aiming at.

### The messenger sent to all mankind

The verse is one of the basic matters of prophethood. The belief that the Prophet was sent to the whole of mankind, and to the jinn as well, is one of the fundamental tenets of the religion.

The mission he was given was not limited to one people or one place or one period, which was the case with the earlier prophets. Each of them came to a particular people, in a particular place, for a limited time. He was sent at the end of the prophets. His coming at the end, for the guidance of all people and all times to come, leaves no room for another prophet after him.

One of the marks of this ummah follows from the same fact. A report of the Prophet says that there will always be a group among the Muslims who stand against the forces working against the religion. They resist sacrilegious thought and practice, and they correct false interpretations of the Book and the sunnah. That group is helped by Allah and is promised the final victory, since such people are the real inheritors of the prophetic mission and carry its duty after him.

Al-Razi drew a further point out of the same fact. Commenting on the command to be in the company of the truthful, he said that the command carries an assurance that a group of the truthful will always be found among the people. Otherwise the command to seek their company would mean nothing. From that he took the principle of consensus, that the presence of such truthful people prevents the ummah from agreeing together on an error.

Another account drew from the verse a proof that he is the last of the prophets, since his message covers all the people of the world and all the ages to come. Some reports add that Jesus will follow the law of the Prophet after his descent from the heavens in the last age. The Book speaks of the finality of prophethood in many places. One of them has the words that the Book has been revealed to him so that he may warn whoever it reaches (6:19). That lays the following of the Book on all the people who come after him, and it lays on them the duty of learning it.

### The two sides of the mission

The words that he is the Messenger to all people are not a comparison drawn between him and the prophets before him. They are the plain statement of a fact. His prophethood has two sides to it. One is direct and the other works through his ummah.

He was sent to convey the message directly to the people living in Arabia (6:92), and the message was carried to the whole world through his community (22:78). This is, in principle, the nature of the task given to every prophet of God. What happened to the religions brought by the other prophets is that they did not stay in their original and pristine condition. It was not possible, then, for those prophets to go on giving good tidings or warning people of what comes after death, which is the main duty of a prophet.

The Bible carries a prediction about the Arab Prophet, that blessing will come to every tribe on the earth through him. It has been possible for his blessings to reach every nation because the religion he brought has been preserved as it was. The religion brought by Moses and by Jesus was distorted. Everyone may hear its call, yet the blessing of it does not travel with the call.

A number of Jewish tribes were settled in Arabia, and they were proud of having the holy Book. Such people resist accepting a truth that comes from outside them, since the feeling that they possess the greatest truth keeps them from accepting any other. The great majority of the Jews were blinded in this way by obstinacy and prejudice. A few were not, among them 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who could look at Islam with an open mind, vouched for its truth without caring for his worldly honour, and surrendered himself to it wholeheartedly.

### The distinctions given to this prophet

The report of the distinctions came at the battle of Tabuk. Imam Ahmad recorded it on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas. The Prophet was engaged in the late night prayer, the tahajjud, and the companions had gathered round him in a circle to keep him safe from any attack by the enemy. When he had finished the prayer he said that he had been given five distinctions on that night which had not been given to any prophet before him. He said it, as the report has it, and he did not say it out of pride.

The first is that his prophethood was extended to all mankind, while the message of the prophets before him was limited to their own people. The second is that his presence put dread into the heart of his enemy and that the dread overtook the enemy from a distance of a month's journey. The third is that the spoils taken from the enemy were made lawful for his people, while they had been forbidden to the peoples before them. The fourth is that the whole earth was made a place of prayer for them, and it was made a means of purification in tayammum. The prayers of the earlier people were confined to their churches and synagogues, and they were not allowed to pray at home or out in the open land. In the absence of water, his people were allowed to use clean soil in place of water. That was another concession the earlier people did not have. The fifth, which he called the most promising and the most helpful of them, is the supplication that every prophet was asked to make and that was certain to be granted. Each prophet used his for some particular aim of his own. He was asked to make such a supplication too, and he chose to keep his for the Day of Judgement. There it will bring great benefit to the people of the declaration that there is no god but Allah.

Another Tradition, reported on the authority of the companion Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, has the Prophet saying that anyone who hears of his appearance must believe in him, be he Muslim, Christian or Jew. Otherwise, he said, that person will be placed in Hell.

The chain of narration of the report of the five distinctions is suitable, and the two Sahihs did not record it. The distinction of the reserved supplication is the one that matters most for the community, since it is kept until a day when all people stand in need.

### The two companions and the word of Abu Bakr

The other well-known report belongs to this verse directly, and it was recorded by Al-Bukhari. Abu al-Darda said that Abu Bakr and Umar had an argument, and that in the course of it Abu Bakr made Umar angry. Umar went off in his anger, and Abu Bakr followed him asking to be forgiven. Umar refused and shut his door in his face. Abu Bakr then came to the Messenger of Allah while the companions were sitting with him, and the Messenger of Allah said that this companion of theirs had made someone angry.

Umar regretted what he had done, and he came to the Prophet, greeted him with the greeting of peace and sat beside him. He told him what had passed, and the Messenger of Allah became angry with him. When Abu Bakr saw what was happening, he said that it was he who had been in the wrong. The Messenger of Allah answered with the words that they should leave his companion alone. He said that when he had declared to the people that he was the Messenger of Allah to them all, they had called him a liar. Abu Bakr alone had declared that he had spoken the truth.

The report is placed with this verse because it turns on the same declaration. The man who stood by the declaration at the moment when it was contested is the one whose standing the Prophet defended, and the anger of the Prophet was for the sake of a companion who had been wronged rather than for himself.

### What the verse asks of a believer

The verse closes with belief and with following. The Prophet is named in it again as the unlettered one, the man who could neither read nor write, whom the earlier Books had promised and given good news of. His description was carried in those books at length, and the promise of him was the reason the men of the Book were told to watch for his coming.

The phrase that he believes in Allah and his words carries the sense of a life in which the man and the message agree. He believed in what he was given from his Lord, and the words of Allah that he believed in cover every Book revealed before him and the Book given to him.

Following him means taking his path and his guidance. The command of following comes immediately after the command of believing, which shows that a person is not excused from acting on what he holds. The law he brought is the road, and the safe arrival is on it. A saying of a spiritual leader of Baghdad has it that no road to Allah stays open to a man except the path the Prophet marked out.

The distinction between the God of the prophet and the God of the philosopher is drawn from this verse by one of the accounts. The God of the philosopher is an abstract spirit, and faith in Him resembles faith in the pull of gravity. Gravity neither speaks nor commands anything. The God of the prophet is living and aware. He addresses human beings, He lays commands on His servants, and He settles reward and punishment on the basis of obedience or disobedience. It is this God who sent the Messenger, and it is this God the verse commands people to believe in.

### In short

- The command to the Prophet is to declare that he has been sent to the whole of mankind. The verse names every colour and every nation, and the jinn as well, and it follows the declaration with the right of the One who sent him over the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.
- The universality of the mission is the ground of the finality of prophethood, since a message for all people and all ages leaves no room for another prophet after him. It is also the ground of the promise that a group within the ummah will always stand for the truth and keep correcting false interpretations of the Book and the sunnah.
- The report of the distinctions came at Tabuk after the tahajjud prayer. The five named in it are the universal mission, the dread cast at a month's distance, and the spoils made lawful. The rest are the earth made a place of prayer with tayammum in place of water, and the supplication kept for the Day of Judgement.
- Abu Bakr alone declared that the Prophet had spoken the truth when he announced his mission. The Al-Bukhari report of the argument between him and Umar ends with the Prophet defending him and asking the people to leave his companion alone.
- Belief in him and following him are both asked for. The order of the two shows that a faith without the practice of the shariah is not enough. The account adds that the God of the prophet is a living God who speaks and commands, unlike the abstract force of the philosopher.

159.text:
Verse 159 turns from the address to all mankind to a group within an earlier community. "There are some among the people of Moses who guide with the truth and establish justice accordingly"

### Phrase by phrase

**"There are some among the people of Moses who guide with the truth and establish justice accordingly"** states that of the Children of Israel there are people who follow the truth and judge by it. They guide people by the truth, and when they pass judgement they act justly according to it.

The Book says the same of such people in other places. One passage speaks of a group among the people of the Book who take their stand for what is right. They recite the verses of Allah in the night hours and prostrate themselves in prayer (3:113). Another says that among the people of the Scripture there are those who believe in Allah, in what has been revealed to the Prophet and in what was revealed to them. They humble themselves before Allah and do not sell the verses of Allah for a small price. Their reward is with their Lord (3:199). Another speaks of those to whom the Scripture was given before this. They believe in the Book when it is recited to them, and they say it is the truth from their Lord. They had been among those who submitted themselves even before it, and they will be given their reward twice over for their patience (28:52-54). Another passage describes those who were given knowledge before it. They fall on their faces in humble prostration when the Book is recited to them, and they say that glory be to their Lord and that the promise of their Lord must be fulfilled. They fall down weeping, and it increases their humility (17:107-109).

### The group that guides by the truth

The question is which of the Israelites the verse means. It means those who followed the commandments of the Torah and the Injil faithfully at the time when those Books were revealed. It also means those who accepted the faith of Islam after the appearance of the Prophet. They did so on the strength of the predictions about him that were carried in the Torah and the Injil. The Book has spoken of this group in a number of passages in terms of praise.

The Book also says that those to whom the Scripture was given before this believe in this Book (28:52). The community of Moses was not one body with a single conduct. Alongside those who were blinded by obstinacy there were people who held to what had been given to them. The verse names them so that the difference is clear.

### The community beyond the river of sand

A narrative is carried by Ibn Jarir and by other reporters about a group of the Israelites who greatly despised the corruption that had spread among their own people. They prayed to Allah for a land of their own, a place cut off from the other tribes. Their aim was to live by the original faith preached by Moses. Allah answered them and settled them in a distant land in the far east, where they lived by that faith with care.

Another favour was granted to those people. In the time of the Prophet they were given the chance to accept Islam at his own hands. On the night of the ascension, the Archangel Gabriel took the Prophet to them on the way to the heavens. They accepted the faith, and the Prophet taught them some surahs of the Book.

The Prophet spoke with them, and the account gives the questions he put to them. He asked them whether they had any means of weighing and measuring, and what other means of subsistence they had. They answered that they tilled the soil and heaped the whole harvest in one place. Each person then took what he needed from the heap. They said that they therefore needed no weights and measures. He asked them whether anyone among them ever told a lie. They said that no one among them lied. It was the established practice among them that any person who spoke a lie was burnt up by a fire from heaven. He asked them why all their houses were of the same kind. They answered that it was to remove the possibility of showing off one's wealth against the wealth of others. He asked them why they had built their graves in front of their houses. They said that it kept death before their eyes at all times.

After the Prophet returned from the heavens to Makkah, this verse was revealed to him. Al-Qurtubi narrated the event along with other suggestions and remarked that the narrative was not authentic. The other account called it an unusual event, but did not reject it. One of the other works gives a plainer statement of the same identification. The community who lead with truth and act upon it are the people who live beyond the river al-Raml.

### What the people of this description are given

The verse draws a picture of a people whose whole concern is the truth. The Lord of the Worlds showed them the road of felicity. He singled them out for nearness to Him and honoured them out of His generosity. Godwariness lives through such people. The path of truthfulness stands firm under their feet, and the fortune of the religion is joined to the blessing that comes with their breathing.

The description of them is the description of the friends of Allah, and of those who travel the road to Him. God's Messenger is reported to have said that the light of one of them, if it were shared out, would take in all the people of the earth. Suppose the light of their hearts were given an open road. Suppose the glitter of that radiance fell on the world and its people. Then every stubborn man would turn into a voicer of the oneness of Allah. Each would trade the sash of unbelief for a belt of love for the religion.

Such people are rare and precious. He does not show them to everyone, and He does not hand them over to this world or to the world to come. He keeps them in His own protection, as a man might keep fugitives, and He nurtures them with love under the domes of jealousy.

The revelation that came to Moses carries the same care. He was told, as the account has it, that he was the speaking companion of the empire. He was told to be careful not to open the oyster of his pain's pearl before those without eyes. He was told not to recite the verses of the passion for His majesty to those who are not privy to them. The same warning covered those who have been dismissed from hearing the reality. He was told that if he wanted to expose the mystery to someone, he should do it to those who are the locus of the covenant of the secrets. Such people are busy night and day serving His threshold, with the tent of their passion pitched in the contemplation of His majesty. Those are the people branded with the mark of most-worthiness by the threshold of Lordhood, the community that guides by the truth and does justice thereby.

That mark belongs among the divine secrets. It is a subtlety of the Lord that came out of the World of the Unseen. It came to rest in one place only, behind the curtain that veils the stages of the clay of the poor. The one who wants to catch a whiff of it is told to go into the curtains of the soul until he reaches the heart. He is told to pass from the curtains of the heart to the spirit, and from the curtains of the spirit to union with the Beloved. He will not see the mark placed anywhere except in the spirit of the friends. The language of the passage is the language of inward states, and the outward meaning of the verse stays what it was. The verse makes plain that among the people of Moses there has always been a group who held to the truth. That group is either the people described in the narrative or those who entered Islam when the Prophet appeared.

### In short

- The verse states that there are people among the Children of Israel who guide by the truth and judge by it. The Book praises such people in other places, among them the party who stand for the right and recite the verses of Allah at night (3:113).
- Those who believe in what was revealed to the Prophet and in what was revealed to them, and who do not sell the verses of Allah for a small price, have their reward with their Lord (3:199). Those who believed before the Book came to them will be given their reward twice over (28:52-54).
- The group meant by the verse are those who followed the Torah and the Injil faithfully when they were revealed. They also include those who accepted Islam when the Prophet appeared, on the strength of the predictions about him in those Books.
- A narrative carried by Ibn Jarir and other reporters tells of Israelites who asked for a land apart from the corruption of their people. The Prophet visited them on the night of the ascension, when Gabriel took him to them. They accepted the faith and were taught some surahs of the Book.
- Al-Qurtubi narrated that account with other suggestions and called it unauthentic. The other account called it unusual without rejecting it. One of the other works identifies the community of the verse as the people beyond the river al-Raml.
- The inner reading of the passage describes such people as the friends of Allah, whose light would embrace the folk of the earth if it were divided among them. It places the mark of that worthiness in the spirit of the friends rather than in any outward show.

160.text:
The verse turns back to the Israelites in the wilderness and names the provisions given to them there. "We divided them into twelve tribes—each as a community." The first provision was water. "And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out. Each tribe knew its drinking place." The second was shade and food. "We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.”" The verse closes with a judgement on their conduct. "They ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We divided them into twelve tribes—each as a community."** describes the order given to the Children of Israel after they came out of Egypt. They were separated into twelve groups. The word used for the tribes in the verse is asbatan, and it stands in the place of the word for the groups themselves. Each of the twelve had its own leader, and all of them were under the charge of Moses. They were settled in the desert of Sinai, away from the polytheistic air of Egypt, and there they were organised into those groups.

The verse answers a question that follows from the division. **"And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out. Each tribe knew its drinking place."** The people asked Moses to call on Allah for water, and he was commanded to strike the rock with the staff that was in his hand. He struck it, and twelve springs broke out of it, one for each tribe, and no tribe shared another's spring. Each group came to know the place that belonged to it.

**"We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.”"** names the second provision. The white cloud overshadowed them in the wilderness, and it served them in two ways. In the day it kept the sun off them, and in the night it gave them light like a lamp. The manna was a substance like gum with a sweet taste, and the quails were the small birds sent down with it. Both were ready for them in front of their tents, and the command that came with them was to eat of what had been provided.

**"They ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves"** states the result. The wrongdoing of the people did not harm Allah in anything. What their disobedience did was to bring ruin on their own souls, since they did not value the blessings given to them as they should have, and they went against the commands of their Lord.

### The differences between the two accounts

This passage has its counterpart in Al-Baqarah, where the same favours are named with more detail. The two passages do not sit in the same setting. The passage of Al-Baqarah belongs to what was revealed in Al-Madinah, while these verses belong to what was revealed in Makkah, and the two narrations differ in the way they are told. That difference is why the two are not simply repeats of one another. Each brings out the lesson that suits the situation it was revealed in.

The favours listed here are favours of need, given to a people who had left a settled land for a desert. The tribes were given their order, then their water, their shade and their food, and with the food came the command to be content with what had been handed to them. The verse then records that, with all of that in front of them, they turned to what had been forbidden to them.

### The springs and the inward reading of them

One of the reports carries a reading of this verse that turns on the meaning of the water. It was said by Ja'far ibn Muhammad that Allah made twelve streams to flow from the wellspring of recognition, and He gave each of them to be the drink of one group, so that the water of the good fortune of the religion was drawn for each group at its own watering place.

The same idea is put briefly in another place in the Book, in the words that if they go straight on the Tariqah, that is the path, then the watering promised for them will be appointed (72:16). The twelve rivers are named in that reading, and the first of them is familiarity and the last is friendship. Between the two are ten others, and they are named as the truthfulness of belief, self purification in deeds, approval of the decree, the eye of certainty, the joy of ecstasy, the lightning of unveiling, the bewilderment of witnessing, the dissolving of the marks that give witness, the observation of togetherness and the reality of solitariness.

The point of the list is what happens to the servant who tastes them. When his spirit tastes these drinks and finds how sweet they are, and when the divine attraction joins with that, he becomes a wellspring of life himself. Whoever takes a drink from his hand will be prosperous for ever. The reading is that of inward states and it stands beside the plain meaning of the verse, which is that water was brought out of a rock for a people in a desert.



One account of the division has it that nine of the tribes and a half settled towards the east, beyond China, on the river al-Raml, which is also called the Jordan, while two tribes and a half were spread over the world. That reading comes from the men of the earlier books, and it does not change what the verse says, that every one of the twelve found its own drinking place when the rock was struck.

### In short

- The Children of Israel were brought out of Egypt and divided into twelve tribes, each with its own leader, and all of them under the charge of Moses.
- The water came when the people asked for it, and Moses was told to strike the rock with his staff, and twelve springs broke out of it, one for each tribe.
- The cloud shaded them by day and gave them light by night, and the manna and the quails came down for them in the wilderness, with the command to eat of the good things provided.
- The inward reading takes the twelve springs as twelve streams from the wellspring of recognition, of which the first is familiarity and the last friendship, and the promise attached to them is the watering given to those who stay on the path.
- The wrongdoing of the people did not harm Allah in anything, and what it did was to bring ruin on their own souls.

161.text:
The next verse carries the command given to the same people when they came to the town. "And ˹remember˺ when it was said to them, “Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please. Say, ‘Absolve us,’ and enter the gate with humility. We will forgive your sins, ˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please."** is the first part of the command given to the Israelites. The town named here is Jerusalem, and one of the accounts names it as the town of Jericho. The people were told to enter it and to eat from whatever they wished, and one reading adds that the permission covered whatever they wished and whenever they wished.

**"Say, ‘Absolve us,’"** is the second part. The word they were told to say carries the sense of a request that the wrong be taken away from them. It is understood as the declaration that there is no deity except Allah, and as the asking of forgiveness for their sins.

**"and enter the gate with humility."** is the third part. The word used for the entering is that of bowing down. The meaning given to it is that they were to enter their place of worship with humility and modesty. They were to bow their heads, remember the majesty and supremacy of their Lord, and admit their shortcomings before Him. That was the path asked of them at the gate.

**"We will forgive your sins, ˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers."** is the promise that came with the command. Their transgression would be wiped out. Those among them who were virtuous in their obedience would be given more than the ordinary measure in reward, in this world and in the world to come.

The command given at the gate carries the whole of the religion in three words. The town is the place of settlement, and the food is the provision. The word to be said is the admission of the wrong, and the way of entering is the manner of the heart when it comes before its Lord. The people were asked to hold all four together, and the promise was attached to the doing of them.

### What the command was meant to teach

The command was meant to bring the people to contentment and gratitude. They had been given a settled town after the wilderness, and the instruction with it was that they should leave aside greed for the pleasures of the world. The manner of the entry speaks to the same thing. Coming into the place of worship with a bowed head is the outward form of a heart that has stopped claiming anything for itself.

### In short

- The people were told to enter the city of Jerusalem, named in one account as the town of Jericho, and to eat from wherever they wished.
- They were told to ask that their wrongs be taken away from them. The word is read both as the declaration that there is no deity except Allah and as the asking of forgiveness.
- They were told to enter the gate with humility and with the head bowed. The meaning is that they were to come into the place of worship with modesty and remember the majesty of their Lord.
- The promise attached to it was that their sins would be forgiven and the reward of the good among them increased.
- The instruction as a whole was meant to bring the people to contentment and gratitude, away from greed for the pleasures of the world. The passage stands with the verses of Al-Baqarah that tell the same story in the setting of Al-Madinah.

162.text:
The third verse tells what the people did with the command. "But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say." The result follows in the same verse. "So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their wrongdoing"

### Phrase by phrase

**"But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say."** states the offence. The word they had been given to say was the word of the seeking of forgiveness, and the command had been given to them by their Lord. The evildoers among them replaced it with another saying. The word they put in its place was the word for a grain, or a grain inside a hair, or a grain in a rite. Those are the forms in which the substitution is reported.

The same people changed the manner of their entering as well. They had been told to enter the gate bowing down. One account says that they went in dragging themselves on their rears, so that the humility asked of them was turned into mockery.

**"So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their wrongdoing."** names the answer to the offence. What came down on them was a chastisement from the heaven, and one account names it as the plague. The punishment was sent for the exchange they had made. They had taken a word of their own devising in place of the word that had been told to them.

### What the change shows

The change touched the heart and not only the tongue. The word set aside carried the admission of the wrong, and once it was dropped nothing was left of the state the command had asked for. Speech of insolence took the place of speech of gratitude, and the path of the people's own devising was given the name of the religion. When they reached that point the grace that had been with them was withdrawn, and blessings were replaced by punishments until they were surrounded on every side. The Book tells the story of the same people in Al-Baqarah as well. The passage here was revealed in Makkah, while the passage there belongs to Al-Madinah, and the two tellings serve the same lesson for the people who hear them.

### In short

- The wrongdoers among the Israelites replaced the word of the asking of forgiveness with a saying of their own. They also changed the way of entering the gate from humility to mockery.
- One account names the substituted words as a grain, a grain inside a hair or a grain in a rite. Several readings add the way they dragged themselves in at the gate.
- A punishment was sent down from the heaven on them for the exchange they had made, and one account names it as the plague.
- The offence touched the heart and not only the tongue, since the word set aside carried the admission of the wrong. The people were left with their own way dressed in the name of the religion.
- The verses were revealed in Makkah while the telling of the same story in Al-Baqarah belongs to Al-Madinah. The two match each other in the order of the favour, the command, the refusal and the punishment.

163.text:
The verse turns to a story the first hearers knew from their own history. "Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath." The next words describe the test they were put under. "During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen." The verse closes with the reason for the test. "In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath."** addresses the Prophet and, through him, the Jews who were with him. They were to be asked about the story of their own people, the Israelites who had defied the command of Allah. The punishment that overtook their forefathers all of a sudden was to stand as a warning to them. The warning covered another matter as well. They were not to go on hiding the description of the Prophet that they found in their books, since a people who did that would meet what their fathers met.

The town is named in the reports. Ibn 'Abbas, whose words came through Muhammad ibn Ishaq, said that it was a village called Aylah, standing between Midian and At-Tur, which is in Sinai. The same identification of the place is given by Ikrimah and by Mujahid, and also by Qatadah and by As-Suddi. The village stood on the shore of the sea, and that sea is the one also called the Red Sea. Ibn Jarir reported these sayings. The Book itself refers to the same event in Al-Baqarah, where the words come that the people who broke the Sabbath are already known (2:65).

**"During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen."** tells how the test worked. On the day when fishing was forbidden the fish came to the surface of the water in great numbers, close to the shore and plainly seen. On the days when fishing was allowed they stayed away. The trial was made by bringing the thing they wanted within reach on the one day when it was out of bounds.

**"In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness."** gives the reason. The test was a trial of a people who had already turned away from the command of their Lord. Ibn Jarir explained the words by saying that the fish were brought near the surface on the day of the prohibition and hidden on the day when taking them was lawful. The trial was meant to bring out what was in the people.

### The trick they used

The people did not simply break the rule out in the open. They turned to a trick. They set up their nets so that the fish would fall into them on the Sabbath and could then be collected and eaten on the following day. In that way they took the catch of the forbidden day while keeping the appearance of the law.

The offence of such a people is greater than a plain disobedience. The one who does a forbidden thing because his desire overcomes him knows what he is doing. The one who does the same thing while arranging a legal form to cover it adds the insult of making the prohibition look as though it had been kept. The people of the town, by the account, joined both wrongs together.

A report on the subject was carried by Ibn Battah from Abu Hurayrah. He said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the believers not to do what the Jews did, and not to make the prohibitions of Allah lawful by the smallest of tricks. The chain of that hadith is a reasonable one, and the warning in it is aimed at the method rather than at one single act.

### What the test brought out

The trial made the inner state of the people visible. They had been given a day set apart and a rule to keep it, and the rule came with a provision that made obedience easy on the other six days. They chose instead to hunt for the catch of the seventh day by a device. In doing so they showed that the command of Allah weighed less with them than the fish.

The lesson the passage draws is the one the verse before it had already given. A people who treat the prohibitions of Allah as a fence to be got around lose more than they gain. The account adds that such a fall takes a person away from the position given to him and puts him down on the level of the animals. The one who lives only by his appetite has given up the thing that made him a man.

### In short

- The Prophet was told to ask the Jews of his time about the town by the sea. The fate of their forefathers was to serve as a warning, and they were not to repeat the fault of hiding the description of him that was in their books.
- The town is named as Aylah, standing between Midian and At-Tur in Sinai. The event is the same one referred to in Al-Baqarah, where the words come that the people who broke the Sabbath are already known (2:65).
- The fish came in numbers to the surface on the Sabbath and stayed away on other days. The trial was meant to bring out a people who had already turned away from the command of their Lord.
- The people took the catch of the forbidden day by setting their nets so that the fish would fall into them on the Sabbath and be gathered on the next day. That is the trick of a people who wanted the fruit of disobedience while keeping the look of obedience.
