- A report carried by Ibn Battah from Abu Hurayrah commands the believers not to do what the Jews did. It forbids them to make the prohibitions of Allah lawful by the smallest of tricks.

164.text:
The next verse shows a group inside the town that spoke up while the rest went on. "When some of ˹the righteous among˺ them questioned ˹their fellow Sabbath-keepers˺, “Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?”" The answer of the preachers comes next. "They replied, “Just to be free from your Lord’s blame, and so perhaps they may abstain.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When some of ˹the righteous among˺ them questioned ˹their fellow Sabbath-keepers˺"** introduces the exchange. The people of the town, one of the Israelite settlements of that region, had separated into three groups. The same story is told in Al-Baqarah, and the account of it here says plainly what the earlier passage had left to be worked out. One group took the fish on the Sabbath and urged others to do the same. A second group neither took the fish nor warned anyone against it. A third group kept away from the fish and also warned the others, and it is this last group that the verse shows answering a question.

**"Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?"** is the question put by the group that did neither. Their argument was that a people headed for destruction or for a severe chastisement had nothing to gain from advice, and that the advice wasted the effort of those who gave it. The same question is reported in the words that Allah is about to destroy them, or to punish them with a torment that is severe.

**"They replied, “Just to be free from your Lord's blame, and so perhaps they may abstain.”"** gives the answer of the preachers. They said that the command to enjoin what is right and to forbid what is wrong had been laid on them. They discharged it so that they would have a defence before their Lord, and so that they would not be taken to account for leaving it undone. The second part of their answer was hope. If the people listened, they would stop taking the fish, and the door of repentance was still open. A person who turns back to Allah is met with acceptance and with mercy.

### The three groups and their ends

The division of the town into three is reported in more than one account. One group committed the prohibition, another forbade it and kept away from it, and a third neither committed it nor spoke against it.

The end of the first two groups is stated in the verses that follow. Those who warned were saved, and those who wronged were seized. The third group is passed over in silence. The reason given for the silence is that the recompense is measured against the deed, and that group had done nothing to earn praise and nothing to bring down blame.

The silence became a question among the early teachers. Ikrimah said that Ibn 'Abbas told him that he did not know whether the people who asked the question were saved. Ikrimah went on discussing the matter with him until he convinced him that they were, and when he had done so Ibn 'Abbas gave him a garment as a gift. The point that settled the question was that those who were seized were named as the ones who did wrong, which leaves the others out of it. The group that neither fished nor spoke had not done wrong in the matter of the fish.

### In short

- The people of the town were divided into three groups, one that took the fish on the Sabbath and urged others to it, one that kept away and warned the others, and one that did neither.
- The group that did neither asked the preachers why they wasted their effort on a people headed for destruction or for a severe punishment from Allah.
- The preachers answered that the command to forbid evil had been laid on them, and that they had discharged it so as to be free of blame before their Lord. They added that the people might yet turn back and stop.
- The verses that follow name the rescue of those who warned and the seizure of those who wronged, and they say nothing of the group that stood aside, since the recompense matches the deed.
- Ikrimah reported that Ibn 'Abbas was at first unsure about the fate of that group, and that once he was convinced they were saved he gave Ikrimah a garment in return for the discussion.

165.text:
The third verse tells what came after the warning had been given. "When they ignored the warning they were given, We rescued those who used to warn against evil and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment for their rebelliousness"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they ignored the warning they were given"** states the point at which the matter was settled. The words are read as meaning that the wrongdoers left what they had been commanded to do, and that the reminder made no difference to them. The warning had been given, and the warning had been refused.

**"We rescued those who used to warn against evil"** names the first result. The group that kept away from the fish and spoke against the practice was saved from the punishment. One account of the passage says plainly that Allah saved the group which had forbidden the disobedience.

**"and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment for their rebelliousness"** names the second result. The people who took the fish and persisted in it were seized by a punishment that is called dreadful. The word used for the punishment carries the sense of a torment that is severe and painful, and the two meanings are given in the reports as near to each other. One account of the passage states that the punishment concerned was firm and that it came on those who had gone past the limits set for them.

### What the two ends show

The passage belongs with the telling of the same event in Al-Baqarah, and it sets the two groups side by side. On one side are the Israelites who had come to hate the evil so much that they spoke against it, and they were taken out of the punishment. On the other side are the people who went on in their rebellion, and they were taken by it. 

The public forbidding of evil is a declaration that the one who does it has carried out the duty laid on him. The passage shows that the duty does not depend on the answer it receives. The preachers were told that the people might yet abstain. When that hope failed, the duty they had performed still stood to their credit, and it stood between them and the punishment.

The word of the account on the point is worth putting plainly. A person is a creature into whom the Creator has put understanding and conscience. When a desire rises in such a person, the understanding weighs it and asks whether the wish should be carried out. The one who puts the bridle of God on himself is the man. The one who does whatever his lower self demands, without stopping to think and without shame afterwards, has left the rank of manhood. That is the sense in which the passage and the verse that follows it speak of the people becoming apes.

### In short

- The verse fixes the moment when the matter was settled, which is the moment the wrongdoers left the command they had been given and refused the reminder.
- The group that kept away from the fish and spoke against the practice was rescued, and one account says plainly that Allah saved the group which had forbidden the disobedience.
- The wrongdoers who took the fish and persisted in it were seized by a dreadful punishment. The word used for it carries the sense of a torment that is severe and painful.
- The forbidding of evil does not depend on the answer it receives, since the duty had been carried out whether or not the people turned back.
- The account draws the line between the man who puts the bridle of God on himself and the one who follows whatever his lower self asks of him. That line is what the next verse speaks of when it names the punishment of the town.

166.text:
The last verse of the passage gives the sentence. "But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"But when they stubbornly persisted in violation"** states what brought the sentence down. The words are read as meaning that the people refused to leave what had been forbidden to them, and that they held to their way out of pride. It was not the weakness of a single moment but a settled refusal to turn. It came after the warning had been given and the example of the preachers had been set before them.

**"We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”"** is the sentence itself. The word attached to the ape in the verse carries the sense of being humiliated, disgraced and driven away. One account of the passage gives the command in the words that they were to be monkeys, brought low. It adds that what Allah willed for them came to pass as He willed it.

The reports explain the sentence in two ways. One line takes it as a change in the outward form of the people, so that they were made into animals of that kind. The other line takes it as a change in their character rather than in their shape. It holds that their hearts and their thinking became like the hearts and thinking of apes instead of those of human beings. The reference to the second reading is given to Al-Qurtubi. It has the support of the words of the verse that describe the people as disgraced, since the disgrace of a people lies in the loss of what made them a people.

### What becoming an ape means

The verse describes a state that a man can reach in this life, and it closes the account of the Israelites who took the fish of the Sabbath. The same passage is told in Al-Baqarah, and this verse adds the sentence that the earlier telling had pointed to. A man who acts again and again against what his understanding and his conscience tell him becomes insensitive to both of them. When that has happened, nothing is left in him of the finer feelings. Whatever desire takes shape in his heart goes straight into action.

The picture given of such a person is drawn in plain terms. If someone comes within his reach, he attacks the honour and the property of that person. If he has a complaint against somebody, he sets about bringing that person down. If he has a difference with somebody, he begins to speak ill of him. If he finds a man standing in his way, he fights him at once. There is no interval in him between the wish and the doing of it, and no shame after it.

The man who keeps the command of Allah over himself is the one who keeps his rank. The one who does whatever his lower self demands has fallen from it, and the verse gives that fall its own name. The sentence came on the town after the warning, after the preachers had done their work, and after the people had refused to turn.

One report belongs to the question that the earlier verse left open. Al-Hakim carried in a hadith that Ikrima referred his opinion back to Ibn 'Abbas, and that Ibn 'Abbas was delighted with it. The opinion was that the group which stood aside was not destroyed. The passage closes with that question settled among the early teachers, and with the punishment resting on the people who took the fish.

### In short

- The sentence came when the wrongdoers refused to leave what had been forbidden to them, holding to their way out of pride after the warning had been given.
- They were told to be apes that are disgraced, and the word carries the sense of humiliation, disgrace and rejection.
- One reading of the sentence takes it as a change in the outward form of the people. Another takes it as a change in their character, so that their hearts and thinking became like those of apes rather than those of human beings, and that reading is given to Al-Qurtubi.
- A man reaches that state in this life by acting against his understanding and his conscience until he becomes insensitive to both, so that nothing stands between a wish in his heart and its doing.
- Al-Hakim carried a hadith in which Ikrima referred to Ibn 'Abbas the opinion that the group which stood aside was not destroyed, and Ibn 'Abbas was delighted with it.

167.text:
The verse tells the Prophet to recall a declaration made against the Israelites. "And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when your Lord declared that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly until the Day of Judgment." The verse then names two of the attributes of Allah. "Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"

### Phrase by phrase

**"when your Lord declared"** turns on the word the verse uses. Which one authority read as meaning that Allah made the matter known. And others read as meaning that He ordained it. Either way the sentence carries the weight of a vow that Allah took upon Himself, and what follows it states what the vow contained.

**"that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly until the Day of Judgment"** names the punishment. The people meant are the Jews, and the torment is one that carries humiliation. The reason for it is given as their disobedience, their defiance of the orders of Allah, and the tricks they used to get around the prohibitions laid on them.

**"Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** closes the verse with two of the names of Allah. The swiftness in punishing belongs to those who disobey Him and defy His law. The forgiveness and the mercy belong to those who turn back to Him. The two are put together in one sentence so that no hearer falls into despair. And the Book often joins encouragement and warning in this way so that the heart keeps both hope and fear.

### The humiliating subjection

The humiliation named in the verse has taken visible forms in the history of the people. Ibn 'Abbas explained it through the tribute that the Jews were made to pay, and the report of that explanation came through Al-'Awfi. The disgrace of being under the rule of others, and the payment of the jizyah, are counted as part of the terrible suffering the verse speaks of.

The payment itself reaches back to Musa. It is reported that he required the Jews to pay the production tax for seven years. And in another report for thirteen. And that he was the first to lay such a charge on them. After him the people fell under one power after another. They were ruled by the Greeks of the line of Kushdanin, then by the Chaldeans. And later by the Christians. And those rulers disgraced them and made them pay the tribute tax. When Islam came and the Prophet was sent, they came under his power and paid the jizyah again.

One account names the rulers who were sent against them. Allah sent Solomon against them, and after him Nebuchadnezzar, who killed some of them and took others of them captive, and who imposed the jizyah on those who remained. They went on paying that tax to the Magians until the time when the Prophet was sent, and he imposed it on them as well. Another account states the position plainly, that the people who lay the cruel torment on them are the Prophet and his community. And that the tax named in the reports is the capitation tax that was laid on them.

The sign of the declaration is plain in the present state of the people. They have been dominated and treated with disdain by others, and history has recorded one persecution after another, from the time of the Prophet Solomon down to the modern age. Their imprisonment under Nebuchadnezzar, their treatment at the hands of the kings who came after him. And their defeat at the hands of the Prophet and of Umar al-Faruq are the examples that are given. A later persecution in the second world war is given in the same record as a fresh instance of the same declaration.

The political standing some of them hold today does not change that reading. The state that was set up in Palestine has been described as a piece of the world powers, created by them for their own political aims against the Muslim ummah. And as a military base of America. Its existence depends on the aid its masters provide, and on the day that aid stops it will not be able to hold its ground for long. The people remain under the rule of others in the sense that matters.

### What comes before the end of the world

The declaration has a future side to it as well. In the last age the Jews will support the False Messiah, and the Muslims, together with Isa the son of Mary, will fight them and kill them. That event belongs to the time just before the end of this world.

The verse then gives the two names of Allah that frame the whole matter. The swiftness in punishment is not a denial of mercy, and the mercy is not a licence to go on as the people were going on. The door of return stays open for the one who repents, and the punishment stays ready for the one who does not.

### In short

- The declaration was that Allah would keep the Jews under powers that would humiliate them until the Day of Judgment. And the reason given is their disobedience, their defiance of His law and the tricks they used.
- Ibn 'Abbas explained the humiliating torment as the disgrace of subjection together with the payment of the jizyah. And Musa is reported to have been the first to lay the production tax on them.
- One account names Solomon and after him Nebuchadnezzar as the rulers sent against them. And it says the tax went on being paid until the Prophet was sent and imposed the jizyah on them himself.
- The record of the people has been one of domination and persecution. And the state set up in Palestine is described as a base of the world powers rather than a sign that the declaration has lapsed.
- The verse closes with swift punishment for those who defy Allah and forgiveness with mercy for those who turn back. And the two are joined so that the heart of a hearer holds both hope and fear.

168.text:
The next verse states the scattering of the same people. "We dispersed them through the land in groups—some were righteous, others were less so. We tested them with prosperity and adversity, so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We dispersed them through the land in groups"** tells how the people were left. The words mean that Allah divided them into communities and sects and scattered them across the earth. The Book states it elsewhere in the words that after Musa had died the Children of Israel were told to dwell in the land. And that when the final promise came near they would be brought out as a mixed crowd gathered from different nations (17:104).

**"some were righteous, others were less so"** describes the mixture inside the scattered people. Some of them were guided aright and some were not righteous. The teachers who worked through this passage of the Book include Mujahid, Qatadah and As-Suddi. And their comments belong with the generations that came after. The jinn made the same declaration about themselves, saying that among them were some that were righteous and some contrary to that. And that they were groups having different ways (72:11).

**"We tested them with prosperity and adversity"** names the two sides of the trial. The good means times of ease, plenty and comfort. And the evil means drought, poor harvest and hardship, along with fear and affliction. The two were used in turn on the same people.

**"so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺"** gives the purpose of the trial. The testing was meant to bring the people back to their Lord. And the hope named in the verse is the hope that they would turn from their wrongdoing.

### What the scattering means

The word used for the dispersal carries the sense of breaking something into pieces. Its plural is the word for a community or a party. So the verse describes a people who were broken into fragments and spread over the earth. The old unity of the people was a favour and the fragmentation is a punishment.

Being joined together as a single body is a blessing from Allah. And being broken into parts that stand apart from one another is a punishment from Him. The Muslims have held the opposite of that state for most of their history. Their own entity began in Al-Madinah in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. And it has been recognised as an organised people in the world since then. Islamic countries stand from the far east to the west, and their presence is given as the plain evidence of that fact.

### The righteous and the ones who were not

The two groups named in the verse are described in more than one way. The righteous among the people were those who followed the commands of the Torah faithfully and did not try to change or distort them. The ones described as other than that include the disbelievers and those who went on disobeying their prophets in an obstinate way. And even killed some of them.

Another reading of the two groups turns on the coming of the Prophet. The righteous are those who believed in him and followed the guidance of the Book that was revealed to him. While the others are those who held to the Torah as the word of Allah but disobeyed it or changed what it commanded. And who in that way sold their eternal salvation for petty gains of this world.

One account of the division gives the scattered people in numbers. It says that nine tribes and a half settled beyond the river al-Raml. While the second group are the remaining believers among the Children of Israel. Another reading of the same words takes the second group to be the disbelievers among them.

### Prosperity and hardship as the two tests

The good and the evil named in the verse came on the people one after another. Wealth and ease were given to them so that it might be seen whether they showed gratitude to their Lord. And when they failed that test they were made to undergo the punishments that the earlier verses of the surah describe.

Their way of thinking had gone so far that they spoke against Allah in both states. In the time of their prosperity they said that Allah was poor and that they were rich (3:181). In the time of their poverty they said that the hand of Allah was shackled (5:64). The two sayings are recorded in the Book as the fruit of the same perversion.

The trial has a wider meaning than the history of one people. Prosperity and poverty, happiness and suffering, are sent to human beings as a test. So that the faith of the created in the Creator and the love of the created for the Creator may be judged. Neither state should carry much weight with a person of understanding, since both are temporary and both come to an end.

A line of poetry is quoted on the point, that neither the happiness that came to a man brought him real benefit, nor did the sorrow make him weep. Since both came as guests to a resolute spirit.

### The warning that the trial carries for the community of the Prophet

The law at work in the verse is not confined to the Jews. The reward for carrying out a task is great when the task is great. And the punishment for failing it is equally great. The Jews had been raised to the position of bearers of the Book. And they were given promises of bounties in the world to come and extraordinary benefits in this world along with them. What they did was to go on disobeying, and to commit their irreligious acts in the name of the religion. The Book had been entrusted to them as a job. And the result of their conduct was that they were removed from that high position. And it was settled that they would go on experiencing the punishment of Allah for as long as the world lasts.

That does not mean that they were given no good days at all. The verses themselves say that there were intervals of good fortune. Those intervals were themselves a kind of curse on the people, in that they gave them the chance to grow more insolent and so become liable for more punishment.

The same law applies to the ummah that was raised to the position after the Jews were removed from it. If Muslims find that they are dominated by those who deny the truth and by those who join partners with Allah. And if their groups have become scattered, then the finding itself calls them back to Allah. Since it shows that they have drawn down His displeasure.

### The travellers and their inward reading

One account reads the scattering as an image of the people of the path who travel the earth. The verse is taken as an allusion to the travellers of the community, the exiles of the Tariqah. Who wander from region to region and from cave to cave to hide their state from people and to struggle for their religion against the harm others do them.

The saying of Al-Mustafa is quoted for that reading. He said that a time would come when those who are religious would not stay safe unless they kept away from people. And that they would be seen like travellers fleeing from people, sometimes in the mountains and sometimes in the desert. The description given of them is that they rush and run and wail across the world, in mountain monasteries and in desert caves, entirely effaced in the ocean of thought. And that they recite on behalf of everyone that they have no home and no possessions.

Two events from the Book are given as witnesses to that reading. The first is the story of the Companions of the Cave. And the second is the stay of the Prophet and of Abu Bakr in the cave. The Book says of that second event that the two were in the cave. And that the Prophet told his companion not to grieve. Since Allah was with them (9:40). Abu Bakr is given the title of the second of the two in that event. And the story is quoted as proof that a believer may be driven into a cave and still be under the care of his Lord.

Another meaning is given for their travelling as well, which is that they were yearning. These people spend most of their days without settledness and without ease. And the hope that keeps them moving is that they may reach some place where they see the mark of the friend, or meet someone who can tell them about the friend.

The prayer of one of the men of the path is quoted on the point, that the homeland of the exiles of Allah is exile and that the question is when that business will end. He asks how the man being tested by his Lord can be thought worthy of relief. And how the man whose homeland is exile can ever reach home. He says that the one who yearns is slain by friendship. And that the shroud of those slain by friendship is the vision of the Beloved.

That reading takes the testing of the verse in an inward sense. The people described are tested with pleasure and with disappointment. And they are neither deceived by the pleasure nor turned away from their Lord by the disappointment. In front of them stands a concern greater than either their pleasure or their disappointment. They are on loan among people, and they are strangers among themselves. Their hearts are joined to their Patron. And with the tongue of poverty and the attribute of brokenness they say that they have come to the Threshold as servants. And that if He wills He may exalt them and if He wills He may lay them low.

### The descent of Isa and the gathering in Palestine

The persecution of the people has gone on without a break. History has recorded that they were laid low by one people after another from the time of Sulayman to the present age. And their treatment by the rulers of later times has followed the same line.

The present state of Palestine raises a question, and the answer given to it rests on the prophecies. The people must come together in one place in the last age. The Prophet ﷺ informed the community that Isa would come down from the heavens before the end of the world, that all the Christians would enter Islam. And that he would fight the Jews and put them to death. The land named for his descent is Syria, and he will make war on the Jews from there.

The people who are due to answer for their conduct are not brought in by police or by any other agency. They are driven to the place of their death by the causes that the will of Allah sets in motion. The gathering of the Jews in Palestine is put in that light. Since it saves Isa the trouble of seeking them out in different parts of the world.

Their present political power is called a delusion that takes in only those who do not follow the ways of the world. The so called state of Israel has been described as a common camp ground of the big powers such as America, Russia and England. It depends on the aid of its masters for its existence, and it has to serve their aims. The people who live under that arrangement are still in real servitude and are deprived of free rule in the true sense of the words.

### In short

- The people were broken into communities and scattered over the earth. And the Book states the same scattering in the words that after Musa they were told to dwell in the land and would later be brought out as a mixed crowd from different nations (17:104). While the jinn said of themselves that among them were the righteous and those contrary to them (72:11).
- Some of the people were righteous and some were otherwise. And the scattering is itself read as a punishment. Since being joined in one body is a blessing of Allah and being broken into parts is a sign of His displeasure. As the Muslims knew from their own entity that began in Al-Madinah.
- The trial came through prosperity and through hardship. And the people spoke against Allah in both states, saying in their wealth that Allah was poor and they were rich (3:181). And saying in their poverty that the hand of Allah was shackled (5:64).
- One inward reading takes the scattering as the state of the travellers of the Tariqah, the exiles who wander to hide their state. And the saying of Al-Mustafa and the stay of the Prophet with Abu Bakr in the cave are quoted for it (9:40).
- The record of the people runs from the time of Sulayman through Nebuchadnezzar and later persecutions to the defeat at the hands of the Prophet and of Umar al-Faruq. And their rule in Palestine is described as a base of the big powers rather than a settled sovereignty.

169.text:
The verse turns to the generations that followed. "Then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture." It then states their conduct with the Book. "They indulged in unlawful gains, claiming, “We will be forgiven ˹after all˺.” And if similar gain came their way, they would seize it." The covenant is put as a question. "Was a covenant not taken from them in the Scripture that they would not say anything about Allah except the truth? And they were already well-versed in its teachings." The verse closes with the better home and with a question to the heedless. "But the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture."** After the generation that held both righteous and unrighteous people, another generation came that had no goodness in it. They inherited the Tawrah from their forefathers and they studied it, and they were entrusted with it by the command of Allah to them.

**"They indulged in unlawful gains, claiming, “We will be forgiven ˹after all˺.”"** describes how the Book was handled. The word used for the gains is the word for something that is bought and sold. And the choice of that word points to how temporary everything owned in this world is. Mujahid said that the people would consume anything available to them in this life, whether it was lawful or unlawful, and that they still wished for forgiveness. Qatadah called them an evil generation. And said that they inherited the Book after their prophets and messengers had gone. Since they had been entrusted with that job by the command of Allah. Their claim took the form that the sins they committed at night would be forgiven during the day. And that the sins they committed in the day would be forgiven at night.

**"And if similar gain came their way, they would seize it."** shows the claim to be empty. The people hoped for forgiveness while committing the same offence again and going on in it. In the Torah there is no promise of forgiveness for persistence in sin, and the verse puts the two things side by side so that the contradiction is plain.

**"Was a covenant not taken from them in the Scripture that they would not say anything about Allah except the truth? And they were already well-versed in its teachings."** states the covenant. A pledge was taken from the people of the Scripture. And its content was that the Book should be made known and clear to mankind and should not be hidden away. The Book records that they threw that pledge behind their backs and bought with it some miserable gain (3:187). The verse adds that their failure was not the failure of the ignorant. They had studied what was in the Book and they knew it, which made their disobedience the greater.

**"But the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand"** closes the verse with encouragement and with a rebuke. What Allah has kept for those who avoid the prohibitions and abandon their lusts and become active in obedience to their Lord is better than any gain of this world. The question asks whether the people who preferred this life to what is with Allah have any sense at all to stop them from their foolish and extravagant ways.

### The words the verse uses

Several words in the passage carry meanings that sharpen it. The word for a successor is used in the form that carries the sense of a deputy or a person trusted with another's work in his absence. And the form used in the verse denotes such a deputy marked by wickedness. As opposed to the good practice of his elders. The word for inheritance is a derivative of the word for the state of being an heir. And the word for the gains carries the sense of something that is bought with money.

The word for nearness lies behind one of the terms in the passage as well, and the feminine form of the same word is used. The same form may also be taken from the root that signifies disgrace, and in that case the word refers to something disgraced.

The final question in the verse has a second reading that turns on the person addressed. It may be read as a question to the people who are absent from the discussion, asking whether they do not understand. And it may be read as a question put to the hearers themselves, asking them whether they do not understand that the better thing should be preferred to the home of this world. The word carrying the question is qilun in one report of the reading, and it is the same word that carries the sense of understanding.

### The generations and what they did with the Book

The record of the generations that inherited the Book is given in a number of reports. Another passage of the Book speaks of the same thing in the words that a posterity has succeeded them who neglected the prayer (19:59).

The clearest picture of their conduct comes through the judges. As-Suddi said that every time the Children of Israel appointed a judge over them, that judge took bribes. The best among the people held a counsel and took covenants from one another that none of them would take a bribe. When one of the judges did take a bribe in return for a judgement. And he was asked what was the matter with him, he answered that he would be forgiven. The rest of his people would then admonish him for what he had done. When that man died or was replaced, the one who came after him took bribes as well. The verse then says of those who admonished that if a chance to loot the world came their way, they would take it.

Another report explains the claim in a plainer way. Ibn 'Abbas said of the words that the people claimed Allah would forgive the sins they kept on committing without turning away from them.

One account gives the wrongdoing in another form. The people accepted the passing goods of this world as a price for distorting the Scripture of Allah. And they gave judgements that were not according to what had been revealed in it. They read the Book but did not act on what was in it, and they convinced themselves that Allah would forgive them their sins. Their failure to act was not caused by ignorance of what was written, since they had studied it and knew it, and so their disobedience was the greater.

One reading of the passage states the offence as the concealment of a particular thing. The generations inherited the Scripture and concealed the traits and description of the Prophet that were in it. And they took bribes and other unlawful goods of this world in exchange for that concealment. The same account says that they studied what was in the Book of the lawful and the unlawful, but did not act on it.

Verse 169 places the whole matter inside the story of the generations, and the account of them is not confined to their dealings with money. One reading describes how the people went on reading the Book while giving it a colour of their own devising through interpretations they made up, until the religion appeared to support the way of life they had chosen. The scene at the beginning of that story is the time of Musa, when the commands were given to the people at the foot of the hill. Their insensitiveness grew to the point where they took satisfaction in declaring that they were a pious community, the progeny of prophets. And that Allah would forgive them for the sake of His favourite servants.

### The covenant and the claim of forgiveness

The covenant named in the verse was a pledge not to say anything about Allah except the truth. It was taken from the people when the Book was given to them. And its content included the duty of making the Book known and clear to mankind and not hiding it. Their conduct went against that pledge at the point that mattered most, since they ascribed to the Book a promise of forgiveness for the man who persists in sin.

The teaching of the passage on forgiveness is plain. The forgiveness of Allah is always there for the one who sees his error, turns to his Lord in repentance, shows remorse for what he has done. And makes a firm promise not to repeat the mistake. The one who goes on in his sins and claims forgiveness at the same time has deceived himself. The Book holds no promise of the kind he relies on. And the home of the world to come is the better home for the man who is mindful of Allah.

### In short

- The generations that came after were a people with no goodness in them. And they inherited the Tawrah and studied it while consuming whatever gains came their way, lawful or unlawful alike. Mujahid and Qatadah are named among the teachers who explained their conduct.
- Their claim was that what they did at night would be forgiven by day and what they did by day would be forgiven at night. And the verse shows the claim to be empty. Since they seized the same kind of gain whenever it came to them again.
- The covenant taken from those who were given the Scripture was that they would say nothing about Allah except the truth and would not hide it. And the Book records that they threw it behind their backs and bought with it a miserable gain (3:187).
- Their wrongdoing was done in full knowledge. Since they had studied the Book. And the reports describe judges who took bribes, answered that they would be forgiven. And were replaced by men who did the same.
- The final question has a second reading and the word behind it is qilun. And the verse closes with the statement that the Home of the Hereafter is better for the mindful. Since forgiveness belongs to the man who repents and not to the man who persists.

170.text:
The verse turns from the generations who failed the Book to the people who held to it. "As for those who firmly abide by the Scripture and establish prayer—surely We never discount the reward of those acting righteously"

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who firmly abide by the Scripture"** speaks of the people among them who were true to what had been given to them. The term is rendered in the reading as those who hold fast to the Book. And the construction of the sentence in the original is the one that opens with the word alladhina, the word for those who. The holding fast spoken of is not the mere keeping of a book on a shelf. It means taking hold of its commands, carrying out what it orders and keeping away from what it forbids.

**"and establish prayer"** singles out the prayer from among the many commands of the Book. The word used is salah. And the establishing of it means performing it as it should be performed and at the times appointed for it. Out of the many doctrines that the Torah carried, the prayer is the one the verse names. Because it is the most significant and the most purposeful of the acts enjoined by Allah. And the most basic way of expressing faith in Him and obedience to Him.

**"surely We never discount the reward of those acting righteously"** is the assurance given to such people. The teachers who worked through the earlier part of the passage, among them Mujahid and Qatadah, explained that the Book was handed to a people as a trust. And this verse is the answer to the ones who kept it. The word used for the act is the one that carries the sense of setting things right. And the promise is that Allah does not let the wages of the reformers go to waste. The sentence is the predicate of the opening construction. And the passage replaces the ordinary pronoun with the plain noun for reformers so that the description is stated in full.

### What the Book meant and who the people were

The Book named in the verse is most probably the Torah. Since the passage before it dealt with the covenant taken over the Torah by the religious leaders of the Israelites and with their distortion of it. Another reading takes it as covering all the Books sent down by Allah, including the Torah, the Injil and the Book given to the Prophet ﷺ. The promise attaches to whoever holds fast to what he was given.

The holding fast has a condition attached to it that is worth stating plainly. Merely keeping the Book of Allah and treating it with respect, without following what it commands, does not fulfil the object for which it was revealed. That is why the verse uses the word for holding fast rather than the word for taking or reading. Holding fast to the Book requires following all of its injunctions and commands.

The people meant by the description are named in one account as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. Who accepted the Prophet ﷺ and the Book that came with him while holding to the truth of what had been revealed before. One account of the passage says of them that they are the people who act on the Scripture. They say of what is lawful that it is lawful. And of what is unlawful that it is unlawful. And they make plain the traits and description of the Prophet that are carried in their books.

### The prayer as the pillar

The place given to the prayer in this verse has been drawn out in the teaching of the community. The Prophet ﷺ called the prayer the pillar of the religion, and the whole edifice of faith rests on it. The one who has set that pillar up properly has built the structure of his faith on a stronghold. The one who is not regular in the prayer is of no account with Allah, even if he is seen reciting the name of Allah at all times. And even if unusual visions come to him and extraordinary acts are seen from him.

The prayer also trains a person for the rest of the worship. Offering it regularly makes a man capable of being regular in the other acts of worship more willingly, and with more ease.

There is a further sign attached to holding fast to the Word of God and to saying the prayer sincerely. The sign is that the person has become a maintainer of peace and harmony among people. Communion with the Book of God and with His worship is what sets a man against the one who disturbs the peace.

### In short

- The verse praises those among the people of the Book who hold fast to the Scripture. And the holding fast means carrying out its commands and keeping away from what it forbids rather than merely keeping the book and respecting it.
- Out of all the doctrines of the Book, the prayer is the one named. And the Prophet ﷺ called the prayer the pillar of the religion. So that the man who sets it up properly has built the whole structure of his faith.
- The Book named in the verse is most probably the Torah and may cover every Book sent down by Allah, including the Injil. And the promise attaches to whoever holds fast to what he was given.
- The people meant by the description are named in one account as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. Who declared the lawful to be lawful and the unlawful to be unlawful and made plain the description of the Prophet in their books.
- The assurance is that Allah never lets the wages of the reformers go to waste. And the sign of holding fast to the Book and saying the prayer sincerely is that a person becomes a maintainer of peace among people.

171.text:
The last verse of the passage returns to the mountain. "And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud and they thought it would fall on them." The command that came with it follows. "˹We said,˺ “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"when We raised the mountain over them"** turns on a word that carries the sense of drawing something up or lifting it. Ibn 'Abbas took the word to signify raising the mountain high. The same event is told in Al-Baqarah. And the Book states it elsewhere in the words that the mountain was raised over the people as part of their covenant (4:154).

**"as if it were a cloud"** describes what the people saw. The word used for the covering means a sunshade or a canopy, and the mountain was held over the heads of the people in that shape.

**"and they thought it would fall on them"** gives the effect on the people. The sense of the words is that they knew and were certain it was going to come down on them. The certainty came from the threat made to them, that the mountain would fall if they refused to accept the rulings that the Torah carried.

**"Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺."** is the command given under the mountain. The words ask for serious and diligent action on what was revealed. And the observing of its teachings means keeping in mind what it carries of reward and punishment and its commands and prohibitions, together with acting on what it declares lawful and unlawful. So that the people might guard themselves against the wrath of Allah.

### The raising of the mountain

The reports of the event agree that the mountain was lifted over the heads of the people. Ibn 'Abbas said of the words that the mountain was raised up, and the statement of the Book about the covenant supports that reading (4:154). Another report from Ibn 'Abbas through Sa'id bin Jubayr says that the angels raised the mount over their heads.

The account that gives the setting came through Al-Qasim bin Abi Ayyub, who reported it from Sa'id bin Jubayr, who had it from Ibn 'Abbas. The report says that Musa later set out with the people for the Sacred Land. He took the Tablets along with him once his anger had subsided. And he commanded the people to hold to the orders that Allah had given him to deliver to them. Those orders fell heavily on the people. And they were unwilling to carry them out until Allah raised the mountain over them in the shape of a canopy. Which happened when the angels lifted it above their heads. An-Nasa'i collected that report. The narrator of it in the chain was Ayyub.

### The promise that was taken under the mountain

The incident explains why the pledge taken at the mountain carried such weight. The people had been given commands they found hard, and they showed their unwillingness to obey them. When the mount was held over their heads they fell down in prostration out of fear and gave their promise to obey the law of Musa.

The report of the town gives its size. The area of the settlement is said to have been three square miles, and the Archangel Gabriel was commanded to raise the Mount of Sinai over it.

The passage lays down a lesson about the seriousness of a pledge. The conditions were made such that the people felt the mountain was about to fall on them. And the purpose was to impress on them that giving a pledge to God is a very serious matter. If they did not fulfil the conditions of the pledge, they were to remember that the other party to it was the majestic Being who could cause the mount to fall on them by His will.

The events that followed are recorded in the same account. The people promised their obedience at the mountain, and the later record of them shows them deviating from the law again and again.

### The question of compulsion in faith

The incident raises a question, since the Book declares elsewhere that there is no compulsion in the religion (2:256). The answer rests on the difference between the two situations. None of the disbelievers was ever forced to accept the faith, and no one is allowed to use force for that purpose. The people under the mountain were not in that position. They had already entered the covenant of faith by their own free will, and they had believed in Allah and in His prophet. When they later moved away from the commands of Allah simply to escape the commitments they had taken on, they were held to those commitments.

The ruling that follows from the incident is that a person who has taken the covenant is liable to the punishments that the law prescribes for the duties he abandons. The compulsion in the story was not a compulsion to believe. It was the holding of a people to a pledge they had already made freely.

### In short

- The mountain was raised over the heads of the Israelites in the shape of a canopy. And they were certain that it would fall on them. And the Book states the same event in the words about the covenant made at the mountain (4:154).
- Ibn 'Abbas read the word of the verse as a raising up. And Sa'id bin Jubayr reported the same from him with the detail that the angels lifted the mount over the heads of the people.
- The report that came through Al-Qasim bin Abi Ayyub and was collected by An-Nasa'i tells how Musa brought the Tablets from Sinai after his anger had cooled. And how the commands fell heavily on the people until the mountain was raised.
- The settlement under the mountain was three square miles across, and the account says the Archangel Gabriel was commanded to raise the Mount of Sinai over it.
- The command that came with the raising was to hold firmly to the Scripture and to observe its teachings, so that the people might become mindful of their Lord.
- The answer to the question about compulsion is that no one is forced to accept the faith. While those who freely take the covenant and then desert it are held to what they promised.

172.text:
The verse takes the hearer back to the beginning. "And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify regarding themselves." The question and the answer follow. "˹Allah asked,˺ “Am I not your Lord?” They replied, “Yes, You are! We testify.”" The verse closes with the reason for the testimony. "˹He cautioned,˺ “Now you have no right to say on Judgment Day, ‘We were not aware of this.’""

### Phrase by phrase

**"when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants"** describes the bringing out of every human being from the loins of his ancestors. One generation came out of the loins of the next, and the whole line of them came out of the loins of Adam. They came offspring after offspring, in the way that human beings multiply. The reading says that they appeared like small ants in the valley of Na'man on the day of Arafah, because of how many they were.

**"and had them testify regarding themselves"** is the testimony the verse is built on. Their witness against themselves was that Allah is their Lord. He is their King, and no deity is worthy of worship except Him. Allah set up proofs of His Lordship before them and gave them the faculty of reason, and then brought the acknowledgment out of their own mouths. Allah created them on the fitrah. Which is the way He built them. As the Holy Qur'an says in the words that the face should be set towards the religion as a man of pure faith. And that this is the fitrah of Allah with which He created mankind. And that there is to be no change in the creation of Allah (30:30).

**"Am I not your Lord?" They replied, "Yes, You are! We testify."** is the exchange itself. One account adds what was said to the angels at that moment, that they were to be witnesses over the people and that the people were to be witnesses over one another.

**"Now you have no right to say on Judgment Day, 'We were not aware of this.'"** gives the purpose of the whole event. The pledge lit the lamp of faith in the hearts of the people, so that a little reflection would be enough for them to recognise their Lord. On that day the plea of ignorance will not help them, since the testimony was taken from them before they were sent into the world.

### What the testimony means

The testimony was taken in two ways at once. It was taken in words, and it was taken by the state the people were made in. The Book shows both kinds elsewhere. The words of testimony are used in the passage where the people say that they bear witness against themselves (6:130). Testimony is also given by a man's own condition, as in the words about those who join partners with Allah. The verse says that it is not for them to maintain the mosques of Allah, since their own disbelief is a testimony against them (9:17). That verse means that their disbelief testifies against them, rather than that they stand and speak the words. Another verse of the same kind says of man that he is a witness to it by his own deeds (100:7).

Asking works in the same two ways. It is sometimes put in words and sometimes in the situation a person is placed in. The Book says that Allah gave the people of all that they asked for (14:34). And that covers the requests a man makes in speech and the needs that are met without a word being spoken.

### The reports of the event

What the verses describe is known as the covenant of Alust. It is the great covenant that the Creator made with all His created beings before they took the form in which they exist.

The reports that follow the event are of two kinds. One kind describes the bringing out of the descendants from Adam himself. The other describes the bringing out of the descendants from the loins of the children of Adam, which is what the verse says. There is no conflict between the two. The direct children of Adam came out of the back of Adam, and the people who came after them came out of the backs of his descendants.

The report of the first kind came through Muslim bin Yasar. Some people asked Umar al-Faruq about the meaning of the verse. And he said that the same question had been put to the Prophet ﷺ and that he had heard the answer. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah first created Adam, then placed His hand on his back and drew out all the righteous among his descendants who were to come into being. Of them He said that they were created for Paradise, and that they would act righteously as those who deserve Paradise act. The second hand was laid on the back of Adam again. Out came all the wicked among his descendants who were yet to come into being. Of them He said that they were created for the Fire, and that they would act wickedly as those who are led to the Fire act.

A man among the companions asked the Prophet ﷺ why people were still asked to do good deeds when the matter had already been settled. The Prophet ﷺ answered that the one created for Paradise begins to do the deeds that make a man worthy of Paradise and dies in that state. While the one created for the Fire goes into the acts that make him liable for the Fire and dies doing the deeds that lead him there. The lesson drawn from the answer is that a man who does not know which group he belongs to should put all his effort into the deeds that are the mark of the people of Paradise. And should hope to be counted among them.

The report was carried by Malik, by Abu Dawud, by Tirmidhi and by Imam Ahmad. The same event is given in another form in the Two Sahihs. Abu Hurairah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that every child is born on the fitrah. And that it is his parents who make him a Jew, a Christian or a Zoroastrian. The Prophet ﷺ compared the matter to animals born with whole bodies, and asked whether any of them is seen with a nose cut off at birth.

Muslim recorded that Iyad bin 'Himar said that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah said He had created His servants as people of the oneness. And that the devils had come to them and turned them from their religion and made unlawful what He had made lawful.

The Tradition that Imam Ahmad reported adds a detail about colour, and the companion named at the head of its chain is Abu al-Darda. The people who appeared first were fair, and those who appeared on the second occasion were black. The companion Abu Hurairah reported the same description through Tirmidhi, and his report adds one more detail. Every child of Adam who was to come into the world, to the last of them, carried a kind of brilliance on his forehead.

The colour and the brilliance point to something in the report that is worth noticing. A spirit has no colour, so the people who came out at that moment were not spirits alone. They had a fine kind of body given to them for the occasion. Since the nourishing that the verse speaks of has to do with a body that passes from one state to another. Spirits do not need that kind of care, since they stay as they were created.

### The report about Adam and Dawud

Another report belongs to the same event. At-Tirmidhi recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah created Adam, He wiped Adam's back and every person He would create from him until the Day of Resurrection fell out of it. A glimmering light was placed between the eyes of each of them, and they were then shown to Adam. Adam asked who they were, and Allah said that they were his offspring. Adam saw a man among them whose light he liked and asked who he was. Allah told him that the man belonged to the later generations of his offspring, and that his name was Dawud. Adam asked how long the man would live, and Allah said sixty years. Adam said that he would give forty years of his own life to the man. When the end of Adam's life came and the angel of death came to take his soul, Adam said that he still had forty years left. He was told that he had given them to his son Dawud. Adam denied it, and his offspring followed him in the denial. Forgetting came over Adam, and it came over his offspring with him. A mistake was made by Adam, and his offspring followed him into it.

At-Tirmidhi said of that report that it is hasan and sound, and that it came through various chains of narration. The name at the head of those chains is Abu Hurayrah, and the report goes back to the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Hakim also recorded it in his Mustadrak, and he said that it is sound according to the criteria of Muslim, although the two did not record it.

Other reports of the same family add that Allah separated the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire at that moment. The report of Anas bin Malik, recorded by Imam Ahmad, has the Prophet ﷺ saying that a man from the people of the Fire will be asked on the Day of Resurrection whether he would pay the whole of what is on the earth as a ransom if he owned it. He will say that he would. Allah will say that He asked him for something far less than that while he was still in the loins of Adam. Which was that he should not join anything with Him in worship. The man insisted on joining others with Him. That report is recorded in the Two Sahihs.

### Why the covenant was taken

The record that Allah keeps is complete without any help from His creatures. His knowledge takes in everything, including the hidden thoughts and intentions of His servants, with no possibility of a wrong judgement. His grace and His perfect justice, however, chose that no one should be punished without the evidence of his own deeds being put before him, in a way that leaves the sinner no choice but to acknowledge what he did.

So He appointed angels to record every act a person does. The Book says that not a word does a man utter but there is a watcher by him ready to record it (50:18). The note attached to that verse in one of the studies of al-Qur'an al-Karim, volume 4, page 969, adds a saying of Ibn 'Abbas. His words are that the guardian angels of a mortal record all that he does, whether the deed is good or evil. The Book adds in another place that everything small and great is written down (54:53). On the Day of Judgement the Balance will be set to weigh the good and the bad deeds of all people. The ones whose good deeds weigh heavy will be given salvation, and the ones whose bad deeds weigh heavier will be punished.

The court of the Day of Judgement will also call witnesses. Some of the wrongdoers will deny what the witnesses say against them. Then their own organs will be given the power to speak and will bear witness to what the man did. The places where the deeds were done will also come forward as witnesses, until the man finds no way to deny the testimony and confesses his evil deeds. The Book refers to it in the words that they will confess their sins (67:11).

None of this was left to law and regulations alone. Allah out of His kindness gave His servants complete guidance through His prophets and His Books, so that they might be saved from eternal punishment. The likeness used for it is the care of kind parents. Who make it necessary for their children to go to school every morning and also make sure that the children have what they need before the time comes. Allah, who is free of any likeness to His creatures, is kinder to His servants than parents are to their children. He did not only set out the laws but made them a source of real guidance. And along with the commands He taught the people how to carry them out with ease and readiness.

Beyond the messengers and the Books, He set a great number of His angels to help people and guide them to the right path. He also placed clear signs of His power and His wisdom all around them. So that their own observation and understanding would be enough to tell right from wrong and to remind them of their Creator. The Book says that on the earth there are signs for those who have firm faith. And that there are signs in their own selves as well. And then asks whether they do not see (51:20-21). The external signs are all around, in the heavens and the earth, the oceans, the mountains, the plants and the trees, and the fruits of different colours and tastes. The internal signs are in the make of a human being, in the way people are reproduced, in their thoughts, their intentions and their feelings of happiness and sorrow. A little reflection on either kind leads a person to the Creator and makes him grateful to Him.

### The pledges taken at different times

Another arrangement made by Allah for the guidance of people was to bring them into covenants with Him through His prophets. The Book refers to a number of such covenants, made with different people in different circumstances. The prophets themselves were made to promise that they would convey the message of Allah to their people regardless of the difficulties and the reproach they met. That group of prophets kept the promise as faithfully as was possible and gave up all they had in the work.

The people of every prophet were made to promise that they would obey their prophet, and in some special cases they were bound to spend their energy on particular commands. Some of them kept the promise and others did not.

The most significant of those covenants is the one in which all the prophets were made to enter regarding the last Prophet. They were bound to follow him and to help him whenever an occasion for it came. The Book mentions that covenant in the words that Allah made the prophets take a pledge about the messenger who would come to confirm what they had. And that they were to believe in him and help him (3:81). One consequence drawn from that pledge is that the followers of the earlier prophets are bound by it. So that they are to believe in the last Prophet, follow him and support him in what he set out to do.

The practice of taking a pledge from those who follow a teacher comes out of this same arrangement. A pledge of this kind is called a bay'ah. And it is the way the prophets, their companions and the spiritual leaders took the commitment of those who came to them. One such pledge is mentioned in the Book, in the words that Allah was well pleased with the believers when they pledged their allegiance under the tree (48:18). That event is known as the pledge of al-Rizwan. The Prophet ﷺ took a pledge of that kind from his companions on many occasions. The pledge of al-'Aqabah was a well known covenant made before the migration with the helpers of Al-Madinah.

The customary way of the Sufis. Who take a pledge from those who follow them, is a covenant taken for practising the commands of Allah regularly and for strengthening belief in Him by frequent remembrance of their Lord. Swearing allegiance to a teacher carries many advantages and draws barakah from Allah. A person who has given his pledge to a spiritual master feels more willing and more inclined to carry out his religious obligations. And he is more careful in seeking the pleasure of Allah.

The same discussion clears away a false notion that is common among people of little knowledge. Putting one's hand into the hand of a teacher or a spiritual leader is not by itself enough for salvation in the world to come. The pledge is a promise to follow the practical guidance the teacher gives. Nothing but the placing of a hand in a hand is of no use at all. And a person who stops there has turned away from the pledge he made. Which may bring down the displeasure of Allah on him.

### What the word for the descendants carries

The verse uses the word for the children of Adam in the phrase that opens the covenant. According to Imam Raghib al-Isfahani, that word is derived from the root that signifies creating. The Book uses the word in a number of places with that sense.

The word therefore covers all created human beings, since the covenant of eternity took in all the descendants of Adam. Nobody who was to come into the world until the end of time stood outside it.

### The questions the event raises

The discussion of the covenant brings up two questions. The first is the time and the place of the event. The second is how the children of Adam could have had the knowledge and the reason to acknowledge Allah as their Lord and Nourisher, when the experience of being nourished comes only after a person has entered the world.

The first question is answered in a report from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, carried through sound sources by Imam Ahmad and Nasa'i. His report places the event at the moment Adam was sent down from the heavens to the earth. The place was the valley of Nauman, which is known as the plain of Arafat near Makkah.

The second question has a plain answer. Allah has the power to do whatever He wills. The same power that made all human beings appear in the size of an ant could more easily give them the knowledge and the reason they needed to recognise the Lord who nourishes them. They appeared with body and soul together in a small size, and with every physical function that a complete human being needs. Reason and understanding are among the most important of those functions, so they were included.

The size of the people at that moment was explained in the report of the companion Abu al-Darda. Who said that they did not appear with their usual size. And that they appeared in the size of a small ant. The matter is not strange even by the measure of the age of scientific knowledge. Science has established that a system like our solar system works in and around the nucleus of an atom. Books of hundreds of pages can be reduced to a small dot by micro filming. It should be no surprise, then, that Allah the All-Powerful reduced the people to the size of an ant on that occasion.

### The question of a covenant that is not remembered

One question is left open by the reports. What value can be attached to a covenant taken before the creation of human beings, when the people who entered it do not remember it after they come into the world?

The first thing to note in the answer is that some individuals have remembered the occasion. The spiritual leader Dhul Nun al-Misri said that he remembered the covenant as clearly as he was hearing it at that moment. Some of the elders reported that they remembered the people who had stood near them at the time. Such cases are rare, and they do not answer the question by themselves.

The real answer is that many acts are effective by their own nature, without anyone remembering them or understanding them. Their effect is imprinted on a person as a matter of course.

The practice of saying the adhan in the right ear of a new born child and the iqamah in his left ear is a plain example of an act of that kind. The adhan is the call to the salah. And it is a bold declaration that Allah is one, that He has no partners. And that He is the greatest of all. The iqamah is the same declaration with the addition that the prayer has been set ready for the people to join. The baby does not understand the meaning of the call and does not remember it when he becomes an adult. The wisdom behind the practice is to revive the pledge he took with Allah. And to plant the seed of faith in his heart by repeating the covenant in his ears. The effect of the act is plain in every Muslim person, even one who is not a good Muslim in practice. He takes pride in calling himself a Muslim and he dislikes being cut off from that identity.

The command to recite the Book even to people who do not know Arabic belongs to the same order. Their hearts are enlightened by the effect of the words, and their faith in Allah is renewed by them.

The wisdom behind the covenant is of the same kind. It sowed the seed of faith in the heart of every human being. That seed takes its nourishment from the soil of the human heart whether or not a person is aware of it. The fruit of the seed shows itself in love and respect for God, and that love and respect is part of human nature. The expression of that love may take unjust forms, such as the worship of false gods, of idols, or of created beings. Whether that worship is rightly directed or wrongly directed, it carries the same love and respect for the Creator within it. The billions of people who live in the world have that respect and love for Allah given to them. And they express it through their worship as their knowledge or their ignorance directs them. Nothing needs to be said about the few who have worn down their natural understanding by following the things of this world until they forgot the pledge they made with Allah.

The Prophet ﷺ stated the matter in a report already quoted, that every child is born on the fitrah and that his parents turn him to their religion. Another report of the Prophet ﷺ says that Allah said He created His servants as people of pure faith, and that they were then led astray by the influence of Satan.

### The two excuses the verse closes off

The words that the hearers are not to say on the Day of Judgement that they were not aware of the matter closes off one excuse. The pledge had lit the lamp of faith in the hearts of the people, and a little reflection was enough to recognise the Lord. The plea of ignorance will not avail on that day.

The next verse closes off a second excuse, which is the plea that the people were only following their forefathers.

### The inward reading of the covenant

One reading takes the event in the tongue of the inner reality and finds in it an allusion to the state of the friends of Allah. It speaks of where their states begin. The compact of friendship was bound with them on the earliest of all days, in the era of the Beginningless. At that hour the Real was present, and the reality was there.

The prayer of longing that goes with that reading is quoted in its own words. How blessed were Layla and the nights when those who loved met with Layla. What a fine day was the day the foundation of friendship was laid. What an exalted time was the time the compact of friendship was made. Desire was awakened in some of them on the first day, and such desire is never forgotten. Those who yearned at the hour of union with the Friend know the crown of life, and they know the direction their days are to take.

The command that goes with the reading is the word of Allah to His Prophet to remind the people of the days of God (14:5). The servants of Allah had forgotten His covenant and busied themselves with other things. The reminder was to take them back to the hour their pure spirits bound themselves in friendship with Him. While their yearning eyes were anointed with the collyrium of the question, Am I not your Lord.

The scene drawn for that day is the assembly of intimacy. Where the spirits and the very persons of the friends drank the wine of passion for their Lord from the cup of love. The near angels of the Higher Plenum are described as saying that these are a people of high aspiration. And that they themselves had never tasted that wine and had not found even its scent. The roaring and the shouting of those beggars rose to Capella, and the Book gives their cry in the words that ask whether there is any more (50:30).

The poetry of that longing is quoted with the reading. The lines say that the lips of the speaker will not stay dry from that wine, which his religion does not forbid, until he returns to nonexistence. The same passage recalls the day when the master of the children of Adam said of a mountain that it loved him and that he loved it.

That reading takes the verse as a description of a bond that a person carries in his deepest self. And it stands beside the plain meaning. Which is that the descendants of Adam were brought out and made to testify to the Lordship of their Creator.

### In short

- The verse describes the bringing out of every descendant of Adam from the loins of his ancestors. And the testimony taken from them that Allah is their Lord and King, with no deity worthy of worship except Him. And that testimony is the first binding of the people to the oneness of Allah.
- They were created on the fitrah. And the Prophet ﷺ said that every child is born on the fitrah and that his parents turn him to their own religion. While another report has Allah saying that He created His servants as people of the oneness and that the devils turned them away.
- The testimony was taken in words and by the state the people were made in. As the Book shows in the words that they bear witness against themselves (6:130), in the words about those who join partners with Allah (9:17). And in the words that a man is a witness to his own conduct (100:7).
- The reports tell of the drawing out of the righteous and the wicked, of the appearance of the people in the size of an ant, of the fair colour and the black colour named in the Tradition of Abu al-Darda, of the brilliance on the foreheads in the report of Tirmidhi. And of the forty years Adam gave to his son Dawud and then denied.
- The event belongs with the other pledges Allah took through His prophets, among them the covenant that all the prophets would follow and help the last Prophet (3:81) and the pledge of al-Rizwan under the tree (48:18). And the inward reading takes the covenant as the bond of friendship placed in the spirits of the friends of Allah.

173.text:
The verse closes off the second excuse. "Nor say, 'It was our forefathers who had associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺ and we, as their descendants, followed in their footsteps." The question the people would put is stated in the same verse. "Will you then destroy us for the falsehood they invented?'""

### Phrase by phrase

**"Nor say, 'It was our forefathers who had associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺ and we, as their descendants, followed in their footsteps.'"** sets out the plea. The people would say that their fathers were the ones who broke the pledge and took partners with Allah. And that they themselves were only their descendants, small and weak after them. Who followed their example.

**"Will you then destroy us for the falsehood they invented?"** is the question that goes with the plea. The people would ask whether they were to be punished for what the idolaters among their forefathers did. And whether their own actions were to be counted for nothing because of the falsehood of others.

### Why the plea cannot stand

The verse stops the people from taking refuge in the claim that they were unaware of the truth. The plea that they were the descendants of their fathers and only followed their path does not carry. And the verse shows why. The people are not punished for the acts of their forefathers. It was their own fault and their own careless attitude that brought the disaster on them.

The covenant had sown the seed of truth in their hearts. It was not difficult for them to reach the conclusion that the stones they shaped into idols with their own hands, or the fire, or the trees, or any other created thing, could not be their creator and had no power to help them in their need.

The same point is put in another way. The awareness of a Creator and a Lord was placed in the soul of a human being so deeply that he never loses it. That awareness is the seed of the oneness of Allah. And it stays in place even when a person worships something else. An animal separated from its parents and raised in a strange place still keeps the marks of its species. And its behaviour in all its dealings comes from its instinct. Human beings hold their God-consciousness in the same way. There is one difference between an animal and a human being. Animals are not able to go against their nature and are compelled to do what their nature urges on them. A human being is free in the matter of action. The awareness is placed in his nature. And at the same time his mind and his conscience point out to him what is right and what is wrong.

Human beings therefore have the power to follow that inner voice. And the power to ignore it and do as they please. The occasions of that choice are the places where a person is on trial. And the decision about Paradise or the Fire rests on the result. A person who listens to the voice of God and does what He tells him through the silent language of nature passes the test. And the doors of Paradise are opened for him after death. A person who ignores the voice of God speaking at the level of nature is held guilty. And he is passed over by God in the measure that he passed over the voice.

That voice of the inner nature is itself evidence of the existence of God. Nobody is left with the excuse of ignorance.
