And nobody can say that he is only doing what has been done since ancient times. A person brings the awareness of God with him from his birth. And it stays with him through every change in his circumstances. Against that, the question is what excuse anyone has for following the path of misguidance.

### The way the reminder reaches a person

The reminder of the covenant reaches each person by the tongue of the one who carries the miracle. And one reading adds that the reminder serves the same purpose for every soul. Which is to bring it back to what it acknowledged within itself.

The dialogue in the verse is put in a form that shows the reasoning of the plea. So that a hearer can see how little weight it carries. The people of the plea say that the error belongs to those who came before them. And that they themselves carry no sin because they had no knowledge of what was done. The verse answers that the knowledge was given to them in their own nature. And that the pledge was taken from them in person.

### In short

- The verse closes off the plea that the people were only following their forefathers. Who had joined others with Allah before them. And that they were small and weak descendants after them.
- The people are not punished for the acts of their forefathers. And the verse lays the fault on their own carelessness. Since the covenant had already sown the seed of truth in their hearts.
- The stone shaped by a man's own hands, the fire, the trees and every other created thing could not be taken for a creator once a person gave the matter any thought.
- The awareness of a Creator is placed in the human soul so deeply that it is never lost. And the animal separated from its parents shows the same thing in the marks of its species.
- A human being differs from an animal in being free to follow that inner voice or to ignore it. And the choice is where he is tried and where the decision about Paradise or the Fire is made.
- The voice of the inner nature is itself evidence of the existence of God. So that no one is left with the excuse of ignorance or with the plea that he was only following the custom of the ancients.

174.text:
The passage closes with a statement of why the signs are set out in this way. "This is how We make our signs clear, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺"

### Phrase by phrase

**"This is how We make our signs clear"** states the way the Book works. The verses are explained in detail. And the story of the covenant is set out in full, just as the signs and the evidences were made clear for the nations that came before. Verse 174 is the closing word of the passage that began with the bringing out of the descendants of Adam.

**"so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺"** gives the purpose. The aim is that the people of Quraish should turn away from the worship of partners and come to the belief that Allah is one and to the worship of Him alone. As they once agreed before they broke their promise. The return aimed at is the return to tawhid. And to the covenant of the oneness that their own selves had acknowledged. The aim is also that people should reflect on the signs and come back from their disbelief. And that they should return to the covenant they made at the beginning.

### What the closing words ask of a hearer

The verse places the whole matter inside the reach of an ordinary person. The signs have been made clear. And the covenant has been told. And the pledges taken from earlier peoples have been recorded so that the reader can see how they were kept and how they were broken.

Anyone who applies his reason to what has been set out can find the truth and save himself from an everlasting punishment. The making clear of the signs is itself a favour to the hearer. Since it removes the ground of every excuse and leaves the way back open for whoever wants to take it.

### In short

- The verse states the way the Book works. Which is that the signs are explained in detail. And it names the purpose. Which is that people should return to the right path.
- The return aimed at is a turning from joining others with Allah to belief in Him alone. And a coming back to the covenant that was made at the beginning. As the people had once agreed before they broke their promise.
- The story of the covenant is told in full so that a reader may reflect on the signs. And a person who applies his reason to what has been set out can find the truth and save himself from an everlasting punishment.

175.text:
The verse turns to a story the hearers knew. "And relate to them ˹O Prophet˺ the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he abandoned them, so Satan took hold of him, and he became a deviant"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And relate to them ˹O Prophet˺ the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs"** is a command to the Prophet to tell the people about a man of the past. The people meant are the Jews who were with him. The story is told so that the fate of that man may serve them as a warning.

**"but he abandoned them"** describes what the man did with what he was given. The expression carries the sense of a creature coming out of its skin, the way a snake leaves its old skin behind and takes no further interest in it. The man put the knowledge and the wisdom he had been granted out of his hand and left it lying behind him.

**"so Satan took hold of him, and he became a deviant"** names the result. So long as the man held the verses of Allah, Satan could not get a hold of him. Once he had thrown that gift away, Satan overtook him and led him to the side of the perverse. He became a companion of Satan and one of those who went astray.

### The man of the story

The story is the story of Bal'am bin Ba'ura. The report of Ibn Mas'ud, carried by Abdur-Razzaq, says that the verse was revealed about him. He was, in those words, a man of the Children of Israel. The same statement came down from Mansur through Shu'bah and through several other narrators. The head of the chain in each case is Ibn Mas'ud.

The identification of the man is given in more than one form in the reports, and the scholars of the community recorded them side by side.

One chain runs from Sa'id bin Abi 'Arubah to Qatadah, and Qatadah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the man was Sayfi, the son of Ar-Rahib. Ka'b, as Qatadah reported him, gave a different name for the place. The man came from Al-Balqla, a province of Jordan. He knew the Greatest Name of Allah, and his home was Bayt Al-Maqdis, where he lived among the tyrants.

Ibn 'Abbas, in the report that came through Al-'Awfi, named him as a man of Yemen. His name was Bal'am bin Ba'ura, and Allah had given him the knowledge of His verses, and he abandoned what he had been given. The description that Malik bin Dinar gave of him is that he ranked among the scholars of the Children of Israel and that his supplication was acceptable. When a difficulty came on the people, they looked to him to lead them in supplication.

One report has him sent by Musa to the king of Madyan, with the task of calling that king to Allah. The king flattered him and settled land and gifts on him. The man then left the religion of Musa and took up the religion of the king.

'Imran bin 'Uyaynah reported from Husayn, and Husayn from 'Imran bin Al-Harith, that Ibn 'Abbas gave the name as Bal'am son of Ba'ura. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said the same. The identification of the man as one of the Children of Israel of ancient times is therefore well known. The say of the early teachers on it is recorded in full. It stands on Ibn Mas'ud, and on a number of the Salaf besides him.

The report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas places him in the city of the tyrants, meaning Jerusalem. His name was Bal'am, and the Greatest Name of Allah was known to him.

### The story as the reports tell it

The setting of the story comes out in the report that runs through Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar, from Salim, from Abu An-Nadr. When Musa entered the land of Canaan in the area of Ash-Sham, which is greater Syria, the people of Bal'am came to him. They said that this was Musa, the son of 'Imran, with the Children of Israel. That he wanted to drive them out of their land, to kill them and to put the Children of Israel in their place. They said that they were his own people and that they had no other place to live. That he was a man whose supplication was acceptable. So he should go out and call on Allah against them.

He answered them with words of warning. He said that Allah's prophet was there with the angels and the believers. He asked how he could supplicate against him when he knew from Allah what he knew. They answered that they had no other place to live, and they went on luring him and begging him until he was tempted by the trial.

He set out on his donkey towards Mount Husban, which stood behind the military camp of the Israelites. When he had gone some way up the mountain, the donkey sat down and refused to move. He got down and struck it until it stood up, and he rode on. The donkey did the same thing a second time, and he struck it again until it stood up.

He went on, and when he tried to supplicate against Musa and his people, Allah made his tongue speak evil of his own people and good of the Children of Israel. His people called out to him and asked what he was doing, since he was praying for the Israelites and against them. He answered that it was against his will, and that the matter was one Allah had decided. His tongue was then made to hang out of his mouth, and he said that he had lost this life and the world to come. The verse was revealed about the story of Bal'am son of Ba'ura.

### The story as the other report tells it

The account that the majority of the scholars trusted most came down through Ibn Marduwaih, on the authority of the companion 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas. The name of the man in that account is Bal'am bin Ba'ura. His home was in Syria, in Canaan near Jerusalem. One report makes him an Israelite by birth. Certain books revealed by Allah were known to him. It is that knowledge the phrase about the one to whom the verses were given refers to.

The event falls in the time that followed the death of Pharaoh and his people. The victory of the Israelites over Egypt had already come. After it Allah commanded the prophet Musa and his people to fight a people called the Jabbarin. The Jabbarin had seen what had happened to Pharaoh and his people. They were greatly frightened when they saw the army of Musa coming towards them.

They came to Bal'am and told him that Musa was a strong man who had come with a great army to drive them out of their land, and that he should pray to Allah to turn him back without a war. Bal'am knew the most gracious name of Allah. He called on Allah with it, and his prayers were generally granted.

Bal'am answered that Musa was the prophet of Allah, with the angels at his back. That no prayer of his could be turned against such a man. He said that he knew the rank Musa held with Allah. That by praying against him he would ruin himself in this world and in the world to come. The people insisted, and Bal'am promised that he would first seek the consent of Allah for such a prayer. That if Allah permitted it he would pray as they asked.

He performed an act to seek the consent of Allah, and in a dream he was forbidden from making that prayer. He came to the people and told them of the prohibition. The Jabbarin then presented him with a gift of considerable value, and he accepted it. After the gift their insistence increased. One report says that his wife advised him to accept the gift and to pray for them. Blinded by the love of wealth and of his wife, he began to pray against the prophet Musa and his people.

That moment was the occasion of an unusual thing. The words he wanted to utter against Musa came out against the people of the Jabbarin themselves, by the will of Allah. They cried out and told him that he was invoking against them. Bal'am said that he was unable to utter a single word against Musa, and that he had no control over what his tongue said.

The Jabbarin met the fate of disaster from the punishment of heaven. The punishment of Bal'am was that his tongue came out from under his mouth until it hung on his chest. He had ruined his life in this world and in the world to come, and he had been stripped of all the spiritual power he had.

The report goes on to the suggestion he made afterwards. He told the people of the Jabbarin that there was one way left by which they might overcome the Israelites. They should decorate their beautiful girls and send them to the Israelites, with instructions that the girls should put up no resistance to whatever the Israelites did. Being away from their homes, the Israelites would be likely to fall into adultery, which is the most detestable act before Allah. A people given to it can never overcome its enemy.

The suggestion was accepted and acted on. A prominent man of the Israelites fell into the trap. The prophet Musa made every effort to stop him, but the man went on in the wicked act. Plague then came on the people as a punishment, and the death toll in one day was seventy thousand people. The man who had committed the sin was killed along with the girl and was hung up by the Israelites in a public place. The people then turned to Allah in repentance and asked His forgiveness, and the disgraceful punishment was lifted from them.

### The man named as the other candidate

Another set of reports holds that the verse was revealed about a man of a later time. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and Zayd ibn Aslam gave another name for the man of the verse. In their report the verse came down about al-Thaqafi, whose full name was Umayyah ibn Abi as-Salt. He had studied the Scriptures, and he knew that a messenger was to be sent around that time. His hope was that he would be that messenger himself.

When Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ, the man envied him and turned against him, and he disbelieved in him. During the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ there was a man of great moral and intellectual distinction by the name of Umayyah ibn Abi as-Salt. When he learned that the holy Books of the Christians and the Jews carried predictions of the coming of a prophet, he formed the idea that he was that prophet.

Then he was told of the claim to prophethood made by the Prophet ﷺ. He heard the discourse revealed to him, found it fine, and was greatly disappointed. From that point he turned into an opponent of the Prophet. The use that should have been made of the superior qualities given to him by Allah was to recognise the Prophet of Allah and then to become his companion. Because of the blessings already given to him, he formed the idea that the blessing of prophethood should have come to him rather than to anyone else. He saw worldly benefit in rejecting the Prophet, while accepting him would have brought benefit in the world to come. Acceptance would have made the angels his fellow travellers. He chose the path of jealousy and pride instead, and on that path nobody was left to give him company except Satan.

One account of the verse names the man as Umayyah Ibn al-Salt and says that he was honoured with knowledge and with good speech. That when he did not believe, Allah took those things away from him. The same report says of the first candidate that he was Bal'am Ibn Ba'ura, who was honoured with the greatest name and then used it to pray against Moses. So that Allah took it away from him.

### The third report of the man

A third report of the man comes from Ibn 'Abbas through 'Ikrimah. In that report the verse concerns a man whose prayers were answered three times over. The man's wife was named al-Basus, and she loved him. She bore him children.

One day she said to him that he should let one of his answered prayers be used for her. He said that one was for her, and asked what she wished for. She said that he should ask Allah to make her the most beautiful woman among the Children of Israel. The prayer was granted and she became as she had asked. When she saw that no woman among the Children of Israel came near her in beauty, she shunned her husband and put her mind on something else.

The man then prayed to Allah to turn her into a barking dog, and that was the second of his prayers spent. Then her children came to him and said that they could not stand the situation, since their mother had become a barking dog and people were insulting them because of her. They asked him to pray that Allah restore her to her first state. He prayed, and she became as she had been before, and all three of the answered prayers were now spent. This is al-Basus, whose ill omen became a proverb. People say of a person that he is more ill omened than al-Basus.

### What the abandoning of the signs means

The verse describes a man who had been given a great gift and let it go. Al-Hasan Al-Basri is reported to have said that the heart of the disbeliever and of the hypocrite is weak and empty of guidance, and that it keeps faltering. The report of the second candidate draws the difference out plainly. The man had the qualities and the knowledge, and the gift itself turned into his trial. The same blessings that could have raised him became the ground on which he fell.

The story also shows how the pledge taken from the people of the Book was broken. The Israelites were waiting for a prophet, and they used to describe his attributes to others. When the Prophet ﷺ appeared, they turned away from him for worldly considerations, just as the man of the story turned away from what he had been given. The verse with which the passage opens speaks to the Children of Israel in their own history and to the Jews of the Prophet's own time at once.

The report that names al-Walibi as its narrator adds one more detail about the man of the city of al-Jabbarin, that his name was Bal'am and that he knew the greatest name of Allah. The report says that when Moses came to that city, the cousins and the people of Bal'am went to him and told him that Moses was a tough man with a huge army who would destroy them if he conquered them. They asked him to pray to Allah to drive Moses and those with him away. He told them that he would lose both this world and the next if he prayed against Moses and those with him. They went on insisting until he prayed against Moses and those with him, and Allah stripped him of what he had been given.

### In short

- The Prophet was told to tell the story of the man who was given the verses of Allah and then abandoned them. So that Satan took hold of him and he became one of the perverse. The expression used for the abandoning is that of a creature coming out of its skin, the way a snake leaves its old skin behind. It shows that the man put away the knowledge he had been given.
- Ibn Mas'ud said through the report of Abdur-Razzaq that the man was Bal'am bin Ba'ura of the Children of Israel. The identification went back to several of the Salaf. The reports also name Sayfi the son of Ar-Rahib, a man of Al-Balqla in Jordan who knew the Greatest Name and lived in Bayt Al-Maqdis with the tyrants. They tell of the man sent by Musa to the king of Madyan who was given land and gifts and turned back from the religion of Musa.
- The long account runs through Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar, from Salim, from Abu An-Nadr. It tells of the donkey that refused to move on Mount Husban, of the words that came out against his own people, and of the tongue that came out of his mouth until it hung on his chest. Many Traditions came down from the Companions and their disciples about the man. The account the majority count as most reliable is the Tradition of Ibn Marduwaih from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, which tells of the Jabbarin, of the dream that forbade him, of the gift he accepted, of the plague that carried off seventy thousand people in one day, and of the repentance that lifted the punishment.
- The passage stands in a series that recalls the covenant made with the children of Adam. The man of the story is set before the hearers as one who did not keep faith with what he had been given. Another set of reports holds that the verse was revealed about Umayyah ibn Abi as-Salt al-Thaqafi, described as a man who hoped to be the prophet himself and turned against him out of jealousy and pride when he was not.
- A report from Ibn 'Abbas through 'Ikrimah tells of a man given three answered prayers, of the wife named al-Basus who asked to be the most beautiful woman of the Children of Israel. Of the loss of all three prayers one after another.

176.text:
The verse states what the man of the story chose and gives the likeness for it. "If We had willed, We would have elevated him with Our signs, but he clung to this life—following his evil desires." The likeness follows. "His example is that of a dog: if you chase it away, it pants, and if you leave it, it ˹still˺ pants." The verse then names what is shown by the likeness and gives the closing command. "This is the example of the people who deny Our signs. So narrate ˹to them˺ stories ˹of the past˺, so perhaps they will reflect"

### Phrase by phrase

**"If We had willed, We would have elevated him with Our signs"** names what was in reach. Had Allah willed, He would have raised the man above the filth of this earthly life by means of the verses He had given him the knowledge of. He would have been raised to the ranks of the scholars by having his way to good deeds made easy.

**"but he clung to this life—following his evil desires"** states what he chose instead. The word used for his clinging carries the sense of inclining towards something and holding to it. The earth in the phrase stands for the globe and all that is on it. The furniture, the machines, the clothes and the food are all gifts of this earth. So that the whole of the worldly possessions of a man are covered by the one word. The man took an interest in the delights of this life and in its display. He went into the desires of life and its joys and was deceived by them, as life has deceived others like him who had no sound understanding and no good mind. The desires named in the verse are read as the craving for leadership. Also as the desires of the lower self by which a man goes into evil things.

**"His example is that of a dog: if you chase it away, it pants, and if you leave it, it ˹still˺ pants."** gives the likeness. The word used for panting means breathing hard with the tongue out of the mouth. The process of drawing in fresh air and letting out used air is necessary for every living being. Allah has made it automatic and easy for the creatures, with the dog as the exception. It is the dog that has to labour hard in its breathing at all times, while other animals make that effort only when they are attacked or when they undergo some strenuous task.

The likeness is read in two ways. Some scholars took it as a description of the end of the man's tongue, which came out of his mouth and flickered there. The man became like the dog whose tongue hangs out whether it is driven away or left alone. One report of the verse says that the likeness is that of Bal'am. Another says that it is the likeness of Umayyah Ibn al-Salt. Others took the likeness as a description of the man and all who are like him in their misguidance, in their persistence on the wrong path. In their inability to benefit from faith or to understand what they are called to.

Two passages of the Book are quoted for that second reading. One is the word that it is the same to the disbelievers whether you warn them or do not warn them, since they will not believe (2:6). The other is the word that it makes no difference whether forgiveness is asked for the hypocrites or not. That even if it were asked seventy times Allah would not forgive them (9:80). Al-Hasan Al-Basri narrated the same reading. The heart of the disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked man is weak, with no guidance in it to steady it, and so it keeps faltering. The likeness of the dog whose tongue is out in both conditions covers the man who has become like that.

The opening of the sentence, with its word for therefore, ties the likeness to what came before it, which is the leaning towards this world and the following of desires. The man who listens to advice and does not take it. Who is left alone and understands nothing, is despicable in both states. No other animal shares that condition with the dog.

**"This is the example of the people who deny Our signs."** widens the likeness from one man to a people. The example of the people who reject the verses of Allah is that they are equated with dogs which have no interest beyond collecting food and satisfying their lusts. Whoever steps out of the area of knowledge and guidance and seeks the satisfaction of his desires and his empty wishes is like that dog, and what an evil example it is.

The Sahih recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the evil example is not suitable for the community. That the one who takes back the gift he has given is like the dog that returns to its own vomit.

**"So narrate ˹to them˺ stories ˹of the past˺, so perhaps they will reflect"** is the closing command, and it is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. He was to tell the Children of Israel the story of a man they knew. What happened to him when Allah allowed him to go astray and expelled him from His mercy.

### What the command to narrate asks for

The stories are to be recited so that the hearers may think about them and take the lesson. The telling of the story of the man was meant for the Children of Israel above all, since they had the knowledge of the man and of what happened to him when he was given the Greatest Name, by which a request is granted when He is asked and an answer is given when He is called upon. The man used that name in disobedience to Allah and called it down on his own party of the people of faith, the followers of Musa the son of 'Imran, the one to whom Allah spoke directly.

The purpose of the account is that they should avoid the behaviour of that man. Allah had given the Jews knowledge and had made them superior to the bedouins around them. He had given them the description of Muhammad ﷺ, by which they could recognise him the way a man recognises his own children. They, among all people, had the most right to follow him, to aid him and to support him, in obedience to their own prophets who had told them of him and had commanded them to follow him.

The warning attached to the passage is that whoever among them defies the knowledge that is in their Books. Or hides it from the servants of Allah, will be given disgrace in this life and humiliation in the world to come to follow it.

### Where the words of the verse point

The words of the passage are taken to carry a general truth. The knowledge of the verses of Allah is what truly raises a man and gives him honour. For the person who turns away from that knowledge and gives preference to worldly desires and possessions, the very same knowledge becomes the ground of his disgrace.

The likeness of the dog is read in that light as well. A man who has taken his knowledge and then gone out after his desires is like an animal whose tongue hangs out in every situation, since he gets no rest from his appetite whether he is treated well or badly. The one who is far from the guidance of Allah pants under blessing and pants under hardship. He is the same man in both states.

The story also carries the truth about a man of the Prophet's own city. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said of the words about the people who denied the signs that they refer to the Israelites of Makkah, who were always longing for someone to be sent to them as a leader calling them to Allah and teaching them the ways of the right path. When the long awaited prophet came to them with signs of the truth so plain that no resistance to them was left, they too slipped away from the commands of the Torah in the way that Bal'am bin Ba'ura had done.

### In short

- Had Allah willed, the man of the story would have been raised above the filth of the earthly life by the verses given to him. But he inclined to the earth, which stands for all the possessions of this world. Followed his own desires, read as the craving for leadership and the pull of the lower self.
- His likeness is the likeness of a dog, an animal alone among living creatures in having to labour at its breathing. The likeness is read both as the tongue that hung out of the man's mouth and as the state of every man who cannot benefit from the call to faith.
- Two passages of the Book are quoted for the second reading, that warning and not warning are the same for the disbelievers (2:6). That seventy appeals for the forgiveness of the hypocrites would not be answered (9:80), since the heart of such a person is weak and empty of guidance.
- The command to narrate the stories was given so that the Children of Israel, who knew the story of the man and of the Greatest Name he was given, should avoid his behaviour, since they among all people had the most right to follow the Prophet ﷺ whom their own prophets had commanded them to follow.
- The Sahih recorded that the evil example is not suitable for the community. That the man who takes back his gift is like the dog that returns to its vomit, while the one who leaves the area of knowledge for his desires is like the animal whose tongue hangs out whether he is driven away or left alone.
- The words of the passage carry a general truth, that the knowledge of the verses of Allah is the honour of the man who holds it. That the same knowledge becomes the ground of disgrace and ruin for the man who turns away from it. The say of Ibn 'Abbas on the people of the likeness was that they are the Israelites of Makkah, who longed for a leader and then slipped away from the commands of the Torah.

177.text:
The verse states the judgement on the people of the likeness. "What an evil example of those who denied Our signs!" The second part names where the harm of their conduct fell. "They ˹only˺ wronged their own souls"

### Phrase by phrase

**"What an evil example of those who denied Our signs!"** repeats the judgement of the likeness in a sharper form. The evil is the example of the people who deny the verses of Allah, in that they are equated with dogs which have no interest beyond collecting food and satisfying their lusts.

**"They ˹only˺ wronged their own souls"** states the effect of their conduct. Allah did not wrong them. They wronged themselves by rejecting the guidance, by refusing obedience to their Lord. By being content with this life that will soon end, while they went after the fulfilment of their desires and the obedience of their lusts.

### The lessons drawn from the passage

The story of the man carries a number of points for the benefit of those who take a lesson from it. The first is that no one should be boastful of his knowledge or proud of his piety. Things change without notice, as they changed for Bal'am Ba'ura. A person should be grateful to his Lord for whatever knowledge and wisdom he has. He should keep asking Allah to make him firm in his faith.

The second is that a person should avoid the situations that threaten his faith and his knowledge. The situations to fear most are those that turn on money, wife and children. The love of these three is the strongest of all the agents of misguidance.

The third is that a person should avoid the company of people who have gone astray. Should be careful about accepting a gift or an invitation from them. Bal'am met his evil fate through accepting the gift of the Jabbarin.

The fourth is that acts of immodesty, adultery and fornication among them, bring ruin and disaster on a whole society. Those who want to be safe from distress must keep their people from such crimes, since the crimes invite the wrath of Allah and His punishment on the whole community.

The fifth is that deviation from the commands of Allah is itself a punishment. That it opens the door to the influence of Satan, which works on a person without his knowledge and leads him astray. Anyone who carries knowledge must be conscious of the treasure he holds. He must seek the help of Allah in protecting it from evil influences, and he must keep correcting himself against error. Al-Hasan Al-Basri described such a heart as too weak to hold on to guidance.

The fifth point comes out of the story itself. The man was a scholar of the Children of Israel by the testimony of the reports. His supplication was accepted before it was turned against him. The lesson drawn for the readers of the passage is that the gift is never a guarantee of safety. That the man who has been given the most is the man who has the most to guard.

### In short

- The verse names the evil of the example of the people who denied the signs of Allah, since they are equated with dogs that have no interest beyond collecting food and satisfying their lusts.
- The people did not harm Allah by their conduct. What they did was to wrong their own souls by rejecting the guidance, by refusing obedience to their Lord and by being content with a life that soon ends.
- The passage carries five lessons for those who take heed of it. A person should not boast of his knowledge or be proud of his piety, since things change without notice, and Bal'am is the proof of it.
- A person should avoid the situations that threaten his faith, especially those that involve money, wife and children, since the love of those things is the strongest agent of misguidance.
- A person should avoid the company of those who have gone astray and be careful with their gifts and invitations. He should work to keep acts of immodesty out of the society he lives in.
- Deviation from the commands of Allah is itself a punishment and it opens the door to the influence of Satan. So anyone who holds knowledge must guard it and keep correcting himself. Verse 176 carries this warning in full, and the words of the story were set down for it.

178.text:
The passage closes with the rule that governs the two ways. "Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. And whoever He leaves to stray, they are the ˹true˺ losers"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever Allah guides is truly guided."** states the first half of the rule. The person whom Allah leads aright is the guided one. Once Allah has led him aright no one can lead him into misguidance.

**"And whoever He leaves to stray, they are the ˹true˺ losers."** states the second half. The person whom Allah leaves to stray has taken on failure, loss and a sure misguidance. No one will be found to guide him.

The rule that covers both halves is that whatever Allah wills comes about. Whatever He does not will does not come about.

### The teaching on guidance and misguidance

Guidance and misguidance both come from Allah. He is the creator of good and of evil, of guidance and of misguidance. The people who are guided are the ones to whom Allah has given guidance. The losers are the ones whom He lets go astray.

The theme is set out in many places in the Book so that human beings may know that Allah created good and evil. That He gave clear instructions by which the two are told apart, together with a kind of free will by which a person chooses one of the two paths. The ones who choose the right path by their own will and do good deeds receive their reward from Allah. The ones who take the other path by their own will and do evil deeds are punished and sent to the Fire.

The wording of the verse carries a point of its own. The people of guidance are spoken of in the singular, while the people who are wrong and misguided are spoken of in the plural. The path of guidance is the one true faith. It was followed by all the prophets from Adam to the last of them ﷺ. The basic message of every prophet was the same in every age. A person of any age who believed in his prophet and followed the teaching that prophet brought is counted by Allah among the people of guidance, whoever he is and wherever he lived. The ways of misguidance, on the other hand, run into the thousands. That is why they are spoken of in the plural.

Another point in the verse is that the people who follow the path of misguidance are named together with their punishment of the Fire, while no reward is named for the people who follow the right path. Of them the verse says only that they are the guided. That is because guidance is itself the greatest of all blessings. It takes in every reward and bounty of this world and of the world to come, so no separate mention of rewards is required.

The likeness given for it is that of a great king who assures a man of his close friendship and of the certainty that he will be heard and trusted. Such a man holds the highest position among the officials. He has no need of a formal rank to go with it. In the same way, when Allah has given a person the title of the guided, that person has been given everything worth having. The say of the elders is that the remembrance of Allah and the worship of Him are themselves the reward of the worship, since the ability to do them is the great favour of Allah.

A person who is engaged in the worship of Allah is receiving the greatest of the rewards of Allah at the same time. The other blessings that wait for him in this world and in Paradise come second to it, since they are the fruit of that guidance.

The same teaching explains a verse in which the believers are promised their reward from their Lord. The reward is expressed there by two different words, one of them for a recompense and the other for a gift. The word that carries the sense of a recompense stands for what is offered in return for a service. The word for a gift stands for what is given without any service or performance at all. The two words together lead to the point that the things which people take to be the rewards of their own attainments are in fact gifts from their Lord, since the very performance that drew the reward was itself a gift from Allah, who enabled the person to do that service.

### The report attached to the rule

A hadith narrated from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud states the same rule in the words of the Prophet ﷺ. The words are the praise of Allah, whom the people praise and from whom they seek help, guidance and forgiveness. The seekers take refuge with Allah from the evils within themselves and from the burden of their evil deeds. The report adds that the one whom Allah guides will never be misled, and that the one whom He leaves to stray will never find anyone to guide him. The witness of the report is that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, without any partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger. The complete hadith was collected by Imam Ahmad and by the collectors of the Sunan and by others.

### In short

- The rule is that the person whom Allah leads aright is the guided one. That once Allah has led him aright no one can lead him into misguidance.
- The person whom Allah leaves to stray has taken on failure and loss. No one will be found to guide him, since whatever Allah wills comes about and whatever He does not will does not come about.
- The wording of the verse speaks of the people of guidance in the singular and of the misguided in the plural, since the path of guidance is the one faith followed by every prophet from Adam to the last of them, while the ways of misguidance run into the thousands.
- The guided are named without a separate reward, because guidance is itself the greatest blessing and takes in every bounty of this world and the next, in the way a man given the friendship of a great king has no need of a formal rank beside it.
- The hadith narrated from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud states the same rule, that the one whom Allah guides will never be misled and the one whom He leaves to stray will never find a guide. The complete report was collected by Imam Ahmad and by the collectors of the Sunan.
- The two words used for the reward of the believers, one for a recompense and one for a gift, show that what people take to be the fruit of their own attainments is a gift from their Lord, since the performance itself was given to them. Verse 178 closes the passage with that rule of guidance.

179.text:
The verse names the people who never use what they were given. "Indeed, We have destined many jinn and humans for Hell. They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with. They are like cattle. In fact, they are even less guided! Such ˹people˺ are ˹entirely˺ heedless"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We have destined many jinn and humans for Hell."** gives the measure of the loss before the verse sets out its cause. The words mean that Allah made a share in the Fire for a great number of the jinn and of humankind. The reports read it in this way. They were set out for the Fire by the sort of deeds that its people do. The work of the creation was known to Allah before any of it existed. A lot of the jinn and of humankind have been made for Hell, since the means of guidance were given to them in full and they did not use them to seek it.

**"They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with."** states where the refusal led. The senses were made for them as a means of gaining guidance, and no benefit was taken from them.

Other passages of the Book speak of other groups in the same way. Of a former people it is said that hearing, sight and hearts were assigned to them, and that none of it availed them, since they used to deny the signs of Allah (46:26). Of the hypocrites it is said that they are deaf, dumb and blind, and so they do not return to the right path (2:18). Of the disbelievers it is said that they are deaf, dumb and blind, and so they do not understand (2:171).

The reports are careful with words of that kind. Such people are not deaf, dumb or blind in their bodies. The loss falls on them in relation to the guidance, and in that respect alone. One passage states that if Allah had known of any good in them, He would have made them listen, and that even then they would have turned away in aversion (8:23). Another states that it is not the eyes which grow blind, but the hearts which are in the breasts (22:46). Another states that when a person turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious, a devil is appointed as his intimate companion. Such a companion holds him back from the path while he thinks that he is guided aright (43:36-37).

**"They are like cattle."** gives the likeness for a people with three losses. They do not take the truth in with their hearing, they do not grasp it with their understanding, and they do not find the guidance with their sight. Grazing cattle take no benefit from their senses beyond what sustains their life in this world, and the people described here stand in the same place.

One passage sets out the likeness as a picture. The example of those who disbelieve is that of a man who shouts at animals that hear nothing but a call and a cry (2:171). When such people are called to the faith, they are like cattle that hear the voice of their shepherd and cannot make out what he is saying.

**"In fact, they are even less guided!"** takes the likeness a step further. Cattle still answer the call of their shepherd, though they do not understand his words, and the people described here do not answer at all. Cattle also fulfil the purpose and the service for which they were made. The disbeliever was made to worship Allah alone, in tawhid, and he disbelieved in Allah and joined others with Him in worship. On that measure, the people who obey Allah are more honourable than some of the angels, while cattle are better than the people who disbelieve in Him.

**"Such ˹people˺ are ˹entirely˺ heedless"** names their condition. They are neglectful of the matter of the world to come and they deny it. They are oblivious to faith in Allah and to the Last Day.

### The decree that stands behind the words

The words about Hell raise the matter of the decree, and the reports answer it in plain terms. Allah knew the work of every creature before the creature existed. He set that work down in writing and kept the record with Him, and the record was made fifty thousand years before the heavens and the earth were created.

Muslim recorded that 'Abdullah bin 'Amr narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a word on the same subject. The Messenger ﷺ spoke of the destination and the due measurement of the creation. Both were decided fifty thousand years before the heavens and the earth were created, and the throne of Allah was over the water at that time. Many hadiths speak on this subject, and the matter of Al-Qadar is of the highest importance. The verse is not the place to set out the whole of it, and the account leaves the question there.

### The question the words raise, and the answer

The words of the verse deny that such people have hearing, sight and understanding, and a question follows from that. In daily life the same people are not blind, deaf or insane. They see, hear and understand the things around them like anyone else. How is the denial to be squared with the plain fact?

The answer turns on the way the creation is arranged. Everything created carries an amount of sensibility that matches the need of its purpose. Nothing that is called inanimate is wholly without life. The stones and the earth were given so little of it that it can hardly be detected, since no duty of growth or movement was laid on them. Human reason itself asks for some kind of perception in the things called inanimate, since there must be a way of communication between the Creator and what He created. A lord who cannot communicate with his creatures for want of sensibility in them would not be their Lord at all. Allah does communicate with all that He created, the living and the lifeless, and that shows a kind of sensibility in the lifeless as well.

The plant kingdom comes next in the order. Its purpose needs growth and nourishment, and its share of perception is greater in degree and matches that need. The animal kingdom follows, and its form of life is more elaborate and more complex. Animals grow and are nourished, and beyond that they move about the earth, seek their food, guard themselves from danger and bring forth their young. The life given to them is greater and more visible than what came before. Their powers are still measured to their task, and they have as much as helps them feed themselves and defend against their enemies.

The human being comes last in the order, and his case is the most serious. To the functions already named he adds the duty of recognising his Creator and the Lord of the universe, of seeking His pleasure by following His commands, and of keeping away from what He dislikes. He is required to contemplate the creation, to use his reason to tell right from wrong, to turn from evil and to do good for the sake of his Lord. He has also been given wide scope to make his life more purposeful and his rank more elevated, and when he advances on that road he can rise above the ranks of the angels. He is answerable for his acts. Eternal peace is promised to him for good, and punishment and distress for evil. He has been trusted with the highest and most perfect degree of life, and the point of it is that he should be busied with what his life was made for. His powers of understanding, hearing and seeing are not meant to be spent on material things alone, the way the animals do.

On that footing the human faculties of understanding, hearing and seeing should work differently from the faculties of the animals. If a man makes no special use of them, he belongs among those who have eyes but do not see, ears but do not listen, a heart but no understanding. The special use of them is telling right from wrong, doing good and keeping away from evil. That is why the Book calls such people deaf, dumb and blind. Their physical ability was never in question. The Book itself affirms that they have knowledge of worldly things, in the verse which says that they know the outward side of this life while they are heedless of the world to come (30:7).

Another passage speaks of the destruction that came on the people of 'Ad and of Thamud, and says of them that they could see clearly (29:38). Those peoples were drawn in by the influences of Satan and went into the evil deeds that brought them to their ruin. They kept the use of their powers within the narrow range of worldly gain, serving the needs of the body, and they stayed heedless of what the spirit demands. A people may make great advances in science and technology. They may conquer space and explore the moon and the other planets, fill the sky with their satellites and tame the forces of nature for their many needs. All of it serves the physical and material life and goes no further to the peace of the spirit. The Book calls such people deaf, dumb and blind because what they heard, saw and understood belonged to this world alone.

The verse closes its picture with the cattle, who put all their effort into the service of their bodily desires, and then adds that such people are much more misled. They are far more unwise than the cattle. An animal is not bound by the laws of the Shari'ah, carries no reward and no punishment for its acts, and is required only to serve the needs of the body, which it does well. A human being is answerable for everything he does, and he will be rewarded or punished according to what he has done. If a man keeps his effort to the material gains of this world and makes no proper use of his faculties, he is less prudent and less wise than the animals.

### The reports on the heart, the eye and the ear

The reports attach one word to each faculty in the verse. The hearts do not understand the truth, the eyes do not see the truth, and the ears do not hear the truth. The eyes do not perceive the proofs of the power of Allah with a perception that carries reflection with it. The ears do not hear the signs or the admonitions in a way that leads to thought and to heed.

The people described are like cattle in their failure to understand, to perceive and to listen, and they are further astray than cattle. Cattle seek what benefits them and keep away from what harms them. Those who are described here walk towards the Fire out of nothing but obstinacy. They are the heedless, the ones who are oblivious to the matter of the Hereafter and who deny it.

One account puts the matter of the making first. A great number of people from humankind and from the jinn were made for the Hellfire, because of the knowledge that they would do the deeds of the people of Hell. Their hearts fail them on the question of benefit and harm, and they cannot tell which of the two lies in a thing. Their eyes are turned away from the signs of Allah, both in their own selves and upon the horizons, and no lesson is taken from what is seen. Their ears are closed to the verses of Allah, and no reflection follows what is heard. Such people are like cattle in the smallness of their sense. The verse puts them further off the mark than the beasts are. Faith in Allah and in the Last Day never enters their mind.

### The truth each person must find

The truth is a thing a man has to discover for himself. Allah has given every person a heart, eyes and ears, and a man arrives at the truth by using them. The one who does not use them will be unable to find the truth, however near it stands. The discovery is the conscious and deliberate act of the man himself. Only the one who has kept the doors of his heart open for it will understand the truth. Only the one whose eyes are not covered with veils of his own making will see it. Only the one who has not blocked his ears will hear its voice. People of that kind recognise the voice of the truth and give themselves up to it.

A man in the opposite case stays without sense, like the animals. The weightiest arguments cannot move him. A flash of the light of Allah appears before him and he cannot see it. A melody of the divine song reaches his ears and he is held back from hearing it. The truth is there for those who are awake. For a heedless man, no truth is truth.

### In short

- The words mean that Allah made a share in the Fire for a great number of the jinn and of humankind. Such people were set out for it by the sort of deeds its people do. The work of the creation was known to Allah before any of it existed, and He set it down in writing in a record kept with Him. That record was made fifty thousand years before the heavens and the earth were created. Muslim recorded from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke of the destination and the due measurement of the creation. Both were decided at that time, with the throne of Allah over the water.
- The hearts, eyes and ears of such people take no benefit from the guidance they were made for. The Book describes them as deaf, dumb and blind in relation to that guidance alone, as it does of the former people who denied the signs (46:26), the hypocrites (2:18) and the disbelievers who do not understand (2:171). The likeness of the cattle is then given for a people who do not take the truth in, do not grasp it and do not see the guidance. It is enough to say that the verse puts them further off than the cattle are, since cattle answer their shepherd and fulfil the purpose for which they were made. The disbeliever was made for tawhid and turned away from it.
- Everything created has been given an amount of sensibility that matches the need of its purpose. That share runs from the stones and the earth, whose sensibility can hardly be detected, through the plants and the animals, to the human being, who carries the duty of recognising his Creator and is answerable for his acts.
- If a man makes no special use of his understanding, hearing and seeing for telling right from wrong, he belongs among those who have eyes but do not see and ears but do not listen. The Book affirms that such people know the outward side of this life while they are heedless of the world to come (30:7). It also told of the people of 'Ad and of Thamud, who could see clearly and yet were destroyed (29:38). The cattle put all their effort into the service of their bodily desires, and the men described here are more misled than they are. An animal is not bound by the laws of the Shari'ah and carries no reward or punishment for its acts. A human being is answerable for everything he does.
- The truth is a discovery each man must make for himself with the heart, eyes and ears he has been given, and for a man who has gone heedless, no truth is truth.

180.text:
The verse turns from the heedless to the remedy. "Allah has the Most Beautiful Names. So call upon Him by them, and keep away from those who abuse His Names. They will be punished for what they used to do"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah has the Most Beautiful Names."** states what belongs to Him alone. The names are the ones that carry the attributes of the highest degree of perfection. Perfection of that kind is not held by anyone besides Allah. A perfect man may always have someone above him in one quality or another, and the Book says that above every man of knowledge there is one more knowing (12:76). The names are His in a way that belongs to no other.

**"So call upon Him by them."** gives the command that follows. The call has two sides. It is praise and remembrance of Allah, and it is a request for help in a time of need. He alone is worthy of the praise and He alone is to be called for relief, so the verse names the one to be called and the words to be used for calling Him. We are not able to choose fitting words for His being, and He has given us the words that suit His glory. The best way to call Him is to call on Him by His beautiful names.

**"and keep away from those who abuse His Names."** orders the Prophet ﷺ to leave the company of the people who turn the names aside. The word used here for that turning aside means to decline from the centre. In the language of the Book it covers any deviation from the correct reading of the words, and any distortion of the message they carry.

The abuse took shape among the idolaters in the names they gave their gods. Al-Lat came from the name of Allah, and al-'Uzza came from al-Aziz, the All Mighty, and Manat came from al-Mannan, the Lord of favours. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid that the people took the name of the first idol from Allah, and the name of the second from the All Mighty. Al-'Awfi reported that Ibn 'Abbas said that to abuse the names includes saying that Al-Lat was derived from the name of Allah. Qatadah said that the abuse lies in joining others with Allah in His names, as when an idol is called al-'Uzza. The word also carries the sense of deviation, wickedness, injustice and going astray. The hollow dug in the side of a grave is called a lahd, because it is a hollow within a hollow, and it is turned towards the Qiblah, the direction of the prayer.

**"They will be punished for what they used to do."** closes the verse. Those who turn the names aside will be given their requital in the world to come for what they did and for what they said in this life. The warning was sent down before the command to fight them.

### The ninety-nine names

The reports on the number of the names are well known. Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah has ninety-nine names, a hundred less one. Whoever counts them and keeps them will enter Paradise. Allah is Witr, the One, and He loves what is odd, the witr. The Two Sahihs collected that hadith.

In the wording that comes through Abu Hurairah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that there are ninety-nine names of Allah, and that whoever learns them by heart shall enter Paradise. Al-Bukhari and Muslim reported it. The teachers then added that the names of Allah are not limited to ninety-nine. They gave the supplication recorded by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad among the proofs. 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught a supplication for the man overcome by sadness or grief. The man says, O Allah, I am Your servant, the son of Your male servant and of Your female servant. My forelock is in Your hand. Your decision about me will certainly come to pass, and Your judgement of me is just. I call on You by every name that You have, the name You called Yourself by, the name sent down in Your Book, the name taught to any of Your creatures, and the name kept with You in the knowledge of the unseen. Then he asks that the Glorious Qur'an be made the spring of his heart, the light of his chest, the remover of his grief and the dispeller of his concern. Allah will take away his grief and his sadness and give him delight in their place.

The Prophet ﷺ was asked whether the people should learn those words. He said that they should and that it is an obligation on all who hear the supplication to learn it. Tirmidhi and Hakim set out the names in detail, one by one.

### The two instructions of the verse

The verse carries two valuable pieces of information. The first is that there is none besides Allah who is worthy of praise and worthy of being called for help. The second is that Allah has given us the words with which to call on Him, since we cannot choose words proper to His being, and we are required to call on Him by the attributes of perfection.

The reports attach a promise to those words. Invocations made with the names are generally granted, and the Book has said, Call on Me and I will answer you (40:60). The most certain way to seek help in a need and relief from distress is to call on Allah and ask Him, and that way does not fail.

The immediate benefit of the prayer is that it is itself a worship, and the reward of that worship is written on the sheet of a person's deeds. The Prophet ﷺ said in a Tradition that invoking Allah is the quintessence of worship. The answer comes in more than one way. Sometimes the very thing asked for is granted. At other times, when a person asks for what is untimely, or for what is not good for him in the knowledge of Allah, he is given something more fitting and more beneficial in its place.

Remembering Allah by glorifying and praising Him is food for a person's iman, the faith in Allah. It magnifies the love of Allah, the respect for Him and the awareness of Him, and it makes the hardship of this world look worthless in a man's eyes.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi and Nasa'i reported through sound chains that the Prophet ﷺ gave words for the man who falls into difficulty or is weighed down by grief. The man says that there is no god but Allah, the Greatest, the Most Forbearing. He says the word again with the great throne named. He says it a third time with the heavens, the earth and the glorious throne.

Hakim reported in his Mustadrak on the authority of the companion Anas that the Prophet ﷺ spoke to his daughter Fatimah al-Zahra. He asked what prevented her from hearing his advice and saying, morning and evening every day, the words that call on the Living, the All Sustaining, by His mercy, and ask Him to set right every situation and not to leave the speaker to his own self even for the wink of an eye. That invocation is an effective remedy for hardship and distress as well.

### The ways the names are turned aside

The deviation from the names of Allah takes more than one form. The first is to call on Allah by names that are not given in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah. The scholars of the ummah agree that it is not permitted to call on Allah by names or attributes of one's own choosing, or to praise Him by names that the Qur'an and the Sunnah have not given. A person may give Him the name Nur, which means light, but he may not use the word white for Him. He may be called al-Karim, the generous, but not by another word of the same meaning that the revelation did not use. He may be called al-Shafi, the one who grants cure, but not by the word for a doctor, even though the two words carry the same sense. The words are refused simply because the Qur'an and the Sunnah have not reported them.

The second form is to abandon one of the names because a person judges it unfit for some situation. That is a failure of respect towards the glorious names.

The third form is to give the names of Allah to people. Some of the names in the list have been used in the Qur'an and the Sunnah for human beings, and those may be used for others. Rahim, Rashid, 'Ali, Karim and 'Aziz are of that kind. Other names stand for what belongs to Allah alone, and their use for anyone else is a deviation. Rahman, Razzaq, Subhan, Khaliq, Quddus and Ghaffar are of that kind, and giving them to another is forbidden in the Shari'ah.

If a person calls another by those names out of a false belief that the other holds the attributes the names carry, the act is unbelief. If he uses them heedlessly, out of ignorance, it is not unbelief, though it comes close to it, and it is counted a major sin.

The naming of children among the Muslims has suffered in this matter. Some have left the practice of giving their children Islamic names, and the modern names they choose carry no Islamic mark, so that a person is not known as a Muslim by his name, all the more when his appearance and his manners carry no such mark either. The names of the early women, Khadijah, 'A'ishah and Fatimah, have been exchanged for other names with no such history. Worse still, the practice has grown of cutting short the names that begin with the word servant of. 'Abd al-Khaliq, 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd al-Quddus are shortened to Khaliq, Rahman, Razzaq and Quddus when the person is called. The attributes of the Creator, the Merciful, the Sustainer and the Pure belong to Allah alone, and using them for another is a major sin. Every time a person calls someone by those names he commits the sin again and makes himself liable to a heavy punishment.

The practice has spread among Muslims with nothing gained by it in this world. It is done out of thoughtlessness about the weight of the error. The verse has warned against it in the words that those people will soon be given their requital for what they have been doing. Many evil deeds are done for some worldly gain, and the man who does them can claim that necessity pressed him. A great number of evil deeds bring no worldly benefit at all, and people fall into them out of carelessness about the commands of Allah and indifference to what He has permitted and what He has forbidden.

### What the names are

The names of Allah are His attributes. By those names He is renowned, praised and recognised. They are names full of blessing and sweet to the hearts. Pure words they are, and they come from a pure Lord. They come from the one Lord in a worthy arrangement. They are the ornament of the tongue and the lamp of the spirit, and the praise of them lasts.

One report carries the words spoken in the first person. He Himself says that His light is His guidance, that the word of His oneness is His word, and that He is He. The servant who gains access gains it with His light, and when he finds the way he finds it with the lamp. The lamp of the Sunnah is lit in the hearts, the lamp of recognition in the secret cores, and the lamp of love in the spirits. Happy is the servant who walks among these three lamps. There is no one more exalted than the man whose heart holds the greatest light and who sees the Friend face to face within it. He also says that the word of oneness is His word and His attribute, and that the name Allah is His name.

The teacher of the Tariqah has words that fit the place. He calls on the One worthy of His own praise, the One grateful for His own giving, the One who shows His own trial as sweet. He confesses that in himself he is incapable of praising Him, that in his intellect he is incapable of recognising His favour, and that in his ability he is incapable of what is worthy of Him. He is a captive to the pain for which Allah is the remedy and a slave of the praise of which Allah is worthy. He does not know what to say of Him. Allah knows. Allah is what He has said of Himself, and what He has said, He is.

The word of the chosen one, MuṣṬafā, agrees with that. He said that he does not count the praises of Allah, and that Allah is as He has praised Himself.

### Why the wrong picture forms

The wrong image of God in a man's mind is the reason he goes astray about Him. A man may accept that Allah exists and still frame an image that does not fit His glory. He imagines close ones of God after the pattern of human beings. He looks at kings and assumes that Allah has deputies and assistants, the way kings have regents and advisers. He takes the decisions of God to be the ones that suit his own desires, whether or not they accord with the justice of Allah. To attribute to Allah what does not fit His majesty and His glory is itself a distortion of His names.

Allah does not seize a man at once for his wrongdoing. He gives him room to take a lesson from the warnings and mend himself, or to grow more fearless until his guilt is well established. The verses that follow take up that delay.

### In short

- The beautiful names of Allah are the ones that carry the attributes of the highest perfection, and no one holds them but He, since even the most perfect man may have one above him (12:76).
- Calling on Allah has two sides, praise and remembrance on one hand and the request for help on the other, and the verse teaches that He alone is to be called and that He has given us the words, since the best way to ask Him is by His beautiful names, with the promise that He answers (40:60).
- Abu Hurayrah reported that Allah has ninety-nine names, a hundred less one, and that whoever counts them and keeps them will enter Paradise, in the hadith collected by the Two Sahihs, while the reports through Abu Hurairah add that whoever learns them by heart shall enter Paradise. The names are not limited to that number, since Imam Ahmad recorded from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud the supplication of the man overcome by grief, which calls on Allah by every name He has, including the name kept with Him in the knowledge of the unseen.
- The abuse of the names began with the idolaters, who took Al-Lat from Allah, al-'Uzza from al-Aziz and Manat from al-Mannan, as Ibn Jurayj reported from Mujahid and as Ibn 'Abbas explained through al-'Awfi, and the word also covers deviation from the centre, the way the lahd is a hollow within a hollow turned towards the Qiblah.
- Deviation from the names has three forms. A person may call on Allah by names of his own choosing, which the scholars of the ummah forbid, since the Qur'an and the Sunnah have given the words. He may abandon a name because he judges it unfit. Or he may give to people the names that belong to Allah alone, such as Rahman, Razzaq, Khaliq, Quddus and Ghaffar, a major sin each time, while 'Abd al-Khaliq, 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd al-Quddus are cut short among the Muslims and the exclusive attributes used for men.
- The names are the attributes by which Allah is renowned and recognised, sweet to the hearts and a lamp for the spirit. One report of them gives the words of the first person, that His light is His guidance and that the lamps of the Sunnah, of recognition and of love are lit in the hearts, the secret cores and the spirits, and the teacher of the Tariqah adds that he cannot praise Allah as He deserves. The chosen one, MuṣṬafā, said the same. The wrong picture a man frames of God, with close ones and deputies after the pattern of kings, is a distortion of the names, and Allah does not seize him at once, but gives him room to mend or to grow more fearless.

181.text:
The verse names the group that answers the truth when it is put before them. "And among those We created is a group that guides with the truth and establishes justice accordingly"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And among those We created is a group"** speaks of some nations among the creations, and the group named is the one that stands on the truth in its words and in its deeds.

**"that guides with the truth"** names their first work. They proclaim the truth and they call others to it.

**"and establishes justice accordingly"** names the second. They hold to the truth themselves and they judge by it.

The verses before this one gave a remedy to the people who made no proper use of their faculties. The remedy was to call on Allah by His beautiful names and to remember Him often by them. The present verse speaks of the people who took the right path and became guides for others. The group is a people who guide others to the straight path and decide their matters according to the truth, which is the divine law.

### The group named in the reports

A number of reports hold that the group named here is the ummah of Muhammad ﷺ. The Two Sahihs record the word of Mu'awiyah bin Abi Sufyan, who said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave the promise that there will always be a group of his ummah who are apparent on the truth. Such a group will not be harmed by those who fail them or oppose them, and matters will go on so until the Hour begins. In another narration the words are that this will hold until the command of Allah comes while they are still in that state. In a third narration the report adds that they will dwell in Ash-Sham, which is greater Syria.

Ibn Jarir reported from his own sources that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse. He then said that the people named in it are his people. They will decide their disputes according to justice and truth, and they will observe justice in all their dealings.

'Abd ibn Humaid reported that the Prophet ﷺ addressed his companions. He said that this verse had been revealed in their favour, and that before them there had been a group of people bearing the same attributes. He then recited the verse about the community of Musa, that among the community of Musa there is a group who guide by the truth and act justly by it (7:159). A group among the Israelites carried the attributes named in this verse, guiding others to the truth and deciding their matters by the law of the Torah. The Muslim ummah carries them as its own mark.

### The way of the verse

The message of the passage has two parts. The first is to guide people to the right path in accordance with the demands of the Shari'ah. The second is to decide all disputes according to the law of Islam.

Those two features are the guaranteed way of success in this world and in the world to come. Any group or individual who follows the truth and does justice in every part of life belongs to the people of truth named in the verse. Such a person does not let personal prejudice in when he judges between people, even for enemies. That was the standing mark of the Muslim ummah in the time when its people held strictly to the demands of truth and justice. They put their own priorities aside when they judged between others. History has recorded unique examples of that practice in the lives of the Companions and of their disciples.

The decline set in from the day the Muslims began to show disregard for those two marks, and it showed itself in every part of their life. A large part of the ummah has fallen prey to personal desires, and its activities, in politics, in society and in education, are driven by worldly gain. Its guiding of others is aimed at some benefit in this world. Many of its family ceremonies carry no Islamic character and show behaviour opposed to the Shari'ah. Some family traditions have been set up in the name of religion, and a person who goes against them or shows dislike for them faces active opposition. People no longer organise themselves purely for the spread of truth and justice.

There is no one to make them see that this course will bring disaster on the Muslims at large. The dignity of the ummah can be restored, and the path of progress found again, only by the way of truth and justice set out in this verse. Effort has to be made to keep those values alive among the Muslims.

### In short

- Verse 181 names a group among the creations of Allah who stand on the truth in their words and their deeds. They proclaim it, call others to it, hold to it themselves and judge by it.
- The group is reported to be the ummah of Muhammad ﷺ. The Two Sahihs record from Mu'awiyah bin Abi Sufyan the promise that a group of the ummah will remain apparent on the truth until the Hour begins. One narration adds that they will dwell in Ash-Sham, which is greater Syria.
- Ibn Jarir reported that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said that the people named in it are his people, who decide their disputes by justice and truth. 'Abd ibn Humaid reported that he told his companions the verse had been revealed in their favour, and that a group before them had carried the same marks, which he joined to the word about the community of Musa (7:159).
- The message has two parts, to guide people to the right path as the Shari'ah demands and to decide disputes by the law of Islam. Those two features are the way of success in this world and the next, and the Companions and their disciples gave the recorded examples of them.
- Disregard for the two marks brought the later decline, with worldly gain driving the affairs of a large part of the ummah and family ceremonies opposed to the Shari'ah. The way back is the truth and the justice of this verse. It is enough to say that the group is named in verse 181 as the answer to the heedless.

182.text:
The verse tells how the delay works on those who reject. "As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend"

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who deny Our signs"** names the people meant. The signs are the revelation given to Muhammad ﷺ and the Book itself. The words came down among the people of Makkah first of all, and the denier named in the reports is Abu Jahl, with his followers after him, and every person who makes a mockery of any punishment sent on them.

**"We will gradually draw them to destruction"** states what the delay brings. The doors of provision are opened for them, and the means of livelihood are spread out, until they are deceived by it all and come to think that they are on the correct path. A passage of the Book gives the same picture. When a people forgot what they had been reminded of, the gates of every pleasant thing were opened for them, and in the middle of their enjoyment of what they had been given they were taken suddenly, and they were plunged into destruction with deep regrets and sorrow. The wrongdoers were cut off at the root, and praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of all that exists (6:44-45).

**"in ways they cannot comprehend"** states that the punishment comes to them without their knowledge of what is being done. One report adds that the punishment came on them in a single day, each of them destroyed in a different way.

### The question the verse answers

A question troubles many minds, and the verse answers it. If prosperity and progress come only by following the way of truth and justice, why are the nations that stand far from the truth seen to be more prosperous, more advanced and more powerful than others?

The answer is that Allah does not punish those who reject His verses at once for their sins. Out of His wisdom and His mercy, He lets them enjoy their worldly life for a while, and then He draws them to their shameful end so gradually that they do not know that they are being led to it. The present prosperity of such nations should not deceive anyone. Their prosperity is not a good sign for them. It is a respite, a period of relief before the punishment is carried out, and the Book has a name for it, istidraj, the drawing on by degrees.

Istidraj is a heavier punishment in disguise. Its most essential element is that a person is not punished for his evil deeds at once. The more he adds to his evil deeds, the more he is increased in prosperity and in worldly possessions, and the increase keeps him from any sense of guilt and from taking warning against his crimes. In the end he is kept from turning to Allah in repentance and from saving himself from the lasting punishment. The state of mind turns a man around, so that he takes illness for health and poison for a remedy. He is left to go on in that perverted life until death overtakes him and draws him to the lasting punishment.

The Book mentions istidraj in many places, and one of them is the passage already quoted about the gates of every pleasant thing (6:44).

The dealing is not limited to the disbelievers. The iniquitous among the Muslims are treated in the same way. It was for that reason that the elders used to fear Allah when they were favoured with prosperity and comfort. They feared that their prosperity might be a sign of istidraj.

### What the delay is for

God does not seize a person at once for his wrongdoing. In the delay a man is given the opportunity either to take a lesson from the warnings of God and reform himself, or to grow still more fearless, so that his guilt becomes well established. The next verse states the length of the rope that is given.

### In short

- The verse names the people who deny the signs of Allah, the revelation and the Book, among them Abu Jahl and his followers, and everyone who makes light of any punishment sent on them.
- Such people are not punished at once.
